text: Welcome to the atlas. The thesis asks one practical question: how can LTX-2.3, a model that turns a text prompt into a video with sound, be made smaller and faster on an Intel CPU and an Intel Arc GPU without spoiling its output? The answer will come from sixteen papers, and this first tab gives the vocabulary they all assume. It moves in order from the pipeline, to diffusion, to transformers, to number formats and quantization, to hardware, to the OpenVINO software stack, to quality metrics and other speed-ups, and ends with a map of all sixteen papers and a glossary. Every paper tab after this one follows the same pattern: a header, a short Before reading section, the big picture, the problem, the method, every equation and figure, the results, and a closing box on what it means for the thesis.

label: Primer
text: The whole thesis fits in this diagram. A prompt goes through the Gemma-3 text encoder once, then the dual-stream diffusion transformer, with a 14 billion parameter video stream and a 5 billion parameter audio stream, refines noise for many steps, sometimes three calls per step. The decoders run once at the end. Read the cost strip at the bottom: the indigo box is both the largest and the most repeated part, so that is what gets compressed first.

label: Primer
text: Memory is simply parameters times bytes per parameter. The teal bars are 16-bit weights, the pale rust bars 8-bit, the solid rust bars 4-bit. The transformer drops from 38 gigabytes to about 10, and Gemma from 24 to about 6. Smaller weights also mean fewer bytes to move at every step, which is where the speed comes from on memory-limited hardware. The thesis results table will pair each of these settings with latency and quality.

label: Primer
text: Diffusion builds a video by removing noise a little at a time. Read left to right: pure noise at timestep one, a clean latent at timestep zero, and every indigo arrow is one full call of the transformer. The gold axis is the timestep, the noise level. Because the same network sees very noisy inputs early and nearly clean ones late, its activations change over time, which is why the diffusion quantization papers keep talking about timesteps.

label: Primer
text: The transformer never touches pixels. A variational autoencoder, or VAE, compresses video into a small latent, and diffusion runs only there. In LTX-Video, one latent token of 128 numbers stands for a block of 32 by 32 pixels over 8 frames, about 192 times fewer values. The dashed encoder is only needed for training or image input; for text to video only the decoder runs at the end.

label: Primer
text: Classifier-free guidance, or CFG, is why one step can cost several transformer calls. The model runs once with the prompt and once with an empty prompt, and the mix pushes the result away from the prompt-free answer so the video follows the text. LTX-2 adds a third, dashed pass for guidance between audio and video. When measuring time per step, count how many passes the pipeline settings actually run.

This is the guidance rule in one line. v hat is the final prediction used for the step. v theta of x t and empty is the model's answer without the prompt, v theta of x t and c is the answer with the prompt c, and s is the guidance scale. The bracket is the difference the prompt makes, stretched by s. Both terms need their own transformer call, which is the cost shown in the figure above.

label: Primer
text: Almost every weight in LTX-2.3 lives in a linear layer, and a linear layer is one matrix multiply, called a GEMM. X holds the activations, one row per token; W holds the weights; Y is the output. The teal W is fixed and stored on disk, while X changes with every prompt and step. Weight-only compression, which NNCF does, shrinks W and leaves X in 16-bit.

label: Primer
text: Attention compares every token with every other token. Queries times transposed keys give an N by N score table, which is then turned into weights with a softmax and applied to the values. The side notes make the point: one thousand tokens give one million scores, six thousand give thirty-six million, per head and per layer. Attention has no weights, so weight quantization does not make it cheaper.

Two rough cost formulas, per layer. Attention needs about four times N squared times d operations, where N is the number of tokens and d the model width. A linear layer needs about two times N times d in times d out. The key difference is N squared versus N: longer or higher-resolution videos make attention grow much faster than the linear layers, which is where FlashAttention-style kernels matter.

label: Primer
text: This is one block of a diffusion transformer, and the model stacks many of them. Tokens pass self-attention, cross-attention to the text, and a feed-forward network, each with a residual shortcut. The gold path shows AdaLN: a small network turns the timestep into scale, shift and gate values that modulate each block. In LTX-2 the dashed input adds cross-attention between the audio and video streams. Nearly every box is made of linear layers.

label: Primer
text: Each row is one number format, drawn to scale, one cell per bit. Floating-point formats split bits into sign, exponent for range, and mantissa for detail; BF16 keeps FP32's range with less detail, FP16 the reverse. INT8 and INT4, in rust, are plain evenly spaced levels, 256 or 16 of them, so they need a separate scale to mean a real value. Bytes per parameter on the right drive the memory table below.

This table turns bit-widths into gigabytes for the two big components of LTX-2.3. Read across a row: bits, bytes per parameter, then memory for the 19 billion parameter transformer and the 12 billion parameter Gemma encoder. The highlighted INT4 row includes a small overhead for one 16-bit scale per group of 128 weights, giving about 9.8 gigabytes for the transformer. These are weight sizes only; activations and runtime buffers come on top.

The first estimate to always make. Memory is about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter. For the transformer at 4 bits, 19 billion times half a byte gives about 9.5 gigabytes. Scales, activations and buffers add to this, so use it as a lower bound and compare it with the IR size on disk and the measured peak memory.

How the grid is chosen. The scale s is the real-valued size of one integer step: the range of the data, x max minus x min, divided by the number of steps, q max minus q min. The zero-point z is the integer that stands for real zero. For asymmetric INT4, q runs from 0 to 15. Symmetric schemes fix z at zero, which is simpler but wastes levels when the data is lopsided.

Quantizing one number. Divide x by the scale s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero-point z, and clamp the result between q min and q max. Rounding causes the small, everyday error; clamping causes the large error for values outside the chosen range. Every quantization method in the atlas is, in some way, a smarter choice of s, z or the rounding.

Dequantizing, which gives the value the model actually computes with. x hat equals s times q minus z. Inside the range, the error between x and x hat is at most half a step. Outside the range, clipping can make it much larger. This trade-off between step size and clipping is exactly what the worked example below shows with real numbers.

label: Primer
text: A worked example of equations four to six. The top line is real values, the rust ticks below are the sixteen INT4 levels. With a range from minus 0.6 to 0.9, the step is 0.1 and zero sits at level 6. The value 0.23 lands on level 8 and comes back as 0.2, an error of 0.03. The magenta 1.3 lies outside the range, is clipped to level 15, and returns as 0.9, an error of 0.4.

label: Primer
text: Granularity means which numbers share a scale. From left to right: one scale for the whole matrix, one per row or output channel, one per group of inputs such as 128, and for activations one per token computed at run time, in gold. Darker shades stand for different scale values. Finer sharing fits the data better but stores more scales. NNCF typically uses per-channel scales for INT8 and group-wise scales for INT4.

label: Primer
text: Two families of quantization. On the left, weight-only W four A sixteen: INT4 weights are expanded to 16-bit inside the kernel and multiplied with untouched 16-bit activations, saving memory and bandwidth. On the right, W8A8: activations are also quantized so the multiply runs in integer arithmetic, which needs matching hardware and makes activation outliers dangerous. The core track of the thesis is the left side, with W8A8 as an optional comparison.

label: Primer
text: The chart on the left shows the typical picture in large transformers: most channels have small values, and a few magenta channels are huge. The bars are illustrative. On the right, a single shared scale must stretch to cover the outlier, so ordinary values squeeze into one or two levels and lose almost all detail. The fixes listed at the bottom are the main ideas of SmoothQuant, AWQ, ViDiT-Q and SVDQuant.

label: Primer
text: Three terms that appear in every paper. Post-training quantization, or PTQ, needs only the trained model and a small calibration set, which for a diffusion model must cover many timesteps. Quantization-aware training, or QAT, retrains with rounding simulated and costs days of GPU time, like QVGen. The bottom strip shows mixed precision: most layers in INT4, a few sensitive ones in INT8 or 16-bit. The pattern is illustrative.

label: Primer
section: Hardware, and why speed is not just FLOPs
text: Two kinds of chips and the memory ladder behind them. A CPU has a few strong cores with vector units and large caches; a GPU has many small cores with matrix units and its own video memory. The pyramid on the right shows the rule: the closer to the cores, the faster and smaller. LTX-2.3 is far too big for any cache, so every step must stream its weights from main memory.

label: Primer

text: The roofline explains when a speed-up is possible. The horizontal axis is how much arithmetic an operation does per byte it loads; the vertical axis is the speed it can reach. On the rising slope an operation is memory-bound, and shrinking its bytes, as INT4 weights do, moves it up. On the flat roof it is compute-bound, and only faster arithmetic helps. Measure where LTX-2.3's layers land on the target Intel hardware.

label: Primer
section: Hardware, and why speed is not just FLOPs
text: A kernel is one compiled routine for one operation. In the top row, three separate kernels each write their result to slow memory and read it back. In the bottom row, one fused kernel does all three steps and keeps the intermediate values on chip. The math is identical but the memory traffic is far lower. OpenVINO performs many of these fusions automatically when it compiles the model.

label: Primer
section: Hardware, and why speed is not just FLOPs
text: Many papers report speed from custom CUDA kernels on NVIDIA GPUs such as the A100, H100 or RTX 4090, using Tensor Cores for their low-bit format. The thesis stack on the right uses only OpenVINO's built-in kernels, CPU vector units and the XMX matrix engines of Arc. The magenta gaps are the reasons a speed-up may not carry over. Quality findings usually transfer, but every speed claim has to be measured again.

NNCF then compresses the weights to INT8 or INT4, with options such as AWQ, scale estimation and GPTQ. The compressed IR is compiled for CPU or GPU and run by the OpenVINO pipeline.
