LTX-Video asks how to make a video diffusion model fast enough to generate faster than real time without losing quality. Its answer is to compress the video so hard in the autoencoder that the transformer only has a few thousand tokens to attend over, and to let the decoder finish the last denoising step. The result is a 1.9 billion parameter model that makes five seconds of video in about two seconds on an H100, and wins most human comparisons. The tab opens with the big picture, then three problems, the method steps, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and finally a thesis box. This is the first of sixteen papers and the first of the two target-model papers, followed by LTX-2. It describes the ancestor architecture of LTX-2.3, so it explains what the thesis will be compressing before the quantization and caching papers explain how.

label: Overview
text: The whole paper in one picture: the top row is a typical video latent diffusion pipeline, the bottom row is LTX-Video. LTX moves patchifying into the VAE and hands the final denoising step to the decoder. For 121 frames at 768 by 512 that cuts the token count from about 47 thousand to about 6 thousand, 7.75 times fewer, and since attention grows with tokens squared, roughly 60 times less attention work. Every later block explains one piece of this diagram.

label: Problem A
text: Token count sets the cost of attention, and the bars make the gap visible. Each bar is the number of transformer tokens for the same five second clip. A standard 8 by 8 by 4 VAE with a 2 by 2 patchifier gives about 47 thousand tokens, a temporally stronger VAE about 24 thousand, and LTX only about 6 thousand. The counts are the tab's own arithmetic from Table 1. This is the first problem the method solves.

label: Problem B
text: The second problem: after a finite number of diffusion steps the predicted latent still holds some leftover noise. A normal decoder was trained only on clean latents, so this residual is out of distribution and turns into visible artifacts, worse at LTX's heavy compression. Other systems fix it with large upsamplers, which cost a lot of runtime. LTX's fix is the denoising decoder that appears in the method steps and in equation u5.

label: Problem C
text: The third problem is about the width of the latent. The left bars show a standard per-channel KL loss, where some of the 128 channels collapse to the prior and carry no information, drawn in grey. The right bars show LTX's fix: one shared log-variance for all channels, which spreads the KL pressure evenly. The bars are illustrative, not measured. Figure 3 later shows that the trained channels really are dense.

This is the recipe in order. First the VAE takes over patchifying and compresses each 32 by 32 by 8 pixel block into one 128-channel latent, trained with four reconstruction losses. Then the decoder is made a small denoiser so it can finish the last step. The transformer is a PixArt-style block with normalisation and rotary positions, and image-to-video works by giving conditioning tokens their own small timestep. Training uses rectified flow with a noise schedule shifted for many tokens.

label: Method 1
text: The VAE training loop at a glance. The encoder maps the input x to a 128-channel latent with one shared log-variance, and the decoder, with noise injected at each layer, produces the reconstruction x hat. Four losses compare the two: pixel MSE, a wavelet L1 over eight sub-bands, LPIPS for perceptual similarity, and the new reconstruction GAN in rust. Together they let the VAE survive 1 to 192 compression, as Figure 16 shows.

label: Method 2
text: Inference runs N minus 1 steps in latent space, then one step straight to pixels. Each DiT box is one Euler step that moves the latent along the predicted velocity, and the gold bar shows the noise level shrinking from 1 down to 0.05. The last box is the decoder, which removes the final bit of noise while decoding. The paper found t one equal to 0.05 clearly preferred over 0. For the thesis, the DiT boxes are where compute and quantization error accumulate.

This pseudo-code is reconstructed by the tab, not copied from the paper. The logic is simple: encode the prompt once with T5, start from pure noise, and if an image is given, place its latent in frame zero with a small timestep. Then loop the transformer, each time subtracting a velocity step from the noisy tokens only. Finally the denoising decoder turns the slightly noisy latent into pixels. The loop body is the part the thesis will quantize and possibly cache.

label: (u1)
text: This is how noise is added in rectified flow. z sub t i is the noisy latent at noise level t i, z zero is the clean latent, and epsilon is Gaussian noise. The noisy latent is simply a straight-line blend: one minus t times the clean latent plus t times the noise. At t equal to 0 it is clean, at t equal to 1 it is pure noise. Every later equation builds on this line.

label: (u2)
text: The goal of the denoiser in one line. f theta is the neural network with weights theta, and given the noisy latent z sub t i and its noise level t i, it should return the clean latent z zero. In practice the network predicts a velocity, from which the clean latent follows directly, as equation u8 defines. Quantizing theta perturbs exactly this prediction.

label: (u3)
text: The sampling schedule: a decreasing list of noise levels, from t N at pure noise down to t one, the lowest level. Generation refines the latent one level at a time along this list. In LTX the transformer covers t N down to t two, and the last level t one is handled by the decoder, as equation u6 states. Fewer levels means fewer transformer passes, which is the other lever on speed.

label: (u4)
text: Standard latent diffusion in two halves. The encoder, script E, compresses a video x zero into a latent z zero, and the decoder, script D, maps a latent back to pixels. Diffusion happens only on the small latent. LTX keeps this structure but changes the decoder, which is what equation u5 introduces next.

label: (u5)
text: The key change: the decoder also takes a noise level. It receives a noisy latent, the blend of clean latent and noise from equation u1, together with t i, and must output clean pixels x zero. It is trained on noise levels from 0 to 0.2 only, so it learns to clean up small residual noise while decoding. This is the fix for the leftover-noise problem in Problem B.

label: (u6)
text: How the denoising decoder is used at inference. Because the decoder changes the size of the data, from latent to pixels, it cannot be applied repeatedly. So it performs exactly one step, taking the latent at the lowest noise level t one and producing the final video x zero. The paper sets t one to 0.05.

label: (u7)
text: The baseline way to pick training noise levels: t drawn uniformly between 0 and 1. LTX replaces this with a shifted log-normal sampler from Stable Diffusion 3 that favours higher noise when there are more tokens, and clamps the tails at the 0.5 and 99.9 percentiles. Figure 10 draws the resulting distributions.

label: (u8)
text: The training target. v is the velocity, epsilon is the noise, and z zero is the clean latent, so v equals noise minus clean latent: the direction of the straight line in equation u1. The transformer learns to predict v. This target is about equally hard at every noise level, which makes training more even than predicting noise.

label: (u9)
text: One sampling step. The next latent, at noise level t minus delta t, equals the current latent z t minus delta t times the predicted velocity v theta. It walks back along the straight line from noise towards the clean latent. Each such step is one full transformer pass, so step count times DiT cost is the inference budget the thesis attacks.

label: (u10)
text: The human-survey metric. The win rate is the number of wins divided by wins plus losses, with skipped votes left out. So 85 percent means that in comparisons where raters expressed a preference, LTX was preferred 85 times out of 100. Table 2 and Figure 15 report this number.

label: (u11)
text: Total VAE compression made explicit. Take the pixels covered by one latent cell, times three colour values, and divide by the number of latent channels. For LTX that is 32 times 32 times 8 times 3 over 128, which is 192. Typical VAEs reach 48 or 96. So LTX's latent is two to four times smaller in raw numbers, as Table 1 lists.

label: (u12)
text: Pixels per transformer token, which is what really sets the token count. LTX has 32 by 32 by 8, so 8192 pixels per token, because its transformer patch size is one. A typical model has an 8 by 8 by 4 VAE plus a 2 by 2 patch, so 1024 pixels per token. That is why LTX sees four to eight times fewer tokens for the same video.

label: Fig. 1
text: Sample outputs, drawn schematically since the originals are photos. The first row is text-to-video from a long prompt, and the next two rows are image-to-video, where the gold frame on the left is the given image and the teal frames are generated over five seconds. The point is prompt adherence and coherent motion. These are the qualities the compressed model must preserve.

label: Fig. 2
text: The holistic denoising idea as a flow. Start with a pure-noise latent of size h over 32, w over 32, and f plus 7 over 8. The transformer denoises it down to noise level t two, then the decoder takes the latent at t one and outputs the clean full-size video. This is the paper's Figure 2 and the visual form of equations u5 and u6.

label: Fig. 3
text: Training makes the 128 latent channels independent, and so dense. Panel a plots cumulative explained variance against principal component: early curves in blue rise fast, meaning a few directions hold everything, while the final curve in rust is almost a straight line, meaning all channels matter. Panels b and c show channel correlations fading from strong to near zero. For the thesis, a dense latent means little redundancy to hide quantization error.

label: Fig. 4
text: The Video-VAE architecture. Panel a is the causal encoder: patchify, then stacks of residual blocks with three downsampling stages, giving a 128-channel latent at 32 by 32 by 8. Panel b is the denoising decoder, whose conditioned residual blocks inject the timestep by scale and shift and add learned noise. The exact patchify split is the tab's inference. The decoder is conv-heavy, which matters when deciding what to quantize.

label: Fig. 5
text: The reconstruction GAN in two panels. In panel a, a normal discriminator sees one image and guesses real or fake. In panel b, it sees the original and its reconstruction side by side, in either order, and must say which is the original. This relative task is easier and more stable, and it also pushes reconstructions closer to the input. It is the rust loss in Method 1.

label: Fig. 6
text: One of the 28 transformer blocks. Latent tokens pass through self-attention with rotary positions and QK normalisation, then cross-attention to T5 text tokens, then a feed-forward network, each with a residual. The timestep enters in gold through AdaLN scale and shift, and in LTX it can differ per token. These attention and feed-forward matrix multiplies are the layers NNCF weight compression will target.

label: Fig. 7
text: Three ways to give tokens positions for rotary embeddings. Panel a uses integer indices, panel b uses fractions of the current size, and panel c, which works best, uses fractions of a fixed maximum size, measured in pixels and seconds. With c, the same place keeps the same code across resolutions, lengths and frame rates. This is part of the transformer design in the method steps.

label: Fig. 8
text: Two heat maps of rotary frequencies, each cell being position times frequency. On the left, LTX's exponential spacing covers a useful range of rotation speeds. On the right, the common inverse-exponential spacing leaves most channels barely rotating. The colours are redrawn, not exact. Figure 17 shows the payoff in training loss.

label: Fig. 9
text: How image-to-video works without extra parameters. The input frame is encoded into one latent frame and placed before the noise tokens. Its tokens get a small timestep t c, often zero, meaning clean, while all other tokens get t equal to 1. Each token keeps its 3-D position. This per-token timestep is why activation ranges vary across tokens in the same step.

label: Fig. 10
text: Training noise levels shift toward high noise as token count grows. Each panel plots the probability of sampling each t: the left for about 256 tokens, the right for about 4096. The shifted curve peaks at higher t, and the teal stretched version that LTX uses is clamped so very low and very high t are still sampled. The shapes are simulated, not copied from the paper.

label: Fig. 11
text: The data pipeline, read left to right and then back. Raw shots are cropped, static clips are removed by a motion check, a CLIP embedding and an aesthetic score are computed, then clips are clustered, de-duplicated, filtered and resized into the final training set. It explains where quality comes from, but it is not relevant to compression.

label: Fig. 12
text: Examples of the internal captioner. Each row is a video, here generated by Sora, with the long structured caption it received: subject, action, setting, camera motion and lighting, ending with the style. The whole training set was re-captioned this way. It explains why LTX works best with long, detailed prompts, which is worth copying in the evaluation prompts.

label: Fig. 13
text: A word cloud of the training captions, with word size roughly showing frequency. Colours, people, camera and background terms dominate, along with the phrase real-life footage. The sizes are approximate. It shows what kind of prompts the model has seen most, which helps in picking realistic test prompts.

label: Fig. 14
text: Two histograms of the training data. Panel a shows words per caption, peaking around 75 to 85 words with a long tail. Panel b shows clip length, mostly under five seconds with a tail to thirty. The bar heights are read off the original plot. Together they say the model is trained on long captions and short clips.

label: Fig. 15
text: Pairwise human preference matrices, text-to-video in panel a and image-to-video in panel b. Each cell is how often the row model beat the column model, and darker is higher. The bottom row, LTX, wins between 72 and 96 percent of its matchups. This is the detailed version of Table 2, and the baseline the compressed model's quality should be compared against.

label: Fig. 16
text: A hard reconstruction case, drawn schematically: a lighthouse covered in scaffolding, full of thin high-frequency lines. With a standard GAN loss the scaffold smears into artifacts, while with the reconstruction GAN it stays close to the input. This is the evidence for the rust loss in Method 1, and a reminder that fine detail is fragile at 1 to 192 compression.

label: Fig. 17
text: Training loss against step for two otherwise identical runs. The rust curve uses inverse-exponential rotary frequencies and stays above the indigo exponential curve for all 140 thousand steps, ending around 0.59 versus 0.58. The gap is small but consistent. It justifies the frequency choice shown in Figure 8.

label: Fig. 18
text: More text-to-video samples, drawn as a schematic grid. Each row is one prompt, and the frames are evenly spaced over five seconds. In the paper, the prompt words the video realises are coloured green, and most of each prompt is green. The takeaway is prompt adherence on detailed cinematic prompts.

label: Fig. 19
text: More image-to-video samples, drawn schematically. The gold frame on the left of each row is the input, and the teal frames are generated. The model keeps the identity and style of the input while adding motion such as turning, walking or camera drift. Identity drift over time is a good thing to check after quantization.

Model specifications side by side, with LTX in the last column. Read down the LTX column: the smallest model at 1.9 billion parameters, but the strongest VAE at 32 by 32 by 8 with 128 channels, a patch size of one, and 8192 pixels per token, four to eight times more than the others. Only MovieGen needs a separate 7 billion parameter upsampler. The table backs the claims in equations u11 and u12.

The headline result: human preference in pairwise tests over 1,000 prompts per task and 20 raters. LTX wins 85 percent for text-to-video and 91 percent for image-to-video, far above Open-Sora Plan, CogVideoX 2B and PyramidFlow. All models ran at the same resolution, length and 40 steps. So speed did not cost quality.

label: Chart A
text: Table 2 as a bar chart: win rate by model, solid bars for text-to-video and outlined bars for image-to-video. LTX's bars, at 85 and 91 percent, clearly tower over the others. It is also the fastest model in the comparison, at about two seconds for 121 frames and 20 steps on an H100.

label: Chart B
text: Table 1 as a bar chart of pixels per transformer token, with VAE compression in the labels. HunyuanVideo and CogVideoX sit at 1024, MovieGen and PyramidFlow at 2048, and LTX at 8192. The latent is also two to four times more compressed in raw size, because its 128 channels are dense. This is the root of LTX's speed.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Use this box as the plan of attack. Target the DiT's linear layers with NNCF weight-only INT8 or INT4 compression first, since with only about six thousand tokens the model is close to weight-bandwidth bound on CPU and Arc. Calibrate across all timesteps, keep the denoising decoder at higher precision at first, and compress T5 cheaply. Judge quality with temporal video metrics, and confirm which of these design points still hold in LTX-2.3.

label: Primer
text: Before any diffusion happens, the video is compressed. The stacked frames on the left are pixels, the VAE encoder in the middle squeezes them, and the grid on the right is the latent, where each cell is one token. The highlighted block of 32 by 32 pixels over 8 frames becomes a single token of 128 numbers. The transformer only ever works on this small grid, and the decoder turns it back into pixels at the end.

label: Primer
text: Fewer tokens pay off twice, because attention compares every token with every other token. Each square's area is the number of token pairs. A typical video model makes about forty seven thousand tokens for a five second clip, LTX-Video about six thousand. That is 7.75 times fewer tokens, and since the cost grows with the square, roughly sixty times less attention work. This is the main source of the paper's speed.

label: Primer
text: Diffusion generates by cleaning noise in small steps. Read left to right: pure noise, then ever cleaner latents, each arrow one full pass through the diffusion transformer, while the gold timestep falls from one towards zero. LTX-Video's twist is the indigo box: the decoder takes the almost clean latent at a noise level of 0.05 and finishes the job while turning it into pixels. The repeated transformer passes are where the thesis saves time and where quantization error builds up.

label: Primer
text: LTX-Video is the first paper tab of the atlas, right after the Start here tab. It introduces the skeleton that LTX-2.3 still uses: a compressing VAE, a diffusion transformer and a denoising decoder. The next tab, LTX-2, adds sound to that skeleton. After that come the quantization papers, then caching and attention speed-ups, and finally VBench, all about making this kind of model cheaper without spoiling the videos.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are latent and token, the diffusion transformer, the timestep, and rectified flow, because the whole method is built from them. T5, RoPE and AdaLN are parts of the transformer that appear in the architecture figure. The H100 entry is a reminder that the paper's two second speed is measured on a data centre GPU, not on Intel hardware.

LTX-2 asks whether one open model can generate a video and its soundtrack together from a single text prompt, with lips, footsteps and music in sync. Its answer is an asymmetric dual-stream transformer: a 14 billion parameter video stream and a 5 billion parameter audio stream that exchange information at every layer, conditioned on a frozen Gemma-3 12B text encoder. This is the exact model family the thesis compresses, so the tab is written as a map of where the weights and the compute sit. It moves from the big-picture component map, to the problem of joint generation and memory, to the method, every equation, every figure, the results, and a closing thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the second target-model paper, after LTX-Video, and everything that follows, from GPTQ to TeaCache to VBench, is a tool applied to it.

section: Big picture: the full component map
text: Almost all of the model's weight sits in three boxes: the video stream at 14 billion parameters, the audio stream at 5 billion, and Gemma-3 at 12 billion, about 31 billion in total. Read the diagram left to right: the prompt goes through Gemma, a feature extractor and two connectors, then both noisy latents are denoised together for N steps, and finally decoders turn latents into sound and frames. For text-to-audio-and-video only the decoders are needed, not the VAE encoders.

A sequential pipeline cannot fix its own first step. On the left, a text-to-video model runs first and a video-to-audio model follows, so the sound can never influence the picture and lip-sync and foley suffer. On the right, LTX-2 runs both streams together and models the joint distribution of video and audio, so information flows both ways. This is the paper's core motivation for the dual-stream design described in the Method section.

Three components hold about 31 billion parameters, and everything else is small. Each bar is one component, measured in billions of parameters; only the video stream, Gemma-3 and the audio stream have numbers from the paper, and the remaining bars are placeholders. Be careful: the conclusion says 13 billion video plus 3 billion audio, which contradicts the abstract. For the thesis, count the weights in the exported OpenVINO models and report those instead.

In sixteen bit precision the model does not fit a sixteen gigabyte Arc A770. The bars are the tab author's estimates, parameters times bytes, for BF16, INT8 and INT4, and the dashed line marks sixteen gigabytes. The DiT needs about 38 gigabytes in BF16, 19 in INT8 and 9.5 in INT4, so weight-only INT4 brings both big blocks under the line. Since Gemma runs only at the start, it can also be offloaded after the text embeddings are computed.

Latency is almost entirely repeated transformer calls. Each box counts how often a component runs per clip: Gemma, the connectors, the VAE decoder and the vocoder run once, while the DiT runs N steps times k passes, where k grows from one with guidance off to three with text and modality guidance. Refinement tiles add even more DiT calls. So speeding up the transformer, by quantization or by caching, gives the largest gain.

The pipeline runs in a clear order. First, video and audio are compressed into latents, audio as one 128-dimensional token per twenty-fifth of a second. Next, the frozen Gemma model turns the prompt into features that are merged across all its layers and refined by one connector per stream. Then the dual-stream blocks denoise both latents together, guided by modality-aware guidance, optionally refined tile by tile at high resolution, and finally decoded into frames and 24 kilohertz stereo sound.

The feature extractor is just one large linear layer. The diagram follows tensor shapes: Gemma's hidden states from all L layers, shaped batch by tokens by width by layers, are normalised per layer, flattened so width times L becomes one axis, and projected by W back to width D. W is trained briefly at the start and then frozen. Because it runs once per prompt, compressing it saves memory, not time.

Guidance makes every sampling step three times as expensive. For one stream, the model is run with full conditioning, with the text dropped, and with the other modality dropped; the two differences are scaled by s t and s m and combined, as in the equation in section four point one, before a single Euler step lowers the noise level sigma. This is why Table 1's timing, measured with guidance off, is a lower bound on real cost.

Peak memory depends on the tile size, not on the final 1080p output. The flow goes left to right: the full DiT first generates a base latent of about half a megapixel, a latent upscaler enlarges it, the result is cut into overlapping tiles in space and time, each tile is refined by the same DiT weights, and the tiles are blended before decoding. On a memory-limited Arc GPU this is what makes high resolution feasible.

The whole inference loop fits in a few lines. The text is encoded once into one embedding per stream. Then, for every noise level, each stream computes three predictions, full, without text and without the other modality, mixes them with the guidance weights and takes an Euler step. After optional upscaling and tile refinement, the latents are decoded. Note that this is the tab author's summary, not an algorithm box from the paper.

This table is a compression plan. Each row is a component with its role, parameter count, how often it runs per clip, and a suggested precision. The two transformer streams run N times k times and hold 19 billion parameters, so they come first for INT8 or INT4 weights. Gemma runs once and is compressed second, mainly to save memory. The small parts, with counts marked not given, stay in sixteen bit because they are cheap but sensitive.

The paper's only displayed equation is its guidance rule. M hat is the guided prediction for one stream, where x is that stream's noisy latent, t is the text condition and m is the other modality's features. It starts from the fully conditioned prediction, then adds s t times its difference from the text-dropped prediction and s m times its difference from the modality-dropped prediction. With both weights zero it reduces to one ordinary pass; otherwise it costs three.

label: (§4.1 values)
text: These are the guidance weights behind every reported result. Video uses a text weight s t of three and a cross-modal weight s m of three; audio uses a stronger text weight of seven and the same cross-modal weight of three. The paper says a larger s m improves synchronisation and semantic coherence. When benchmarking on CPU or Arc, keep these settings fixed so the quality and speed numbers are comparable to the paper's.

This equation reconstructs the feature extractor from the paper's prose; the paper gives no formula. For each Gemma layer l, the hidden state h l is centred by subtracting its mean mu l and then scaled. All L layers are concatenated side by side and multiplied by the learned matrix W, which maps width times L down to width D, giving the embedding e. The exact scaling statistic is not specified, so treat the details as approximate.

label: (A1*)
text: Training uses the standard rectified-flow objective, written here in its usual form because the paper only names it. The noisy latent z sigma is a straight-line blend of the clean latent z zero and Gaussian noise epsilon, weighted by the noise level sigma. The network v theta, given the condition c, is trained to predict the velocity, epsilon minus z zero, with a squared-error loss, separately for audio and video. Signs and time conventions may differ in the real code.

label: Fig. 1
text: The architecture is two parallel denoisers joined in the middle. Read it from the outside in: audio as a mel spectrogram and video each pass through their own VAE encoder and receive noise, while text passes through the encoder, feature extractor and one connector per stream. N dual-stream blocks then denoise both latents, exchanging information through audio-visual cross-attention, and each stream has its own prediction and loss. This is the training view of the component map above.

label: Fig. 2a
text: Each backbone block runs the same four operations in both streams. Top to bottom: self-attention within the stream, text cross-attention, audio-visual cross-attention in the dotted box, where the links cross between streams, and a feed-forward network. Both streams share the text hidden state and have the same depth; only their width differs, with the audio stream narrower. That asymmetry is why the audio stream costs 5 billion parameters instead of 14.

label: Fig. 2b
text: The cross-modal link aligns sound and picture in time, not in space. Queries, keys and values are projected and modulated by the stream's own timestep, then a temporal-only rotary position encoding is applied to queries and keys. Video queries attend to audio keys and values on the left, audio queries attend to video on the right, and each output is gated by the other modality's timestep. These small modulation and gate layers are precision-sensitive when quantizing.

label: Fig. 3
text: Cross-attention maps show that the model finds the source of each sound in the frame. The schematic shows four clips at three frames each, with V2A maps on one side and A2V maps on the other, averaged over heads and layers. Attention follows the passing car, switches from the first speaker to the second to both, and locks onto the lips in the close-up. This is the paper's qualitative evidence that the bidirectional design actually synchronises the two modalities.

label: Fig. 4
text: Text conditioning uses every Gemma layer, not just the last one. Gemma-3 12B produces a tokens-by-width activation at each of its L layers, the feature extractor merges them into one embedding, and learned thinking tokens replace the padding positions. A small bidirectional transformer connector then refines the sequence for one stream, and there is one connector per stream. For quantization this means an error in early Gemma layers still reaches the DiT.

label: Fig. 5
text: Modality guidance pushes the prediction along two independent directions. Start at the fully conditioned output M of x, t, m; move away from the text-dropped prediction by the weight s t, then away from the modality-dropped prediction by the weight s m. The end point is the guided output M prime. Arrow lengths are illustrative. It is the geometric picture of the guidance equation in section four point one.

label: Fig. A1a
text: The training pipeline is the only place the VAE encoders are needed. Audio, as a mel spectrogram, and video are encoded into latents and noised, and the denoiser, conditioned on text, learns to match each modality's velocity field with a flow-matching loss, the objective in equation A1. For the thesis this figure mainly shows which parts can be left out of the exported inference graph.

label: Fig. A1b
text: This is the inference pipeline, the one exported to OpenVINO. Start from noise in both latent spaces, run the denoiser N times with text conditioning, then decode: the audio VAE decoder and an upsampling vocoder produce sound, and the video VAE decoder produces frames. Every box here becomes an exported model, and only the denoiser repeats, which is why it is the main compression target.

label: Fig. A2
text: One stream of one block, in full detail; audio and video share this layout. The latent passes through RMS norm, a timestep-driven scale and shift, self-attention with rotary positions, a gate and a residual add, then text cross-attention, then audio-visual cross-attention with the other branch, then a modulated and gated feed-forward network. The timestep AdaLN feeds every scale, shift and gate, and those small layers are the usual candidates to keep in high precision.

LTX-2 is about eighteen times faster per step than Wan 2.2, despite having more parameters. On an H100 at 720p with 121 frames, Wan 2.2 with 14 billion parameters takes 22.3 seconds per step for video only, while LTX-2 with 19 billion takes 1.22 seconds for audio and video. The paper credits its compact latent space. Note that guidance was off, so real runs with modality guidance cost up to three times more.

The eighteen times speed-up is plain when the bars are drawn to scale. The horizontal axis is seconds per diffusion step on an H100, and lower is better: Wan 2.2 reaches 22.3 seconds while LTX-2 barely leaves the axis at 1.22. This is the paper's main efficiency claim, and it gives the baseline setting, 121 frames, 720p, guidance off, to reuse when reporting CPU and Arc timings.

LTX-2 generates the longest continuous clips in its comparison, up to twenty seconds with synchronised stereo audio. The table lists each model, whether it is open or proprietary, and its maximum clip length: Sora 2 reaches sixteen seconds, Veo 3 twelve, and Ovi and Wan 2.5 ten each. Longer clips mean more latent tokens, which matters for memory and attention cost when running on Intel hardware.

LTX-2 leads on clip length, at twenty seconds against sixteen for Sora 2 and ten for the open alternatives. Each bar is one model's maximum continuous length in seconds. The paper's limitations section adds that beyond about twenty seconds the output drifts in time, loses synchronisation or loses scene variety, so twenty seconds is a practical ceiling, not just a record.

The guidance settings are the same for every result in the paper. Each row is a stream with its text weight and cross-modal weight: video uses three and three, audio uses seven and three. Audio leans more than twice as hard on the text prompt as video does. These values repeat equation 4.1's settings in table form, and they fix the three-pass cost per step that the thesis benchmarks should state.

The quality claims are rankings and preferences, not numbers. In human studies LTX-2 was significantly preferred over the open model Ovi and judged comparable to Veo 3 and Sora 2, and in the Artificial Analysis rankings of November 2025 it placed third for image-to-video and fourth for text-to-video, ahead of Sora 2 Pro and Wan 2.2. Because no numeric scores are given, the thesis needs its own metric, such as VBench, to measure quality loss after compression.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Act on this in four steps. First, compress the 19 billion parameter transformer with NNCF weight-only INT8 or INT4, calibrating data-aware methods on activations from several noise levels. Second, compress Gemma for memory and check the feature-extractor output. Third, keep the decoders, vocoder, connectors and the AdaLN modulation layers in sixteen bit with an ignored scope, and reduce guidance passes with caching. Finally, count parameters in the actual exported models, since the paper describes LTX-2, not 2.3.

label: Primer
text: LTX-2 never generates pixels or sound waves directly. Read the drawing from left to right: noisy video and audio latents enter the dual-stream transformer, which removes a little noise per step while sigma, the noise level, falls from one to zero. Only at the end do the video decoder and the audio decoder with its vocoder turn the clean latents into frames and stereo sound. The transformer is the box that runs many times, so it is the main target.

label: Primer
text: Attention comes in two flavours in this paper. On the left, self-attention: tokens of one stream look at each other, with three dimensional positions for video and time only for audio. On the right, cross-attention: queries from the video stream read keys and values from the audio stream, matched only by time. LTX-2 uses cross-attention to read the text and to let the two streams exchange information in every block.

label: Primer
text: Guidance is why one denoising step can cost three transformer passes. The model runs once with full conditioning, once with the text dropped and once with the other stream dropped, then combines the three with two weights, s t for text and s m for the other modality. Video uses three and three, audio seven and three. The paper's speed table switches guidance off, so real generation is slower than those numbers suggest.

label: Primer
text: LTX-2 sits between LTX-Video and GPTQ. LTX-Video gave the family its compressed video latent and fast transformer. LTX-2 adds an audio stream, a Gemma-3 text pipeline and guidance per modality, and it is the family of LTX-2.3, the thesis model. From GPTQ onward, the remaining fourteen papers are tools for shrinking or speeding up the blocks this report describes.

These fourteen terms cover what the report takes for granted. The most important are the diffusion transformer, the VAE latent, the timestep sigma and classifier-free guidance, because they explain where compute goes. RoPE and AdaLN appear inside every block, and AdaLN layers are small ones likely to stay in high precision. The H100 is the NVIDIA data-centre GPU used for the speed numbers, which will not transfer directly to Intel hardware.

GPTQ asks whether a huge trained language model can have its weights squeezed to three or four bits in a few GPU hours, without retraining and without losing quality. Its answer is yes: round the weights one column at a time and push each rounding error onto the columns not yet rounded, guided by second-order information from a small calibration set. The tab opens with the big picture, then the problem of plain rounding and slow exact solvers, then the method and its three speed tricks, every equation, the paper's figures, the result tables, and finally a box on what this means for the thesis. Among the sixteen papers, GPTQ is the first of three quantization foundations for large language models, followed by SmoothQuant and AWQ. The diffusion quantization papers later in the atlas, and NNCF's int4 weight compression, build directly on its error compensation idea.

Rounding errors should not be thrown away but paid back. On the left, round to nearest, or RTN, rounds each weight alone, so the errors pile up and 3-bit OPT one hundred seventy-five B reaches a perplexity of about seven thousand. On the right, GPTQ rounds column j and then nudges the full-precision columns to its right, using the inverse Hessian built from calibration inputs. This one picture is the whole paper; everything later makes it accurate and fast.

Plain rounding is acceptable at four bits and catastrophic at three. Bars show WikiText2 perplexity for OPT one hundred seventy-five B, where lower is better. RTN at four bits costs about 2.2 points, and at three bits the model is destroyed, with the bar clipped at a perplexity of about seven thousand three hundred. GPTQ stays within 0.03 at four bits and 0.34 at three bits. This gap is the problem the method section solves.

The accurate older method, OBQ, is far too slow for billion-parameter layers. The log-scale bars count operations for one square layer twelve thousand two hundred eighty-eight wide, the width of OPT one hundred seventy-five B. OBQ scales with rows times columns cubed; GPTQ needs about twelve thousand times fewer operations. The counts are illustrative, derived from the cost formulas, not measured. This motivates the shared column order introduced a few blocks later.

Speed is not the only obstacle: the numbers themselves go bad at scale. Starting from a healthy, positive definite inverse Hessian, repeatedly applying the removal update of equation five lets round-off error build up until the matrix becomes indefinite. From then on the compensation pushes weights the wrong way and the layer is ruined. The paper says this almost certainly happens in a few layers of models beyond a few billion parameters, which motivates the Cholesky trick.

The first trick is to quantize columns in the same fixed order for every row. OBQ picks a greedy order per row, so each row keeps its own inverse Hessian to update, once per weight. Because the Hessian depends only on the inputs X, a shared order means all rows share one inverse, updated once per column. The paper finds arbitrary order is about as good as greedy on large layers, and the cost drops to the formula in the equations section.

Here is the core loop in motion. Each panel is one step t: column t, in indigo, is rounded, its error is scaled and multiplied by row t of the inverse Hessian, and that correction is subtracted from the teal columns to its right, which absorb it. Rust columns are already frozen. After the last column the whole matrix is quantized, giving Q. This is the picture behind Algorithm 1.

The second trick keeps the same arithmetic but reorders it for the GPU. Updating the whole weight matrix after every column is memory-bound, because each update touches everything but does little math. Since rounding column i only needs the updates to column i, GPTQ keeps updates inside a block of one hundred twenty-eight columns, then applies one large matrix multiply to the rest. Same operation count, about ten times faster in practice.

The third trick fixes the numerical drift from figure four. Quantizing column q only needs one row of the shrinking inverse Hessian, from the diagonal onward, and those rows are exactly the rows of the upper Cholesky factor, up to a square-root scale. So one stable Cholesky call, plus one percent dampening, gives every row in advance and replaces the error-prone chain of equation five. The error is then divided by the diagonal entry of U.

GPTQ never holds the whole model on the GPU. It loads one Transformer block of six linear layers, runs the calibration set through it to build a Hessian per layer, quantizes each layer, then re-runs the inputs through the now quantized block to feed the next one. Using inputs that already carry earlier quantization error gives a noticeable accuracy gain at almost no cost. For a diffusion transformer, the same loop would run over its blocks.

The recipe walks through the network one block at a time. Each linear layer gets its Hessian, which is damped, inverted and turned into a Cholesky factor once. Then the columns are swept in blocks of one hundred twenty-eight: round, push the error inside the block, and after the block update everything else in one go. Grid parameters are fitted on the already updated weights. Finally, the quantized block produces inputs for the next.

Algorithm 1 is the entire quantizer for one layer, and it combines all three tricks. It takes the damped inverse Hessian, replaces it by its Cholesky factor once, and then loops over blocks of B columns. Inside a block it rounds each column, divides the error by the diagonal entry, and subtracts that error times the matching Cholesky row from the remaining columns of the block. The saved block errors then update all later columns with one matrix multiply.

Equation one is the goal for each layer. Find quantized weights W hat, restricted to the grid, that minimise the squared difference between W times X and W hat times X, where W is the full-precision weight matrix and X holds the layer inputs from the calibration samples. It matches layer outputs, not weights, so errors on unimportant directions are cheap. Every later equation is a way to solve this problem approximately and quickly.

H sub F equals two times X sub F times X sub F transposed. This is the Hessian, the curvature, of the layer objective for one row, restricted to F, the set of weights still in full precision. It tells how costly an error in each direction is. The key point is that it depends only on the inputs, not on the weights, which is why all rows can share it once the column order is fixed.

Equation two is the OBQ rule that GPTQ inherits. The first part picks the weight whose rounding error squared, divided by its diagonal entry of the inverse Hessian, is smallest. The second part, delta F, shifts all remaining weights by minus that scaled error times the matching column of the inverse Hessian, cancelling its effect on the output. Quant means rounding to the nearest grid point. GPTQ keeps the update but drops the greedy choice.

Equation three removes a quantized weight from the problem without inverting a new matrix. It subtracts from the inverse Hessian an outer product of its q-th column and q-th row, divided by the q-th diagonal entry, which is one step of Gaussian elimination, and then drops row and column q. The paper prints the subscript as minus p but means minus q. Repeated use of this update is what drifts numerically at scale.

This line is the cost argument in one step. OBQ costs on the order of rows times columns cubed per layer. With a shared column order GPTQ costs the larger of rows times columns squared and columns cubed. That is a speed-up by a factor of the smaller dimension, thousands of times for large models, and it is what makes one hundred seventy-five billion parameters feasible in hours.

Equation four is the block version of the update in equation two. Instead of one weight, a whole index set Q, such as one hundred twenty-eight columns, is quantized together. The correction delta F is minus the block error times the inverse of the Q by Q sub-block of the inverse Hessian, times the matching columns. This is the lazy batch update that applies once per block in Algorithm 1.

Equation five removes many rows and columns from the inverse Hessian at once, the block version of equation three. It subtracts the Q columns times the inverse of the Q by Q sub-block times the Q rows. Applied over and over through a large layer, it accumulates round-off error and can make the matrix indefinite, as figure four shows. That failure is why GPTQ switches to the Cholesky form.

Dampening adds lambda times the identity to the Hessian, with lambda equal to one percent of the average diagonal value. This small boost keeps the matrix well-conditioned, so inverting it and taking a Cholesky factor stay stable even when some input directions are almost never used. It is a cheap safety step and a setting worth keeping in mind in NNCF's GPTQ options.

This identity is the heart of the Cholesky trick. Row q of the upper Cholesky factor of the inverse Hessian, from the diagonal onward, equals the row GPTQ needs from the shrinking inverse, divided by the square root of its diagonal entry. So instead of updating the inverse column after column, one Cholesky factorisation computed at the start gives every needed row, stably. Algorithm 1 uses exactly these rows.

label: Alg. 1
text: The input to Algorithm 1 is H inverse, the inverse of two X X transposed plus lambda times the identity. X is the layer's calibration inputs and lambda the one percent dampening. It is computed once per layer, then replaced by its Cholesky factor. Its size depends only on the number of input columns, which keeps the cost modest even on a CPU.

Grouping costs a few extra bits. The average bits per weight, b bar, is about b plus sixteen plus b, divided by g, because each group of g weights stores a sixteen-bit scale and a b-bit zero point. Three-bit with groups of one thousand twenty-four adds about 0.02 bits, groups of one hundred twenty-eight add about 0.15, and two-bit ranges from about 2.2 to 2.6 bits. These figures are derived from the text.

label: A.2.1
text: Perplexity is the language quality score in all the tables, and lower is better. It is the exponential of minus the average log probability the model gives each true next token, over N tokens, using non-overlapping segments of two thousand forty-eight tokens. A perplexity of eight means the model is roughly as unsure as choosing among eight words. The paper describes it in words; the formula is the standard one.

label: Fig. 1
text: GPTQ tracks full precision across model sizes, while plain rounding falls apart. Each panel plots WikiText2 perplexity against parameter count on a log scale: OPT at four bits on the left and BLOOM at three bits on the right. The RTN curve spikes, to one hundred ten for OPT sixty-six B and five hundred seventy-one for BLOOM one hundred seventy-six B, while GPTQ hugs the FP16 line. It summarises tables three and four.

label: Fig. 2
text: The paper's own sketch of the procedure matches Algorithm 1. On the right is the inverse Hessian in Cholesky form, computed once. On the left, a bold block of consecutive columns is quantized one column at a time, with the white column being the current one. The blue weights to the right are updated only once the block is finished. Compare it with the lazy-batch and Cholesky figures above.

label: Fig. 3
text: Zero-shot task accuracy tells the same story as perplexity. The plots show LAMBADA accuracy against model size for OPT and BLOOM, where higher is better. At four bits even RTN mostly holds, except OPT sixty-six B. At three bits RTN drops to about zero, while GPTQ keeps most of the accuracy, and bigger models lose less. The data come from tables thirteen and fourteen.

label: Fig. 4
text: Grouping closes most of the remaining four-bit gap. Curves show WikiText2 perplexity for OPT models from 1.3 to 30 billion parameters: plain row-wise four-bit GPTQ, groups of one thousand twenty-four, groups of one hundred twenty-eight, and FP16. The g128 curve sits closest to FP16. The grouped curves are redrawn from the plot, so read their shape, not exact values. This is the basis for int4 with group size one hundred twenty-eight in NNCF.

On the largest models bits can be traded for quality smoothly. The horizontal axis is average bits per weight including group overhead, the vertical axis WikiText2 perplexity, with FP16 dashed. Two-bit with groups of thirty-two gets within about 0.6 points, and three-bit with groups of one hundred twenty-eight comes within 0.1 to 0.15. The data come from tables five and seven, with bit counts computed from the grouping formula.

Low-bit weights make token generation faster because decoding at batch one is memory-bound. For OPT one hundred seventy-five B, latency drops from 589 to 130 milliseconds per token on A6000 cards, 4.53 times faster, and from 230 to 71 milliseconds on A100s, 3.24 times faster, while needing far fewer GPUs. The gain comes from moving fewer bytes, which matters for the thesis because video diffusion is mostly compute-bound.

GPTQ is a fast approximation, not the most accurate solver on small models. On ResNet eighteen and fifty for ImageNet, it performs on par with AdaRound, BRECQ and OBQ at four bits, and slightly worse at three bits, for example 74.87 versus 75.32 for BRECQ on ResNet fifty. The table exists to show that the speed tricks cost little accuracy before the paper scales up to language models.

Quantization time stays practical even at the largest scale. On one A100 GPU, full GPTQ takes about twenty-one minutes for OPT thirteen B, 1.6 hours for sixty-six B and 4.2 hours for one hundred seventy-five B, and 3.8 hours for BLOOM one hundred seventy-six B. Earlier accurate methods would need weeks, which is the gap the shared order and lazy batching close.

This is the paper's main table. Rows are full precision, RTN and GPTQ at four and three bits; columns are OPT sizes from one hundred twenty-five million to one hundred seventy-five billion; cells are WikiText2 perplexity, lower being better. GPTQ wins almost everywhere, and at three bits RTN explodes into the thousands while GPTQ stays near FP16 for large models, for example 8.68 versus 8.34 at one hundred seventy-five B.

The BLOOM family confirms the OPT result on a different architecture. Cells are WikiText2 perplexity, lower being better. At four bits GPTQ improves on RTN at every size, and at three bits RTN reaches five hundred seventy-one for the one hundred seventy-six B model while GPTQ gets 8.64, against 8.11 for FP16. As with OPT, larger models tolerate quantization better.

This summary covers only the two giant models, across three perplexity datasets and LAMBADA accuracy. Four-bit GPTQ is nearly lossless, three-bit GPTQ loses a little, and three-bit RTN is broken. The last two rows add grouping: three-bit with groups of one thousand twenty-four or one hundred twenty-eight reaches 8.45 perplexity on OPT, close to the four-bit result. Grouping is the cheap lever the thesis box recommends.

Latency is measured per generated token for OPT one hundred seventy-five B at batch size one. Three-bit GPTQ with a custom kernel runs 4.53 times faster on A6000 cards, dropping from eight GPUs to two, and 3.24 times faster on A100s, dropping from five to one. The speed-up relies on memory-bound matrix-vector products, so it will not transfer directly to a compute-bound video transformer.

Two-bit quantization becomes usable with small groups. Cells are WikiText2 perplexity for the two giant models. Smaller groups help steadily: OPT goes from 9.58 with groups of one hundred twenty-eight to 8.94 with groups of thirty-two, just above the 8.68 of plain three-bit and against 8.34 for FP16. This extreme regime shows how far error compensation plus grouping can go.

Dropping OBQ's greedy order costs almost nothing. GPTQ is compared with full OBQ on BERT base, scored by SQuAD F1 where higher is better, and on OPT one hundred twenty-five M, scored by perplexity. The two are close, and at three bits GPTQ is even better, with a perplexity of 53.85 against 69.32. This backs the claim in the shared-order figure that arbitrary order is about as good.

On PTB perplexity for OPT, the pattern repeats. GPTQ at four bits stays close to FP16, RTN has an outlier at sixty-six B with 225.66, and at three bits RTN is in the thousands while GPTQ stays usable, reaching 12.86 against 12.01 at one hundred seventy-five B. This appendix table shows the main result does not depend on the WikiText2 dataset.

BLOOM on PTB perplexity gives the same ranking. GPTQ beats RTN at every size and bit width, and the margin is largest at three bits, where the one hundred seventy-six B model scores 15.57 with GPTQ against 107 with RTN and 14.59 in FP16. Like the other appendix tables, it confirms robustness across datasets.

OPT on C4 perplexity shows the same pattern, with one caveat. The calibration samples come from C4's training split, so this test is not fully zero-shot. GPTQ still wins clearly: at three bits the one hundred seventy-five B model scores 10.67, against 10.13 for FP16 and about four thousand six hundred for RTN.

BLOOM on C4 perplexity, again not fully zero-shot because calibration used C4 training text. GPTQ tracks FP16 closely at four bits and stays reasonable at three bits, with 12.27 against 11.71 for the largest model, while RTN at three bits jumps to five hundred ninety-eight. It rounds out the appendix evidence.

LAMBADA accuracy for OPT, where higher is better, is the data behind figure three. Three-bit RTN falls to about zero for most sizes, while three-bit GPTQ keeps 76.19 percent on the one hundred seventy-five B model, slightly above FP16's 75.59. OPT sixty-six B is a weak spot for both methods, echoing its outlier in the perplexity tables.

LAMBADA accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better, is the second half of figure three. Four-bit GPTQ is close to FP16 throughout, and at three bits the one hundred seventy-six B model keeps 65.10 percent with GPTQ against 0.17 with RTN. Smaller models lose more, again showing that scale makes quantization easier.

PIQA accuracy for OPT, a physical common-sense task where higher is better. Four-bit GPTQ matches FP16 almost exactly, for example 81.00 against 81.07 at one hundred seventy-five B. Three-bit RTN sits near fifty percent, which is chance for this two-choice task, while three-bit GPTQ reaches 80.03 on the largest model.

PIQA accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better. At four bits RTN and GPTQ are both close to FP16, so easy tasks hide differences. At three bits the gap opens on the largest model: 77.70 with GPTQ against 53.32 with RTN and 79.16 in FP16.

ARC-easy accuracy for OPT, grade-school science questions where higher is better. Four-bit GPTQ is close to FP16, and at three bits it keeps 65.36 on the one hundred seventy-five B model while RTN drops to about the level of random guessing. Small models are noisier, including one GPTQ entry above FP16 at 1.3 B, so read trends rather than single cells.

ARC-easy accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better. For small BLOOM models RTN at three bits sometimes scores higher than GPTQ, a reminder that zero-shot accuracy on small models is noisy. On the one hundred seventy-six B model the usual order returns: 62.84 for GPTQ against 28.87 for RTN.

ARC-challenge accuracy for OPT, the harder science set where higher is better. Scores for small models are near chance for every method. For large models GPTQ holds up, with 41.04 at three bits on one hundred seventy-five B against 43.94 in FP16, while RTN falls to about 24.

ARC-challenge accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better. Differences among small models are within noise. On the largest model, three-bit GPTQ reaches 40.70 against 24.74 for RTN and 44.97 in FP16, the same large-model pattern seen in every other table.

StoryCloze accuracy for OPT, choosing the right ending to a short story, where higher is better. Four-bit GPTQ matches or slightly beats FP16 on the largest model, and three-bit GPTQ reaches 78.04 against about 46 for RTN, which is below chance on this two-choice task.

StoryCloze accuracy for BLOOM, higher being better, closes the appendix. Four-bit GPTQ stays within about half a point of FP16 on the largest model, and three-bit GPTQ gets 75.37 against 48.50 for RTN. Across all these tasks the conclusion is the same: GPTQ keeps large models usable at three bits.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Treat GPTQ as a ready-made option in NNCF rather than something to implement. Turn on the GPTQ flag in int4 weight compression with group size one hundred twenty-eight, and feed it calibration inputs gathered across prompts, denoising timesteps, and both the video and audio streams of LTX-2.3. Keep sensitive layers in int8 or FP16. Expect memory savings more than speed, measure latency on the Intel hardware, and report RTN, GPTQ and AWQ side by side as an ablation.

label: Primer
text: Storing a weight in four bits means it may only take one of sixteen evenly spaced values. The green dots are the original full precision weights, and the rust arrows snap each one to its nearest level, which is plain round to nearest. The gap between levels is the scale, delta. With grouping, every block of weights, often one hundred and twenty eight, gets its own scale, which is the group size set in NNCF.

label: Primer
text: Not every rounding error hurts the layer equally, and the Hessian shows which ones do. Each grey dot is an allowed pair of quantized values for two weights. Points on the same indigo ellipse change the layer output by the same amount, and the ellipse's shape comes from the calibration inputs. The nearest point, in rust, is worse than a farther point along the long axis. GPTQ uses this by rounding one column and nudging the rest.

label: Primer
text: When a language model writes one token at a time, each weight is fetched from memory and used for a single multiply add, so the chip mostly waits for data. The bars show how many bits must be read per weight: sixteen for full precision, four or three after GPTQ. That is where the paper's speed ups come from. A video diffusion transformer reuses each weight across thousands of tokens, so for the thesis expect memory savings first.

label: Primer
text: GPTQ is the first quantization paper in the atlas. Before it, the two LTX papers describe the model the thesis compresses. GPTQ shrinks only the weights, to three or four bits, and corrects rounding errors using calibration data, while activations stay in full precision. SmoothQuant, next, tackles eight bit activations. The indigo arrow points to the thesis toolchain: NNCF's int4 weight compression has a GPTQ option, and the idea returns in the Wan two point two paper.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are round to nearest, the simple baseline GPTQ beats; the Hessian, built from calibration inputs, which ranks weight errors; group size, the per block scales that recover most four bit accuracy; and perplexity, the language model quality score where lower is better. The hardware entries are NVIDIA GPUs, not Intel devices, so treat the paper's speed numbers as context, not as predictions.

SmoothQuant asks why large transformers break when both weights and activations are cast to eight-bit integers, and how to fix that without retraining. Its answer is to divide each troublesome activation channel by a scale and multiply the matching weight row by the same scale, so the product stays identical but both sides become easy to quantize. That gives W eight A eight, meaning eight-bit weights and eight-bit activations, running on ordinary integer matrix kernels. The tab moves from the big picture, to the outlier problem, to the smoothing method and its equations, then every figure from the paper, the results tables, and a closing box on what this means for LTX-2.3 with NNCF. Among the sixteen papers it is the second of three language-model quantization foundations, after GPTQ and before AWQ. GPTQ and AWQ compress weights only, while SmoothQuant is the one that makes activations quantizable too.

label: Overview
text: The whole paper in one picture: move the difficulty, do not change the math. On the left, a few activation channels, drawn in magenta, are about a hundred times larger than the rest, so a single eight-bit scale wastes almost every level. On the right, each activation channel is divided by s and the matching weight row multiplied by s, done offline. The activations flatten, the weights get slightly bumpier but stay easy, and the output is unchanged.

label: P1
text: Outliers steal the grid. With one step size set by the largest value in the whole activation matrix, a normal channel whose maximum is only one percent of that value lands on just two or three of the two hundred fifty six integer levels. The drawing shows eight levels for clarity. This is the core problem the paper states in Section 3, and the effective-levels equation further down puts a number on it.

label: P2
text: Accuracy against OPT model size for different ways of scaling the activations, taken from Table 1. Per-tensor and per-token eight-bit activations collapse to about thirty three percent, close to random guessing, once models reach six point seven billion parameters. Only per-channel scaling, marked with a star because it is simulated, stays on the FP16 line. That tells us the outliers live in fixed channels, which is the observation the whole method builds on.

label: P3
text: Why per-channel activation scaling cannot simply be used. In an integer matrix multiply, the sum runs over the input-channel dimension, C i, inside the kernel, so only scales along the token rows and the output columns can be pulled out afterwards, as in equation 2. A per-input-channel scale would have to be applied inside the sum. SmoothQuant's escape is to push that scale into the weights offline, the one place where it costs nothing.

label: M1
text: The migration strength alpha decides how much of the outlier burden slides from activations to weights, shown on the paper's toy example with X channel maxima of 2, 16, 2 and 9. At alpha zero the activations keep their spike of 16; at alpha one the weights inherit it. At alpha one half both sides end up with maxima of 2, 4, 2 and 3, so the worst ratio drops from eight times to two times, as the derived equation predicts.

label: M2
text: Where the scale actually lives. The division by s is folded into whatever produced X, such as the LayerNorm gamma and beta or a previous linear layer, and the multiplication by s goes into the weight rows before quantization, so nothing extra runs at inference. The gold box, the tab's own annotation, shows NNCF inserting an explicit Multiply node when nothing can be folded, which is the case for LTX-2.3's adaptive LayerNorm.

The recipe runs in five stages, all offline except the last. First, measure the largest absolute value of every input channel on 512 calibration sentences. Then pick alpha by a quick search, which gives about one half for OPT and BLOOM and higher values for Llama-style models. From alpha, compute the scales, fold them into the previous operation and the weights, quantize every linear layer and attention product to eight bits, and finally run on standard integer kernels.

The procedure as pseudocode written by the tab, since the paper has no algorithm box. For each smoothed linear layer, the attention QKV input and the first feed-forward input, it collects activation channel maxima and weight row maxima, turns them into a scale with equation 4, and folds that scale in with equation 3. Then every matrix multiply is quantized to eight bits, while LayerNorm, Softmax, activation functions and residual adds stay in FP16.

The basic symmetric quantizer used throughout the paper. X bar, the integer version of the floating-point activation X, is X divided by the step size delta and rounded. Delta is the largest absolute value in X divided by two to the power N minus one, minus one, which is 127 for eight bits. Delta from calibration is called static, delta measured at run time is dynamic. Because the largest value sets delta, outliers hurt everything else.

label: (–)
text: The shape bookkeeping for a linear layer. Y equals X times W, where X has T rows, one per token, and C i columns, the input channels. W has C i rows and C o columns, the output channels. The important detail is that C i is the inner dimension that gets summed over, so later arguments about which scales can leave the kernel all refer back to these three names.

label: (–)
text: A back-of-the-envelope count of how many integer levels a channel really uses. It is two to the eighth, or 256, times m i over m, where m i is that channel's maximum and m is the maximum of the whole matrix. When outliers are about a hundred times larger, ordinary channels get only two or three levels. This is the numeric form of the grid picture in P1 and the reason naive W8A8 collapses.

How an eight-bit matrix multiply is dequantized. The integer product of X bar and W bar is computed first, then multiplied on the left by a diagonal matrix of per-token step sizes, delta X, and on the right by a diagonal matrix of per-output-channel step sizes, delta W. Both scales sit on the outer dimensions, so they can be applied after the integer kernel. A scale along the inner input-channel dimension cannot, which is the constraint SmoothQuant is designed around.

The smoothing identity, the heart of the method. X is multiplied by the inverse of diag of s, which divides each activation channel j by s j, and W is multiplied by diag of s, which multiplies weight row j by the same s j. The two cancel, so Y equals X hat times W hat exactly. Because the division can be folded into the previous operation offline, the model gains easier activations at no runtime cost.

label: (–)
text: The two extreme choices of scale, shown side by side. Setting s j to the maximum of activation channel j makes every smoothed activation channel peak at one and dumps all the difficulty into the weights. Setting s j to one over the maximum of weight row j does the opposite and leaves everything in the activations. Figure 10 shows that both extremes lose accuracy, which motivates the balanced formula in equation 4.

The paper's scale formula. For each input channel j, s j equals the maximum absolute activation in that channel raised to the power alpha, divided by the maximum absolute weight in row j raised to the power one minus alpha. Alpha, the migration strength, runs from zero to one: one half splits the difficulty evenly, and larger values push more of it into the weights. This single knob is what the steps block tunes and what Figure 10 sweeps.

label: (Fig. 5)
text: Equation 4 at alpha equal to one half, written the way Figure 5 annotates it. The scale is the square root of the activation channel maximum divided by the weight row maximum. X hat is X with each channel divided by its scale, and W hat is W with each row multiplied by it. Applied to the toy example this gives scales of 1, 4, 1 and 3.

label: (derived)
text: A derived line the tab adds, not printed in the paper. After smoothing, the maximum of activation channel j becomes the old activation maximum to the power one minus alpha times the old weight maximum to the power alpha, and the weight maximum is the mirror image. At alpha one half both equal the square root of the product, which is what the paper means by giving weights and activations the same quantization difficulty.

label: Fig. 1
text: Model size and accelerator memory over time, on a log scale from 2017 to 2022. Language models grew about ten thousand times, from 0.05 billion parameters to 530 billion, while GPU and TPU memory grew only from 16 to 80 gigabytes. The widening gap is the motivation for the paper. The point positions are approximate, since the plot is redrawn.

label: Fig. 2
text: The intuition in two panels, where horizontal lines are quantization levels. In the original panel, one activation outlier stretches the range to 10, so normal values crowd into the bottom level or two, while weights with a range of 0.1 fill their grid. After smoothing, both X hat and W hat span their grids well. This is the qualitative version of the effective-levels argument, and the shapes are redrawn.

label: Fig. 3
text: The two scale layouts an eight-bit matrix multiply supports. Per-tensor uses one step size for all of X and one for all of W, which is cheapest. Vector-wise uses one step per token row of X and one per output channel of W. Neither allows scales along the inner input-channel dimension. These are the granularities that the O1, O2 and O3 settings in Table 2 choose between.

label: Fig. 4
text: A real OPT-13B layer, redrawn as heatmaps where darkness shows magnitude relative to each panel's maximum. The original activations have a few channels above 70, visible as magenta columns that stay large across all tokens, while the original weights are flat. After smoothing, the activation panel peaks near 10 with faint stripes, and the weights gain thin ridges in the same channels but remain easy. The cell values are synthetic; the pattern follows the paper.

label: Fig. 5
text: The paper's worked example at alpha one half. Activation channel maxima are 2, 16, 2 and 9, weight row maxima are 2, 1, 2 and 1, so the scales come out as 1, 4, 1 and 3. The activation range shrinks from 16 to 4 while the weight range grows from 2 to 4, and the two are now equally easy. The product is unchanged, and all of this happens offline.

label: Fig. 6
text: A precision map of one transformer block. Every compute-heavy operation, meaning the query, key and value projections, both attention matrix products, the output projection and the two feed-forward layers, takes eight-bit inputs, drawn in rust. Light element-wise operations such as LayerNorm, Softmax, ReLU and residual adds stay in FP16, drawn in teal. Quantizing the attention products too is what separates SmoothQuant from weight-only methods, and it maps directly onto a DiT block.

label: Fig. 7
text: Average accuracy against OPT model size. Naive W8A8 and ZeroQuant are fine up to 2.7 billion parameters, then crash to about thirty three percent from 6.7 billion on, exactly where outliers emerge. SmoothQuant O3 stays on the FP16 line at every size. LLM.int8 also matches FP16, but only by keeping outlier channels in floating point, which makes it slow. The points for the two smallest models are read from the plot.

label: Fig. 8a
text: Latency and memory for OPT-13B in PyTorch on one A100, with sequence length on the x axis and a batch of four. SmoothQuant is fastest at every length, for example 223 milliseconds against 296 for FP16 at length 512, and it roughly halves memory. LLM.int8 is slower than FP16, the cost of its mixed-precision path. This is the first speed evidence for the efficiency half of the paper's claim.

label: Fig. 8b
text: The same PyTorch comparison for OPT-30B. At sequence length 256, SmoothQuant takes 228 milliseconds against 343 for FP16, or 1.51 times faster, and at length 128 memory drops from 56.6 to 28.9 gigabytes, 1.96 times less. The gains grow with model size, since bigger layers are more dominated by matrix multiplies. Values are read from the paper's bar labels.

label: Fig. 9a
text: OPT-13B running in FasterTransformer, a highly optimised inference engine, on one A100. SmoothQuant O3 is up to 1.45 times faster, going from 181 to 125 milliseconds at sequence length 1024, and memory falls from 30 to 19 gigabytes. The point is that the speed-up survives even against a strong FP16 baseline, not only against plain PyTorch.

label: Fig. 9b
text: OPT-30B in FasterTransformer on one A100. SmoothQuant O3 reaches the paper's headline speed-up of 1.56 times, 186 against 119 milliseconds at sequence length 512, and memory is roughly halved, from 64 to 37 gigabytes. Together with Figure 9a it shows the gain holds across lengths from 128 to 1024 tokens.

label: Fig. 9c
text: OPT-66B in FasterTransformer, where the comparison changes: FP16 needs two GPUs while SmoothQuant fits on one. Latency is essentially equal, 490 against 489 milliseconds at length 1024, and memory drops from 139 to 74 gigabytes. Halving the hardware at the same speed is a different kind of win from raw speed-up.

label: Fig. 9d
text: OPT-175B in FasterTransformer. SmoothQuant on four GPUs beats FP16 on eight, 720 against 848 milliseconds at length 1024, while memory falls from 389 to 200 gigabytes. Half the GPUs and still faster is the strongest serving result in the figure set, and it anticipates the 530 billion parameter result in Table 10.

label: Fig. 10
text: LAMBADA accuracy of OPT-175B as the migration strength alpha sweeps from 0.1 to 0.9, with separate lines for weight-only, activation-only and full eight-bit quantization. When alpha is small, outliers stay in the activations and anything with eight-bit activations collapses to zero. When alpha is large, the weights become too hard and anything with eight-bit weights collapses. Only 0.4 to 0.6 keeps W8A8 near the FP16 level of 74.7 percent. The shape is redrawn from the plot.

label: Chart R1
text: Average accuracy over seven zero-shot tasks for OPT-175B, from Table 3. Naive W8A8, ZeroQuant and Outlier Suppression all fall to about thirty six percent, essentially random. LLM.int8 and all three SmoothQuant settings stay within half a point of FP16's 66.9 percent. The difference is that SmoothQuant gets there with pure eight-bit kernels, which is the accuracy half of the paper's claim.

label: Chart R2
text: Latency for OPT-13B and OPT-30B at two sequence lengths, from Table 11. Coarser activation scaling is faster: per-token dynamic, O1, is slowest of the three, per-tensor dynamic, O2, is quicker, and per-tensor static, O3, is quickest. All three beat FP16, while LLM.int8 is slower than FP16 in three of the four cases. Since accuracy barely differs between O1 and O3, the static setting is the natural default.

Table 1 tests which activation granularity keeps OPT accurate. From 13 billion parameters up, per-tensor and per-token eight-bit activations fall to about thirty three percent, while per-channel scaling matches FP16 within about two tenths of a point at every size. The catch, marked in the caption, is that per-channel activation scales do not fit an integer matrix multiply. This table is the evidence behind P2 and the motivation for smoothing.

Table 2 defines the baselines and the three SmoothQuant settings compared in every result. All SmoothQuant variants use per-tensor weights; they differ only in the activations, going from per-token dynamic in O1, to per-tensor dynamic in O2, to per-tensor static in O3.
