section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Use SmoothQuant only when trying full eight-bit activations for LTX-2.3; weight-only compression with nncf compress weights does not need it. With nncf quantize and the transformer model type, NNCF already applies smoothing, so sweep its alpha as in Figure 10 rather than trusting the default. Calibrate on several prompts times several denoising steps, expect explicit Multiply nodes around adaptive LayerNorm, and benchmark W8A8 against weight-only on Arc and CPU before choosing.

label: Primer
text: Rounding to eight-bit integers gives a ruler with two hundred fifty six ticks, and one step size is set by the largest value. Without an outlier the ticks are fine and every dot keeps its detail. Add one value at sixty and the step stretches so far that all the ordinary values near zero share just a few ticks. That lost detail is exactly the error SmoothQuant sets out to remove.

label: Primer
text: There are two ways to quantize a linear layer. Weight-only methods like GPTQ, AWQ and NNCF's compress weights store the weights in few bits but turn them back into sixteen-bit floats before multiplying, so they mainly save memory. W eight A eight also rounds the activations to eight bits, so the multiply itself runs on fast integer units. Activations are only known at run time, and that is where the outliers appear.

label: Primer
text: Activations form a matrix with one row per token and one column per channel, and granularity says which numbers share a step size. One scale for everything lets the outlier column ruin all values. One scale per token row still mixes the outlier into every row. One scale per channel column would fix it, but it cannot be pulled out of a fast integer matrix multiply. SmoothQuant moves that per-channel factor into the weights instead.

label: Primer
text: SmoothQuant is the fourth paper in the atlas. GPTQ, just before it, compresses weights only. SmoothQuant adds the activation side by shifting outlier scale from the activations into the weights, which gives W eight A eight. AWQ, next, comes from the same lab and reuses per-channel scaling for four-bit weight-only models. Later diffusion papers like PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q and SVDQuant build on this smoothing, and NNCF uses it in its full integer path.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are outlier channel, W eight A eight, the difference between static and dynamic scales, and per-tensor versus per-token versus per-channel granularity. The hardware and benchmark names matter too: the results come from NVIDIA A100 GPUs and the FasterTransformer library, and accuracy is measured on language tasks such as LAMBADA and WikiText, not on images or video.

AWQ asks how to squeeze a large language model's weights down to four or three bits without retraining and without losing accuracy. Its answer: only about one percent of weight channels really matter, they are found by looking at activation sizes, and they are protected by scaling them up before rounding, so every weight stays in one simple INT4 format. The tab moves from a big picture diagram to the problem, the method and its kernels, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a thesis box. This is the fifth of sixteen papers and the last of the three language model foundations, after GPTQ and SmoothQuant. It is the most directly usable for the LTX-2.3 study, because NNCF offers AWQ as an option in INT4 weight compression. The diffusion papers that follow adapt these ideas to image and video transformers.

The whole paper fits in these two panels. On the left, plain round to nearest gives every weight the same rounding error, but that error is multiplied by the input, so channels with large activations hurt the most. Keeping them in FP16 fixes accuracy but mixes formats, which is slow. On the right, AWQ multiplies those weights by a scale s and divides the input by s, so the product is unchanged while the salient error shrinks by about one over s, and all weights stay INT4.

A handful of input channels dominate the error. The left chart is illustrative: each channel's error is roughly activation size times step size times rounding error, and about one percent stand out. The right bars are real, from Table 1, for OPT six point seven B at three bits. Keeping one percent in FP16 chosen by activation brings perplexity from 23.54 to 11.39, near FP16's 10.86; choosing by weight size or at random barely helps. The method is built on this observation.

Here are the three existing options AWQ wants to beat, each with its weakness. Plain round to nearest at three or four bits wrecks small models, for example OPT one point three B goes from a perplexity of 14.62 to 119. Keeping one percent in FP16 is accurate but gives an irregular layout with no fast kernel. GPTQ's second order reconstruction can overfit its calibration data, costing 2.3 to 4.9 perplexity when tested on a different domain. AWQ aims for accuracy, one uniform format, and robustness at once.

The method has two halves. Offline, a small slice of the Pile runs through the model, the average activation size per input channel is measured, and a grid search over alpha picks the scale with the lowest layer output error; clipping is then tuned. At inference, the inverse scale is folded into the previous operation, such as a LayerNorm, so the stored INT4 weights feed an ordinary uniform matrix multiply. Equations four and five are the loss and search shown here.

The procedure is deliberately cheap. It only needs forward passes on a small generic calibration set, to cache each layer's inputs and measure how large each channel's activations are. From that it tries twenty strengths of scaling, quantizes, and keeps whichever gives the smallest output error. Clipping is then set, the inverse scale disappears into the previous operator, and plain low bit weights are stored with FP16 group scales. There is no backpropagation and no weight reconstruction, which is why AWQ generalizes well across domains.

Scaling up the salient channels is not free, which is why AWQ searches rather than fixing s. In the left chart the indigo curve, the salient error factor, keeps falling as s grows, while the rust curve, the share of groups whose maximum and so step size changes, keeps rising and hurts the other weights. The right chart shows perplexity for OPT six point seven B is best at s equals two, 11.92, and worse again at four. Equation five's alpha search finds this balance automatically per layer.

The tab reconstructs this box from sections 3.2 and 5.1, since the paper has none. For each linear layer it measures the mean activation size per input channel, then tries twenty values of alpha from zero to one, using the statistic raised to alpha as the scale, quantizing the scaled weights and measuring output error against full precision. The best scale wins, clipping is applied, the inverse scale is folded into the preceding operator, and weights are stored at four or three bits in groups of 128.

Fewer bytes only become speed if the kernel is built for it. There is no hardware instruction that multiplies INT4 by FP16, so TinyChat unpacks and dequantizes the weights inside the matrix multiply kernel, in registers, and never writes full precision weights back to memory. It also fuses small operations like LayerNorm and attention pieces into single kernels, because on an RTX 4090 each tiny FP16 kernel takes about as long as its launch overhead. In this project, the OpenVINO CPU and GPU plugins play this role.

This sets up the notation. y equals w times x is a normal linear operation, where w is a group of weights and x is the input. The second form, y equals Q of w times x, is the same operation with only the weights quantized, Q being the quantizer, while the activations x stay in FP16. This is weight only quantization, the W4A16 setting that the rest of the paper and NNCF's INT4 compression use.

Equation one is the basic quantizer. Q of w equals delta times the rounded value of w divided by delta, so weights are snapped to a grid of evenly spaced levels. Delta, the step size, is the largest absolute weight in the group divided by two to the power N minus one, where N is the number of bits. Because delta depends on the group maximum, a group of 128 weights shares one step size, which is the detail equation two exploits.

Equation two is the key trick. Multiply one weight w by a scale s greater than one, and divide its input x by the same s. Mathematically the product is unchanged, but now the weight is rounded at a larger size, so after dividing by s its rounding error is relatively smaller. Delta prime is the group's new step size, which may differ slightly from delta if the scaled weight becomes the group maximum.

These are two empirical facts that make the argument work. First, the rounding error of a single weight is spread roughly evenly between zero and one half, so its average is about 0.25 and does not depend on scaling. Second, scaling one weight rarely changes the group maximum, so delta prime is about equal to delta. The step size and the input are FP16 and add no error. Equation three and the ratio that follows rely on both facts.

Equation three writes out the output error before and after scaling. Before, it is delta times the rounding error of w over delta, times x. After, it is delta prime times the rounding error of the scaled weight, times x, times one over s. The first line shows why saliency comes from activations: the error grows with the size of x, so channels with large inputs contribute most. The second line shows the extra factor one over s that scaling adds.

Dividing the two errors gives the ratio: new error over original error equals delta prime over delta, times one over s. With delta prime about equal to delta and s greater than one, the salient weight's error shrinks by roughly one over s. The catch is the other weights in the group, which see their step size grow by delta prime over delta. Table 2 measures exactly this trade off.

Equation four turns the idea into an optimization. The best scale vector s star is the one that minimizes L of s, the size of the difference between the quantized layer output and the full precision output W times X. Here W is the weight matrix, X is the cached calibration input, and diag of s is a diagonal matrix of per input channel scales whose inverse is folded into the previous operator. Because Q is not differentiable, the paper solves it by the simple search in equation five.

Equation five shrinks the search to one number. The scale is s X raised to the power alpha, where s X is the average activation size per input channel. Alpha between zero and one sets how strongly salient channels are protected: zero means no scaling, one means scaling fully by activation size. The best alpha is found by trying twenty grid points and keeping the one with the lowest loss from equation four.

These roofline numbers explain the speed up. Arithmetic intensity is operations done per byte loaded. On an RTX 4090, with 165 TFLOPS and one terabyte per second, anything below 165 operations per byte is memory bound. FP16 token generation sits near one, reaching about one TFLOPS; four bit weights raise it to about four, so throughput rises about four times. A video diffusion transformer processes many tokens at once and sits much higher, so expect a smaller latency gain.

This is the packing rule from section 4.2. For a SIMD register of two to the n bits, weights that share a byte should be one eighth of two to the n positions apart. For a 128 bit ARM NEON register this means pairing weight i with weight i plus 16, and on GPUs eight weights are stored in the interleaved order zero, two, four, six, one, three, five, seven. It is an engineering detail that makes unpacking cheap; Figure 4 illustrates it.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Use AWQ through NNCF by calling compress weights with an INT4 mode, group size 128, a calibration dataset, and awq set to true, then check which transformer linears it actually matched, since AWQ needs a preceding operation to absorb the inverse scale. Calibrate on many denoising timesteps and prompts, because activation sizes change with noise level. Expect mainly memory savings, since a video diffusion transformer is largely compute bound; compare against W8A8 and keep sensitive layers in INT8 or FP16.

label: Primer
text: Everything in AWQ is stored in one simple format, W four A sixteen with group size one twenty eight. Each run of one hundred twenty eight weights shares a single step size, and every weight becomes one of sixteen whole number levels. At run time those codes are multiplied back by the step size and the math happens in FP16, so the activations are never touched. Plain round to nearest is this recipe with no tricks, the baseline AWQ beats.

label: Primer
text: Each position of the input vector is a channel, and it multiplies one row of weights. Rounding gives every weight a similar small error, but in the output that error is multiplied by the input it meets. A few channels, shown in magenta, carry large inputs on almost every token, so errors on their weights do the most damage. AWQ calls these salient channels and finds them from average activation size, which is the whole idea behind the paper's name.

label: Primer
text: Speed-ups in this paper come from memory traffic, not arithmetic. When a chatbot generates text, each new token must read every weight once and does only about one multiply-add per weight, so the processor mostly waits for memory. Four times smaller weights mean roughly four times less waiting. A diffusion transformer step like LTX-2.3's handles thousands of tokens at once, closer to the context stage, so there INT4 weights mainly save memory.

label: Primer
text: AWQ is the fifth paper in the atlas and the last language model foundation. GPTQ showed four bit weights can work by correcting errors, and SmoothQuant showed outliers can be moved with a per-channel scale. AWQ uses that scaling for weight-only four bit, chooses it from activation statistics, and needs no backpropagation. Q-Diffusion comes next and brings timesteps into the picture. For this project, AWQ is the awq option in NNCF weight compression.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are weight-only quantization with group size one twenty eight, salient channels, and the calibration set, a few text samples used only to measure activation sizes. Perplexity on WikiText-2 is the main accuracy score, where lower is better. The hardware names, RTX 4090, Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi, mark the range of devices from desktop GPU down to a tiny ARM computer.

Q-Diffusion asks why ordinary post-training quantization, which works well on classifiers, falls apart on diffusion models, and how to fix it without any retraining. Its answer: calibrate on inputs sampled evenly across every denoising step, and give the two halves of each U-Net skip concatenation their own quantizers. With these two changes, four-bit weights and eight-bit activations, called W four A eight, stay within about 2.3 FID points of full precision, while naive quantization collapses. The tab starts with a big-picture drawing, then the two problems, the method with its algorithms, every equation and figure, the result tables, and a box on what this means for the thesis. Among the sixteen papers, this is the first of the diffusion-specific quantization group, after the general LLM methods GPTQ, SmoothQuant and AWQ, and it is the ancestor that PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q, SVDQuant and the later video methods build on.

Both of the paper's fixes fit in one picture. On top, the gold bars show how wide the U-Net's input range is at each denoising step: wide while the image is still noise, narrow near the end. Naive quantization calibrates on one step; Q-Diffusion samples every c-th step. At the bottom, a skip concatenation joins a large-range deep tensor with a small-range shallow one, so Q-Diffusion gives each half its own scale. Keep these two ideas in mind; everything below expands them.

A small error at each step becomes a large error at the end. The same quantized U-Net, theta q, is applied T times, and each step takes the previous step's slightly wrong output as its input, so the magenta error band grows along the chain. In effect, a sampler with T steps acts like a network T times deeper. This is the first reason diffusion is harder to quantize than a classifier, and Figure 3 later measures the growth directly.

One scale cannot serve two very different populations. The input channels of a shortcut convolution come in two groups: deep features with a range of about 40 and shallow features with a range of about 1. A four-bit quantizer has only sixteen levels, so a scale sized for the deep half puts nearly all shallow values into bin zero, and their information is lost. This is the second problem, the one shortcut splitting in Equations 6 to 8 solves.

Here is fix number one as a pipeline. First, run the full-precision model from random noise and keep samples from every c-th step, building a calibration set of 5,120 inputs. Second, apply the standard BRECQ recipe: reconstruct each block in turn so its quantized output matches the full-precision output, with AdaRound learning how to round each weight. Third, learn activation step sizes with LSQ. The novelty is the calibration data, not the optimiser, which is reused from earlier work.

Fix number two costs nothing at inference time. Concatenating along input channels means the convolution is really two partial matrix products added together: X1 times W1 plus X2 times W2. So each half can have its own activation scale and its own weight scale, s1 sized for X1 and s2 sized for X2, and the output is the same sum, with no extra operations. The drawing is the visual form of Equation 8.

The recipe runs in a fixed order. First choose the sampler and the calibration interval, then run the full-precision model and collect inputs at the chosen steps, including time embeddings and, for Stable Diffusion, both conditional and unconditional text features. Next, split the shortcut layers, then reconstruct weights block by block with AdaRound, and only afterwards calibrate activation step sizes. Fragile operations like SoftMax, SiLU and GroupNorm stay in full precision, and Stable Diffusion attention scores use sixteen-bit integers.

Algorithm 1 is the unconditional version of time-step-aware calibration. The first loop walks through the denoising steps and, whenever the step number is a multiple of c, stores n intermediate inputs from the full-precision model. The second loop visits the blocks one by one and fits the weight quantizers against the full-precision outputs. An optional third loop then fits activation step sizes. The key design choice is that calibration data comes from the model's own trajectory, so no training images are needed.

Algorithm 2 is the same procedure for text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion. The only change is in the sampling loop: each stored sample is a triple of latent, text feature and time step, and it is stored twice, once with the prompt's conditional features and once with the unconditional ones, because classifier-free guidance runs both branches at inference. That is why Table 4 lists twice as many Stable Diffusion samples as prompts. This is the version that maps onto LTX-2.3, which also uses guidance.

Equation 1 is the forward diffusion step, which adds noise. It says x t, the image at step t, is drawn from a Gaussian centred at the square root of one minus beta t times the previous image x t minus one, with variance beta t times the identity. Beta t is the noise schedule, a small number between zero and one. After enough steps, x T is pure Gaussian noise. This is background; it is not quantized, but it defines what the U-Net sees.

Equation 2 is the learned reverse step, the part the network performs. P theta of x t minus one given x t is a Gaussian with mean mu tilde, computed by the network, and variance beta tilde times the identity. Sampling starts from pure noise x T and applies this step repeatedly. The important point for quantization is that each output becomes the next input, which is exactly why errors accumulate, as Figure 2 and Figure 3 show.

Equation 3 shows where the network enters the reverse step. The mean mu tilde equals one over the square root of alpha t, times the current image x t minus a scaled copy of epsilon theta, the noise predicted by the U-Net. The scaling factor is one minus alpha t over the square root of one minus alpha bar t. Epsilon theta is the quantized part, so any quantization error in the predicted noise flows straight into the next image.

Equation 4 gives the variance of the reverse step and defines the helper symbols. Beta tilde t equals one minus alpha bar at t minus one, divided by one minus alpha bar at t, times beta t. Alpha t is one minus beta t, and alpha bar t is the product of all alphas up to step t. These are fixed schedule constants, not learned and not quantized; they complete the diffusion background before the paper turns to quantization.

Equation 5 is the basic uniform quantizer used for both weights and activations. Divide w by the step size s, round to an integer, clip between c min and c max, then multiply by s again to get w hat, the de-quantized value. With four bits there are only sixteen integers available. Plain linear quantization uses round-to-nearest; Q-Diffusion keeps the same form but lets AdaRound learn whether each weight rounds up or down, and learns the clipping range too.

Equation 6 splits the activation quantizer of a shortcut layer. Q X of X, the quantized input, is formed by quantizing X1, the deep part with c1 channels, with its own quantizer, quantizing X2, the shallow part with c2 channels, with another, and then concatenating the two. This directly answers the range clash in Figure 3: the small shallow values now get a scale that fits them instead of being rounded to zero.

Equation 7 applies the same split to the weights. The weight matrix W has one row per input channel, so it divides into W1, the c1 rows that multiply the deep features, and W2, the c2 rows that multiply the shallow features. Each part gets its own weight quantizer. This matters because Figure 7 shows the weights are bimodal too, with W1 small and W2 much larger, so one shared weight scale would waste precision.

Equation 8 explains why splitting is free. The quantized input times the quantized weights equals the quantized X1 times the quantized W1, plus the quantized X2 times the quantized W2. The input has c in channels, equal to c1 plus c2. Because a matrix product over concatenated channels is just the sum of two smaller products, the layer computes the same amount of work with two scales instead of one, which is why the paper reports negligible overhead.

text: This appendix equation defines a non-uniform alternative the authors tried and rejected. N t, the number of calibration samples taken from step t, is set to s t divided by the sum of s t over all steps, times the total N of 5,120. Here s t is the pixel-wise standard deviation of x t, so noisier steps get more samples. Table 7 shows it did slightly worse than plain uniform sampling, which supports the paper's simple choice.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Act on this box when building the NNCF calibration set: hook the LTX-2.3 transformer's inputs during full pipeline runs and keep samples from many steps across the trajectory, including both guidance branches, exactly as in Algorithm 2. Weight-only int8 or int4 hardly depends on this, but W8A8 does. Shortcut splitting does not apply directly to a DiT, yet the lesson does: give mixed-range tensors separate quantizers or higher precision. And regenerate calibration data if the sampler or step count changes.

label: Primer
text: A diffusion model does not produce an image in one pass. It starts from pure noise and runs the same U-Net again and again, each time on its own previous output. The gold bars show the input range shrinking from about plus or minus 4.5 to plus or minus 1.8 as the picture appears. So a quantizer tuned at one step fits the other steps badly, which is the first problem Q-Diffusion solves.

label: Primer
text: Quantization needs a scale, and calibration is how it gets one. A few example inputs pass through the model, record the range of each tensor, and turn that range into a step size. W four A eight means four bit weights with sixteen levels and eight bit activations with two hundred and fifty six. If the calibration inputs give a range that is too wide, small values all round to zero.

label: Primer
text: A U-Net shrinks the image in an encoder, grows it back in a decoder, and copies encoder features across through skip connections. Inside a decoder block those copied features are concatenated with the deep features from below. In the paper the deep half reaches about plus or minus forty while the copied half stays near one, so one shared four bit scale wipes out the small half. That is the second problem the paper fixes.

label: Primer
text: GPTQ, SmoothQuant and AWQ quantize language models, which have no denoising steps. Q-Diffusion is the first paper in the atlas about diffusion models. It adds two things: calibration data drawn from every part of the denoising trajectory, and separate quantizers for the two halves of a skip concatenation. PTQ4DiT comes next and moves these ideas to diffusion transformers, the family LTX-2.3 belongs to. Its calibration recipe feeds directly into the NNCF setup.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are post-training quantization, which compresses a trained model without retraining, the calibration set that sets the scales, and W4A8. For results, remember that FID compares generated and real images and lower is better, while CLIP score measures how well an image matches its prompt. Note that the paper reports model size and bit operations, not measured speed on hardware.

PTQ4DiT asks why standard post-training quantization breaks on Diffusion Transformers and how to fix it without retraining. Its answer: a few input channels carry huge values, activation outliers and weight outliers rarely share a channel, so each channel is rescaled to meet in the middle and choose the calibration timesteps carefully. On DiT-XL/2 for ImageNet, W eight A eight nearly matches full precision, and W four A eight reaches an FID of 7.09 where Q-Diffusion gets 15.31. The tab runs from the big picture and the problem, through the method, every equation and every figure, to the result tables and a thesis box on LTX-2.3 with NNCF. Among the sixteen papers it is the second diffusion-specific quantization paper, after Q-Diffusion and before ViDiT-Q. It borrows the SmoothQuant idea from the language-model group and adapts it to transformers with timesteps.

label: Overview
text: The core trick is to move each extreme to where the other tensor is calm. Magenta marks activation outliers, and weight outliers sit in different channels. A per-channel scale shrinks the loud activation channel and grows the matching weight row, so both end at the geometric mean of their two ranges, here dropping the maxima from about 6 to 2.4 and 5.5 to 2.3. The product stays identical, and the scales are folded into existing layers before quantization. The numbers are a toy example.

label: Problem
text: Two things break plain quantization on DiTs. In panel a, a uniform grid must stretch to cover one salient channel, so at four bits only about two levels are left for the bulk of the values, unless the outlier is clipped. In panel b, the salient activation magnitude climbs toward the end of sampling, so a range calibrated at one timestep clips late steps and wastes resolution early. These are exactly the two problems that channel balancing and timestep-aware calibration address.

label: Method
text: Here the two method steps are worked with toy numbers. On the left, channel-wise salience balancing takes each channel's activation and weight maxima, for example 12 and 1, and moves both to their geometric mean of about 3.5, so the worst channel falls from 12 to 3.5. On the right, the calibration step weights each timestep by the exponential of minus rho, the rank correlation between activation and weight salience. Because rho lies between minus one and one, weights differ by at most about 7.4 times.

label: Method
text: The balancing costs nothing at inference because both scales are folded in offline. The weight scale is multiplied into the linear layer's weight once and stored. The activation scale is pushed into the small MLP that produces the adaLN scale and shift, for the QKV projection and the first feedforward layer, or into the preceding attention matmul for the output projection. The second feedforward layer, after GELU, is left unbalanced. After this step, ordinary integer matmuls run with no new operations.

The recipe has three phases. First, collect statistics: sample 25 or 10 timesteps from the full-precision model's own trajectories, 32 samples each, and record per-channel maxima of activations at every timestep and of weights once. Second, compute the scales: rank-correlate the two, turn the negative correlations into softmax weights over timesteps, average the activation maxima with those weights, then take the geometric mean with the weight maxima. Third, fold the scales in and run a standard Q-Diffusion-style quantizer calibration.

The algorithm is the same pipeline written as five stages. Preparation measures salience per channel, per timestep for activations and once for weights. The Spearman calibration stage decides how much each timestep counts and produces one blended activation salience per channel. Balancing turns that into the two diagonal matrices. Re-parameterization folds them into the weights and the adaLN MLP offline. Quantization then runs on the already balanced tensors, so the deployed model has the same structure and cost as a plain quantized DiT.

This is how a DiT injects the timestep and class. An MLP maps the condition c to two vectors, gamma, a per-channel scale, and beta, a per-channel shift. The adaptive layer norm then normalizes the tokens Z, multiplies each channel by one plus gamma, and adds beta. This matters later because the output of adaLN is the input X to the QKV and feedforward layers, which gives the method a free place to hide its activation scale.

This is the standard uniform b-bit quantizer. Divide x by the step size delta, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point lambda, and clamp the result between zero and two to the power b minus one. The step size is set by the range being covered, so one huge value makes delta coarse for every other value. That is the failure shown in the problem figure, and every later equation is about shrinking the range before this quantizer is applied.

Channel-wise salience balancing in one line. X tilde is the activation matrix multiplied on the right by a diagonal matrix B X, which rescales each input channel column. W tilde is the weight multiplied on the left by a diagonal matrix B W, which rescales the matching weight row. Choosing the two so they cancel keeps the layer output unchanged, as equation twelve shows, while reshaping what the quantizer sees.

Salience is simply the largest absolute value in a channel. For activation channel j, s of X j is the max of the absolute values in that column; for weights, s of W j is the max over row j. The index j runs over the d in input channels. The paper uses the maximum because the range is what sets the quantization step, and the problem figures show the channels with the biggest maxima also carry the biggest error.

The balanced salience of channel j is the geometric mean of its activation salience and its weight salience, the square root of their product. If activations peak at 12 and weights at 1 in that channel, both end up at about 3.5. This is exactly SmoothQuant with alpha equal to one half. It is the target value that the balancing matrices in equations six and seven are built to reach.

The activation balancing matrix is diagonal, with entry j equal to the balanced salience divided by the activation salience of that channel. Where activations are loud, the ratio is below one and the channel is shrunk; where they are quiet, it is above one and the channel is enlarged. After multiplying, every activation channel has maximum equal to its balanced salience from equation five.

The weight balancing matrix mirrors equation six: entry j is the balanced salience divided by the weight salience of channel j. Multiplying the two entries gives s of X j times s of W j over the product of the same, which is exactly one, so the two matrices are inverses. After balancing, activation and weight channel j share the same maximum, the geometric mean. The exact inverse property is proven in equations fifteen and sixteen.

This inequality is the payoff of balancing. The overall salience of a tensor, s sub o, is its largest channel maximum. The larger of the two overall saliences after balancing is never bigger than before. When activation and weight outliers sit in different channels, it is much smaller, because each outlier is paired with a small partner. Since the quantization step follows the overall range, this means finer steps for both tensors at the same bit width.

label: —
text: An unnumbered helper definition. The overall salience of a tensor is the maximum of all its channel saliences, so for X it is the largest value among s of X one up to s of X d in. With per-tensor activation quantization, this single number sets the step size for the whole tensor, which is why one loud channel hurts everyone. Equation eight is stated in terms of it.

Now time enters. For each timestep t, the activation salience vector collects the per-channel maxima s of X j at that step, one entry per input channel. The weight salience vector s of W does the same for weights and does not depend on t, since weights are fixed. These two vectors, compared step by step, are the inputs to the Spearman calibration in equations ten and eleven.

The temporal salience s rho is a weighted average of the per-timestep activation salience vectors. Each timestep t contributes its vector times a weight eta t, and the result is one salience value per input channel. It replaces the single-timestep activation salience in the balancing formula, so the scales work across the whole denoising process rather than being tuned to one step. The weights come from equation eleven.

The timestep weights are a softmax of minus rho. Rho is Spearman's rank correlation between the activation salience vector at step t and the weight salience vector. Low or negative correlation means outliers sit in different channels, so balancing works well, and that timestep gets a larger weight. High correlation means outliers coincide and cannot be cancelled, so that step gets less say. The sum in the denominator just makes the weights add to one.

Balancing is exact in full precision. X tilde times W tilde equals X times B X rho times B W rho times W, and since the two diagonal matrices multiply to the identity, this is just X times W. So the model is mathematically unchanged; only the ranges that the quantizers see are different. Equations fifteen and sixteen spell out the proof.

This shows where the activation scale hides. Instead of an extra multiply, the adaLN output is rewritten: layer norm of Z times B X rho plus gamma tilde, plus beta tilde, where gamma tilde and beta tilde are gamma and beta already multiplied by B X rho. The constant one from equation one simply becomes B X rho. Because gamma and beta come from an MLP, the scaling can be baked into that MLP, as equations eighteen to twenty-one show.

From the appendix, this is the refined balanced salience actually used. It is the same geometric mean as equation five, but the activation salience is now the Spearman-weighted temporal salience s rho from equation ten rather than a value from one timestep. The square root of s rho of channel j times s of W j gives the target range for that channel across all denoising steps.

This is the proof that the refined balancing matrices are exact inverses. Multiplying B X rho and B W rho entry by entry gives, for each channel, the balanced salience squared divided by s rho times s of W. Since the balanced salience is the square root of that same product, each entry equals one and the product is the identity matrix. This makes the equivalence in equation sixteen hold.

The equivalence stated fully. X tilde times W tilde is regrouped as X times the product of the two balancing matrices times W. Equation fifteen showed that product is the identity, so the result is X times W. In words, balancing changes nothing in full precision, and any quality change after quantization comes only from how well the new ranges quantize.

The appendix restates adaLN. The linear layer's input X is the layer norm of the latent tokens Z, multiplied channel-wise by one plus gamma and shifted by beta. Z has n tokens and d in channels. This is the starting point for showing that an activation-side scale can be absorbed upstream instead of being applied as an extra operation.

The scale and shift come from the last layer of the conditioning MLP, which is affine: c times weight matrices W gamma and W beta, plus biases b gamma and b beta. Because it is a linear map plus bias, multiplying its output by a diagonal matrix is the same as multiplying its weights and biases. That is what makes the offline fold in equations twenty and twenty-one possible.

Applying the activation scale to adaLN's output distributes over its three parts. X tilde, which is X times B X rho, equals layer norm of Z times the sum of B X rho and gamma times B X rho, plus beta times B X rho. The constant one becomes B X rho, and gamma and beta are each rescaled. This matches equation thirteen and sets up the weight edit that follows.

The offline edit itself. Multiply the columns of the MLP weights W gamma and W beta, and the biases b gamma and b beta, by the diagonal activation scale B X rho. This is done once before deployment. The next equation checks that the edited MLP now outputs the already scaled gamma and beta.

This verifies the fold. Running the condition c through the edited MLP gives c times the scaled weights plus the scaled biases, which factors into the original MLP output times B X rho, which is gamma and beta each times B X rho. So the modified adaLN produces the balanced activation directly, with no extra multiply at inference. This closes the argument that the method has zero runtime overhead.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: The practical reading for the thesis: the balancing half of PTQ4DiT is SmoothQuant with alpha one half, which NNCF already offers, so a W8A8 run on LTX-2.3 can use it by setting the smooth quant alpha to about 0.5 and checking which MatMuls are smoothed. The timestep half becomes a calibration-set decision: collect transformer inputs from 10 to 25 denoising steps. For weight-only int4, look at NNCF's AWQ and scale estimation instead, and remember the paper covers images, not video with audio.

label: Primer
text: Inside a Diffusion Transformer block, the timestep and the class go through a small network that outputs a scale and a shift for every channel. Adaptive layer norm applies them to the normalised tokens, and the result, called X, is exactly what the quantized linear layer receives. Remember this path: PTQ4DiT later hides its own activation scaling inside that small network, which is why its method adds no cost at inference.

label: Primer
text: A four bit quantizer has only sixteen evenly spaced levels, and they must stretch to cover the largest value. With values near plus or minus one, many levels are used. Add a single value of twelve and the step grows twelve times, so the ordinary values fall on about two levels. W four A eight means four bit weights and eight bit activations, and this loud channel problem is what the whole paper attacks.

label: Primer
text: Spearman's rho compares two lists by their rankings, not their raw values. On the left, the loudest activation channel is also the loudest weight channel, so rho is high and balancing cannot help. On the right, the outliers sit in different channels, so rho is low and one tensor can absorb the other's extreme. PTQ4DiT turns minus rho into a softmax weight for each timestep when it averages activation statistics.

label: Primer
text: PTQ4DiT sits between Q-Diffusion and ViDiT-Q. Q-Diffusion taught us to calibrate diffusion models across many timesteps, but on U-Nets. PTQ4DiT brings quantization to Diffusion Transformers, borrowing SmoothQuant's per-channel scaling with alpha of one half and adding timestep weighting. ViDiT-Q then moves to video transformers, where it replaces static scales with per-token dynamic ones and mixed precision.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important are adaptive layer norm, the timestep-driven scale and shift; salience, the largest value in a channel; W four A eight, the bit setting; and Spearman's rho, a correlation on ranks. For results, FID and sFID are lower is better, while Inception Score and Precision are higher is better. All experiments use DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

ViDiT-Q asks why quantizers that work for language models and image U-Nets fall apart on text-to-video diffusion transformers, and how to fix that. Its answer is that the numbers sharing one scale vary along tokens, the two classifier-free guidance halves, timesteps and channels, so it adds per-token dynamic activation scales, a two-stage channel balancing, and a mixed-precision search judged by the right quality metric per layer group. That gets W eight A eight and W four A eight video and image generation close to FP16 quality, with measured GPU speed-ups. The tab runs from the big picture and the problem, through the method, every equation and every figure, to the result tables and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the third diffusion quantization paper, after Q-Diffusion and PTQ4DiT and before SVDQuant, and the first built for video transformers like LTX.

A single static scale is why naive W4A8 turns video into noise, and ViDiT-Q replaces it with three targeted fixes. Follow the lower path left to right: each token gets its own scale computed on the fly, channels are balanced by a fixed scaling and then a Hadamard rotation, and a metric-aware search puts the most sensitive layers at eight bits. The rest of the tab unpacks each numbered fix in turn.

Quantization error here is mostly rounding error, and one outlier makes it large. The top bar shows min-max scaling: the sixteen four-bit levels must stretch to reach the outlier, so the step s is big and most ordinary values share about three levels. The lower bar shows a smaller, balanced group where the same sixteen levels sit close together. Every fix in the paper is a way to shrink the spread inside a group.

A static tensor-wise scale is really one enormous group, because DiT activations vary along four axes at once. The cube shows tokens and channels, with timesteps stacked behind and the conditional and unconditional guidance halves side by side. The four labels name the variations: between tokens, between guidance halves, across timesteps, and outlier channels whose strength changes with time. Each axis later gets its own remedy in the method section.

Groups must lie along the summation axis of the matrix multiply, otherwise the integer kernel cannot use them. Weights get one scale per output row and activations one scale per token, both spanning C in. Q-DiT's per-input-channel groups are accurate but force floating-point casts inside the sum, so they are slow. Because token scales come from each token's live min and max, they automatically track every timestep and guidance half.

Channel imbalance has a fixed part and a part that changes with the timestep, so ViDiT-Q uses two tools. The adaLN scale-shift table is constant, which a SmoothQuant scale with one alpha, fused into the previous operation, can handle. The timestep embedding adds a moving part, which an online Hadamard rotation spreads evenly. This is the design behind fix number two; the next block shows why both halves are needed.

Scaling and rotation together beat either one alone. The bars show incoherence, roughly the largest weight divided by the average, for one MLP layer: 40.75 originally, 17.77 with static scaling, 12.83 with QuaRot rotation, and 5.02 with ViDiT-Q's static-dynamic combination. With only sixteen levels at four bits, a ratio near thirteen still wastes most levels, so only the combined method is small enough.

This is the part of ViDiT-Q most worth replicating: each layer is judged by the metric it actually damages. Cross-attention is scored by CLIPSIM for text alignment, spatial self-attention and feed-forward by DOVER VQA for visual quality, and temporal attention by FlowScore for motion. Layers compete only within their group, and the whole analysis repeats for four timestep ranges, with group budgets of 5.54, 4.05 and 4.34 bits averaging five bits.

The procedure moves from coarse to fine. First, the method picks one metric per quality aspect and confirms with a heatmap that each layer type mainly hurts one of them. Then, for each timestep range, it splits the total bit budget between groups using a cheap MSE test, ranks layers inside each group with their own metric, and greedily promotes the most sensitive layers from four to eight bits until the group budget is spent.

Two pieces of pseudocode, both reconstructed by the tab because the paper has no algorithm box. Algorithm A is the offline search: reference videos, per-group budgets from MSE, per-layer sensitivity from the group metric, then greedy promotion to eight bits, repeated per time range. Algorithm B is what one quantized linear layer does at run time: fixed scaling, Hadamard rotation, per-token quantization, an integer matrix multiply, and one rescale back to floating point.

The usual quantization objective replaces the real task loss with a simpler proxy. On the left is the task loss between the full-precision network f FP and the quantized network f q. On the right is the sum over all L layers of the squared weight error, W minus Q of W, plus the squared activation error, X minus Q of X. The paper argues this layer-wise proxy is not enough for visual generation, which motivates its metric-decoupled search.

Dequantization maps an integer back to a real value. x hat, the approximation of x, equals the scale s times the integer x int minus the zero point z. The key point is that s and z are shared by every element in the group, so the whole design question is which elements should share them.

Equation two is the b-bit uniform quantizer. Divide x by the step s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point z, then clamp to the range zero to two to the b minus one. Error comes from two places: clamping values that fall outside the range, and rounding the ones inside. The next equation shows that with min-max ranges only rounding is left.

With min-max scaling the step s is the group's maximum minus its minimum, divided by two to the b minus one, so nothing is ever clipped. The rounding error then lies between minus half a step and plus half a step. The takeaway is that error grows directly with the spread inside a group, which is the central claim of the error analysis.

Mu-coherence, borrowed from QuIP, measures how spiky a group is. It says the largest element is at most mu times the group's Frobenius norm divided by the square root of the group size g, which is roughly mu times the average magnitude. A large mu means one value towers over the rest, making the group hard to quantize. The incoherence numbers in figures 3 and 8 are this idea in practice.

Equation three is SmoothQuant channel scaling. The output Y stays the same when the activations X are divided channel by channel by s and the weights W are multiplied by s. Each s i is the activation channel maximum to the power alpha, divided by the weight channel maximum to the power one minus alpha. Alpha decides how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. ViDiT-Q uses this as the static half of its balancing.

Rotation is the other balancing tool, used by QuaRot and SpinQuant. Q is an orthogonal matrix, so Q times Q transpose is the identity, and multiplying X by Q and the weights by Q transpose leaves the output unchanged. The rotation mixes channels, spreading an outlier's energy across many of them. ViDiT-Q uses a Hadamard matrix as Q, applied online as the dynamic half of its balancing.

A small fix to how VBench's dynamic degree is read. The first term is the relative change of the quantized score f Q against the FP16 score f FP. Quantization jitter makes videos look more dynamic, so a higher raw value is not better. The radar chart in figure 10 therefore plots one minus this relative change, so that matching FP16 scores highest.

Each output element y is the sum, over the C in input channels, of weight w i times input x i. Because the integer kernel adds these products directly, all elements in the sum should share quantization parameters. This single line is the reason for the per-output-channel weight and per-token activation grouping in figure 19.

Expanding the quantized product shows why the grouping is hardware friendly. Substitute the dequantized weight and activation, and the main term becomes s w times s x times an integer matrix multiply of W int and x int, followed by one floating-point rescale. The remaining three terms are zero-point corrections that can be precomputed or cheaply added. The integer multiply is where the speed-up comes from.

This turns sensitivity runs into the heatmap of figure 20. For layer type l and metric m, delta is the relative drop, full-precision metric minus quantized metric, divided by the full-precision value. The drops are standardized with a z-score, then a softmax over metrics makes each layer type's column sum to one. The paper describes this in words, so the formula is the tab's reconstruction.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Copy ViDiT-Q's sensitivity method, not its CUDA kernels. Group LTX-2.3's linear layers by role, including the audio branch and audio-video cross-attention, give each group one metric, rank layers by quantizing them to int4 one at a time, then keep the sensitive ones at int8 or in NNCF's ignored scope while compressing the rest with compress weights. Keep the runs cheap with short low-resolution clips, and report memory and latency separately, since weight-only compression on Intel hardware mainly saves memory.

label: Primer
text: Quantizing means rounding every number to one of a few levels, and the range decides how fine those levels are. The scale is set from the smallest and largest value in a group, so one magenta outlier stretches the range and the ordinary teal values share only about four levels. Eight bits give two hundred fifty six levels, four bits only sixteen. W four A eight means four bit weights and eight bit activations.

label: Primer
text: Which numbers share one scale matters as much as the number of bits. On the left, a single static scale covers the whole activation matrix and is fixed in advance from calibration data. On the right, ViDiT-Q gives every token its own scale, measured live at each step, so it adapts to timesteps and guidance passes. Notice the magenta column: per token scales cannot fix an outlier channel, which is why the paper adds channel balancing.

label: Primer
text: A video diffusion transformer runs the same blocks about twenty times, once per denoising step, shown in gold. Frames are cut into patches, and every patch is a token. Each block has spatial attention, temporal attention, cross attention to the text, and a feed forward network. The timestep enters through adaptive layer norm, and classifier free guidance runs every step twice. These are the four sources of variation that ViDiT-Q is designed around.

label: Primer
text: ViDiT-Q follows Q-Diffusion, which handled timesteps in U-Net models, and PTQ4DiT, which moved to image transformers. It is the first method built for text to video transformers. It borrows SmoothQuant style scaling and Hadamard rotation, and adds three pieces in indigo. The metric decoupled mixed precision search is the part to reuse for LTX-2.3 with NNCF. SVDQuant and DVD-Quant come next.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are static versus dynamic quantization, per token and per channel grouping, and channel balancing, because the whole method is built from them. The metric names matter too: CLIPSIM for text match, VQA for visual quality, and FlowScore for motion. Keep in mind that the speed-ups come from custom GPU kernels on an A100, which OpenVINO cannot use.

SVDQuant asks how to make a twelve billion parameter diffusion transformer like FLUX.1 genuinely faster, not just smaller. Its answer is W four A four, four-bit weights and activations, made possible by smoothing activation outliers into the weights and then letting a small sixteen-bit low-rank branch from an SVD absorb the weight outliers, so only a flat residual is quantized. A companion engine, Nunchaku, fuses that branch into the four-bit kernels. The model ends up 3.6 times smaller and about three times faster than weight-only NF4, with better images. The tab runs from big picture and problem through the method, every equation and proof, every figure and the results tables, to a thesis box on OpenVINO. Among the sixteen papers it follows Q-Diffusion, PTQ4DiT and ViDiT-Q, builds on SmoothQuant and GPTQ, and is extended to video by the SVDQuant-GPTQ note on Wan 2.2.

The whole method fits in one picture. Smoothing first divides the activations by a per-channel factor lambda, which pushes their outliers into the weights. A small sixteen bit low-rank branch, L one times L two, then takes over those weight outliers. What is left, the residual R, is flat enough to quantize to four bits, and a four bit GEMM multiplies it with the four bit activations. Every later section explains one part of this diagram.

Two problems motivate the paper. On the left, a single outlier sets the quantization range, so most values fall into only one or two of the sixteen four bit levels. On the right, weight-only four bit saves memory but still runs a sixteen bit multiply, so it gives no speed-up. Real speed needs both weights and activations in four bits, which is why outliers must be handled first.

Proposition 4.1 splits the W4A4 error into four factors: the size of the input, the size of the weight, and the quantization error of each. SVDQuant attacks them in pairs. Smoothing shrinks the input and its quantization error, and replacing W by the small residual R shrinks the weight term. Read this diagram as the reason for each of the method's steps.

Smoothing makes activations easy by pushing their outliers into the weights, and the SVD then pulls the few dominant directions of that harder weight into a small sixteen-bit branch; since smoothing made the spectrum spiky, rank sixteen to thirty-two suffices. Only the flat residual goes to four bits with GPTQ, after a short refinement loop re-balances the split. Nunchaku fuses the branch into the kernels, and a few sensitive layers stay in sixteen bits.

The offline recipe runs once per layer. A small set of COCO prompts serves as calibration data. The method searches the smoothing strength alpha by output error, smooths the weight, takes the top r singular vectors as the sixteen bit branch, and quantizes the residual with GPTQ. It can then repeat the decomposition on what quantization left behind and keep the best result.

This pseudocode is reconstructed from Section 4.2 and Appendix D, since the paper prints no algorithm box. For each candidate migration strength alpha, it smooths the layer, takes a rank r SVD of the smoothed weight, and quantizes the residual. The inner loop re-fits the low-rank part to whatever the quantized residual missed, and the version with the smallest output error on calibration prompts wins. At runtime the layer is just a sixteen-bit path plus a four-bit path, added together.

This is the basic quantizer used throughout the paper. Take a tensor X, divide it by a scale s X, and round to the nearest integer to get the integer tensor Q X. The scale is the largest absolute value in X divided by q max, the largest integer the format allows. One big outlier therefore stretches the scale and wastes levels for every other value, which is the whole problem SVDQuant attacks.

q max is the largest representable magnitude: two to the power k minus one, minus one, for a signed k-bit integer, so seven for INT4, and six for the FP4 format E2M1 used by NVFP4. Multiplying the integers back by the scale gives Q of X, the dequantized tensor. With only seven positive levels at four bits, how the scale is set decides almost everything.

A linear layer multiplies activations X by weights W. In low precision, both are quantized, the integer matrices are multiplied on fast integer hardware, and one final rescale by s X times s W restores the magnitude. The key point is that both operands must be at the same low bit-width to get the speed-up, which is why the paper insists on W4A4 rather than four-bit weights only.

This defines the error the paper tries to shrink: the Frobenius norm, meaning the square root of the sum of squared entries, of the gap between the true output X times W and the quantized output. X has b rows of tokens and m input channels, W maps m inputs to n outputs. Every later equation is a way to bound or reduce this number.

Proposition 4.1 splits the layer error into pieces. The first term is the size of X times the weight quantization error; the second is the activation quantization error times the size of W plus its own error. So the output error stays small only if both X and W are small in magnitude and both quantize well. That is why outliers on either side hurt, and it motivates attacking both.

Smoothing, borrowed from SmoothQuant, divides each input channel of X by a factor lambda i and multiplies the matching row of W by the same factor. X hat times W hat equals X times W exactly, so nothing changes mathematically. What changes is where the outliers live: X hat becomes flat and easy to quantize, while W hat inherits the spikes, the problem seen in Figure 3b.

Here the smoothed weight W hat is split into two parts: L one times L two, a rank r product where L one is m by r and L two is r by n, plus a residual R. With r much smaller than m or n, the low-rank part is cheap to store and run in sixteen bits. The next equation shows why only R then needs quantizing.

Equation five is the SVDQuant layer itself. The output X times W equals X hat times the low-rank part plus X hat times the residual. The first term runs in sixteen bits and carries the outliers; only the second term is quantized, as four-bit X hat times four-bit R. This is the two-path picture from the big-picture diagram.

The cost of the extra branch is m times r plus n times r values, divided by the m times n values of the full weight. For a 3072 by 3072 layer with rank thirty-two that is about 2.1 percent more parameters and compute. The branch is cheap in arithmetic; Figure 6 shows the real cost is memory traffic, which Nunchaku fixes.

Equation six says the error of the whole SVDQuant layer is exactly the plain quantization error of the residual product, X hat times R. The sixteen-bit branch adds no error at all. So the question reduces to making X hat and R easy to quantize, and equation eight then says how to do that for R.

This is a mild regularity assumption for Proposition 4.2: the expected largest entry of R is at most a constant c times the expected Frobenius norm of R. In words, R has no extreme outliers compared with its total energy. The paper checks it for Gaussian entries two blocks down.

Proposition 4.2: under that assumption, the expected quantization error of R is at most c times the square root of the number of entries, divided by q max, times the expected size of R. The practical message is simple: a smaller residual means a smaller four-bit error. Minimising the norm of R is therefore the goal, and the SVD is the optimal tool for it.

For a residual with normally distributed entries, the constant c in equation seven is the square root of log of the number of entries times pi, divided by the number of entries. It shrinks as the matrix grows, so the regularity condition is easy to satisfy for large layers. The proof in Appendix A.2, equations twelve to fourteen, derives this value.

The SVD writes W hat as U times Sigma times V. Keeping the first r columns of U times Sigma gives L one, and the first r rows of V give L two. The Eckart, Young, Mirsky theorem guarantees this truncated SVD is the best possible rank r approximation, so it leaves the smallest residual R, exactly what equation eight asks for.

The size of the residual equals the square root of the sum of the squared singular values from index r plus one onward, while the full weight includes all of them. If the first few singular values sigma i are huge, removing them removes most of the energy. Figure 5 shows smoothing makes W hat exactly like that, which is why rank thirty-two is enough.

This is the smoothing factor for input channel i: the largest activation magnitude in that channel raised to alpha, divided by the largest weight magnitude in that row raised to one minus alpha. Alpha, the migration strength, decides how much difficulty moves from activations to weights. Unlike SmoothQuant, SVDQuant searches alpha per layer to minimise output error measured after the SVD step, using calibration prompts.

This is the appendix restatement of Proposition 4.1, identical to equation four: the layer error is bounded by the size of X times the weight error, plus the activation error times the size of W plus its error. It is repeated here only to set up the proof that follows.

label: proof A.1
text: The proof of Proposition 4.1 uses one trick and two standard inequalities. Add and subtract X times Q of W, split the norm with the triangle inequality, then use the fact that the norm of a product is at most the product of norms. Finally, Q of W is written as W minus its error, and the triangle inequality is applied once more. Nothing here is specific to diffusion models.

This restates equation seven in Appendix A.2: the expected maximum entry of the residual R is at most a constant c times its expected Frobenius norm. It is the no-extreme-outliers assumption on which the residual error bound of Proposition 4.2 rests.

This restates equation eight in Appendix A.2: the expected quantization error of R is bounded by c times the square root of its size, over q max, times its expected norm. The proof block that follows derives it.

label: proof A.2
text: The proof of Proposition 4.2 factors the scale out of the error and bounds each element's rounding error by one step, giving the scale times the square root of the number of entries. The scale is the maximum of R over q max, and the regularity assumption turns that maximum into the norm of R. One step is a loose bound, since rounding error is at most half a step, but the conclusion holds.

For Gaussian entries with standard deviation sigma, the expected largest absolute entry grows only like sigma times the square root of two times log of the number of entries. This is a standard maximal inequality from Massart, and it is the first ingredient for computing the constant c.

The Cauchy, Schwarz inequality gives a lower bound on the Frobenius norm of R: it is at least the sum of absolute entries divided by the square root of the number of entries. This is the second ingredient for the Gaussian constant c.

For a normal entry, the expected absolute value is sigma times the square root of two over pi, the mean of a half-normal distribution. Summing over all entries turns the lower bound from equation thirteen into sigma times the square root of two times the size over pi.

Chaining equations twelve to fourteen shows that the expected maximum of R is at most the Gaussian constant c times the expected norm of R. So the regularity condition of Proposition 4.2 holds for Gaussian residuals, closing the proof that a smaller residual gives a smaller four-bit error.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: This is how one SVDQuant layer would look inside an OpenVINO model. Every piece is a standard operation: a Multiply by one over lambda, two small MatMuls for the low-rank branch, a compressed four bit MatMul for the residual, and an Add. So the layer can be exported without custom ops. What is missing is a W4A4 matrix multiply and a fused kernel, so on Intel hardware the gain would be quality at four bit weights, not speed.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Treat SVDQuant as a quality tool for int4 weight-only or W8A8 on OpenVINO, not a speed-up. The clean experiment is to smooth and split each layer in PyTorch, keep L one and L two in f16, compress only the residual with NNCF, and compare against NNCF int4 with and without lora correction. Calibrate on a few LTX denoising trajectories, and measure the unfused branch overhead on Arc and CPU instead of assuming five to ten percent.

label: Primer
text: Any matrix can be split into a few big directions plus a small leftover, and the singular value decomposition finds the best split. On the left, W equals two thin sixteen bit matrices, L one and L two, plus a residual R. On the right, the singular values are sorted by size: keep the tall ones, and the flat tail becomes R. SVDQuant quantizes only R to four bits, so a spiky spectrum is exactly what it needs.

label: Primer
text: W four A four means four bit weights and four bit activations, and only that combination speeds up the arithmetic. In the top row, weight-only quantization such as NF4 unpacks the weights to sixteen bits before multiplying, so the file shrinks but the math does not. In the bottom row, both inputs are four bit and the multiply runs on four bit hardware. Diffusion models are compute-bound, which is why the paper insists on quantizing activations too.

label: Primer
text: An extra branch that is tiny in arithmetic can still cost time, because every separate GPU program reads its inputs from memory and writes its outputs back. The top row shows three kernels, each making its own trips to memory; in the paper that costs about eighteen percent per step. The bottom row fuses everything into one pass, which is what the Nunchaku engine does. On OpenVINO, check whether this pattern gets fused rather than assuming it.

label: Primer
text: SVDQuant is paper nine in the atlas. It follows ViDiT-Q, which reached eight bit activations on diffusion transformers but broke at four. It borrows smoothing from SmoothQuant and uses GPTQ on the leftover weights, then adds its own idea: a sixteen bit low-rank branch that holds the outliers so they are never rounded. DVD-Quant comes next, and paper twelve later reuses SVDQuant with GPTQ on the Wan two point two video model.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are the singular value decomposition, rank, and smoothing, because together they are the method. W four A four versus weight-only, and compute-bound versus memory-bound, explain why the authors want four bit activations. NF4 and NVFP4 are the four bit formats compared, Nunchaku is their fused engine, and LPIPS, ImageReward and FID are the quality scores in the results.

The question behind DVD-Quant is whether a video diffusion transformer can be quantized to four-bit weights and low-bit activations without any calibration data at all. The answer is yes, on HunyuanVideo with 50 steps: at W four A four, meaning four-bit weights and four-bit activations, it reaches an Imaging Quality of 61.82 against 64.78 for the full-precision model, runs 2.12 times faster on an RTX 4090, and uses 3.68 times less memory. It has three parts: a closed-form weight grid search called BGR, a rotation plus live scaling for activations called ARQ, and a per-step switch between four-bit and eight-bit activations called delta-GBS. The tab moves from the big picture to the two problems, then the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box. It is the tenth of the sixteen papers, in the diffusion quantization group after SVDQuant and before QVGen.

The key move is to throw away the calibration pass. In the top row, usual video post-training quantization runs the model on calibration prompts over all 50 timesteps and freezes one set of scales, which breaks at W4A4 because activation ranges shift from step to step. In the bottom row, DVD-Quant derives weight grids offline from the weights alone and activation scales online from each step's live tensor, with delta-GBS choosing four or eight bits per step. The rest of the tab unpacks these three boxes.

The first problem is on the weight side. Weights follow a bell-shaped distribution, but MinMax spreads its sixteen four-bit levels evenly from the smallest to the largest value. A tiny fraction of extreme weights, about 0.3 percent, pulls the range wide, so outer levels sit nearly empty while the dense centre gets too few levels. BGR, the first part of the method, fixes exactly this by clipping the tails and refining the grid.

The second problem is on the activation side. The curve is the largest activation magnitude across the 50 denoising steps, and the flat line is a single scale fixed from calibration. Wherever the curve rises above the line, values are clipped; wherever it falls below, quantization levels go unused. The shape is illustrative, but the point motivates ARQ, which recomputes scales at every step instead of trusting one static number.

BGR is two nested loops. The outer loop tries progressively tighter clipping bounds on the weights, starting each try from a MinMax grid of the clipped values. The inner loop alternates three closed-form updates: the step size by least squares from equation 4, the zero-point from equation 5, and re-rounding the weights from equation 6, until the error stops improving. The grid with the lowest reconstruction error wins. It needs no gradients and no data, and the output is an ordinary INT4 grid with one scale and zero-point per output row.

Algorithm 1 is BGR written out. It first sets a shrink step equal to the weight range divided by n, then for each i from one to n clips i shrink steps off both tails and builds a MinMax grid on the clipped weights as a starting point. From there it repeats the least-squares step size, the zero-point update and re-rounding, measuring the Frobenius reconstruction error each time, and stops when the improvement falls below epsilon. Across all clipping levels it keeps the step size and zero-point with the smallest error. Everything runs offline on the weights only.

ARQ handles activations in two moves. First, the activation X and the weight W are both multiplied by a Hadamard matrix H, which leaves the layer output unchanged but spreads a few massive outliers across all channels. Second, per-channel scales s j are taken from the current step's rotated activation, so channels that rotation made larger are evened out. The rotated weights are quantized offline with BGR. The paper's real kernels use block-wise scales that match Tensor Core tiles, and all reported results use that variant.

Delta-GBS spends eight bits only when the output is changing fast. The bars track the accumulated relative L1 change of the model output since the last reset. When it crosses the threshold delta, that step runs with eight-bit activations and the counter resets; otherwise it runs at four bits. Early steps change quickly and get mostly A8, later steps drift slowly and get mostly A4, averaging about six bits. The picture is a schematic replay of equation 11 with delta at 0.1.

The pipeline splits into one offline stage and one per-step loop. Offline, every linear weight is rotated by the Hadamard matrix and quantized to INT4 with BGR, and these weights never change again. At each denoising step, the activations are rotated, their block-wise scales are read from the live tensor, and delta-GBS decides whether this step uses four or eight bits. The chosen standard W4A4 or W4A8 kernel then runs and the result is rescaled. No mixed-precision kernel is needed, only a switch between two existing ones.

Equation 1 is ordinary asymmetric quantization, the baseline everything else builds on. Each weight in W is divided element-wise by the step size delta, rounded to the nearest integer, shifted by the zero-point z, and clamped into the range from zero to two to the b minus one, where b is the bit-width. For four bits that range is zero to fifteen. W q is the resulting integer matrix.

Equation 2 goes back from integers to real numbers. The dequantized weight, W hat, is the step size delta times the integer weights W q minus the zero-point z, element by element. The gap between W and W hat is the quantization error that BGR later tries to minimise in equation 3. This is also the form OpenVINO uses when it decompresses INT4 weights at run time.

This is the MinMax recipe for the grid, computed separately for each output row of W. The step size delta is the row's range, max minus min, divided by two to the b minus one, so the levels span exactly the extreme values. The zero-point z is minus the rounded ratio of the minimum to delta, so the smallest weight maps to integer zero. Figure 2 shows why this is wasteful for bell-shaped weights, and BGR uses it only as a starting point.

Equation 3 states what BGR really optimises. Among all choices of step size delta and zero-point z, pick the pair that makes the Frobenius norm of W minus its dequantized version as small as possible, the Frobenius norm being the square root of the sum of squared errors. MinMax does not solve this; it is just a first guess. Equations 4 to 6 give the alternating closed-form updates that approximately solve it.

Equation 4 updates the step size when the integers and zero-point are held fixed. For each row it divides the inner product of W q minus z with the real weights W by the inner product of W q minus z with itself. That is the textbook least-squares fit of a single scale factor, so it has an exact answer with no iteration or gradients. It is the first update in the inner loop of BGR.

Equation 5 updates the zero-point with the new step size delta prime held fixed. The zero-point is temporarily treated as a real number, solved as the average integer value minus the average weight divided by delta prime, then clamped into the valid integer range and rounded. The overlines are printed in the paper without a definition; reading them as row averages is the natural interpretation, not a stated fact. This is the second update in BGR's inner loop.

Equation 6 re-rounds the weights on the updated grid. It is the same formula as equation 1, only with the new step size delta prime and zero-point z prime: divide, round, add the zero-point, clamp to the four-bit range. With new integers in hand, BGR goes back to equation 4 and repeats until the reconstruction error stops falling.

Equation 7 is the clipping step of BGR's outer loop. W c is W with every value below the minimum plus delta l raised to that bound, and every value above the maximum minus delta u lowered to that bound. Delta l and delta u are the lower and upper shrink amounts. Cutting off the rare extreme weights lets the sixteen levels concentrate on the dense centre shown in figure 2.

Equation 8 is simply MinMax applied to the clipped weights W c. Delta c is the clipped range divided by two to the b minus one, and z c is the matching zero-point. This grid is the starting point that the inner loop of Algorithm 1 refines with equations 4 to 6, one start per clipping level.

Equation 9 shows what earlier video quantization methods do, borrowed from SmoothQuant. Each input channel of X is divided by a scale s i and the matching weight row is multiplied by it, so the product is unchanged but activation outliers move into the weights. The scale mixes the largest activation and the largest weight with a migration strength alpha. The catch is that the activation maximum comes from a calibration set and stays fixed, which is exactly what figure 3 shows failing across timesteps.

This block states the rotation trick ARQ relies on. An orthogonal matrix Q times its transpose gives the identity, so inserting a Hadamard matrix H and its transpose between the activation X and the weights leaves the output Y unchanged: X times W transpose equals X H times H transpose W. The paper also prints a determinant-style condition that looks garbled, so treat that part loosely. The useful fact is that rotation is free in exact arithmetic and spreads outliers before quantization.

Equation 10 is ARQ in full. The activation is rotated, X tilde equals X H, and each channel's scale s j is its largest absolute value in the current tensor; lambda is the diagonal matrix of those scales. The quantized activation X hat is the rotated activation divided by lambda and then quantized, while the weights are rotated and quantized with BGR. The output multiplies X hat, lambda and W hat transpose. Because the scales come from the live tensor, no calibration set is needed.

This line comes from the middle panel of figure 2 and makes one point: the scale matrix lambda depends on the timestep. The output at the first step uses lambda at t zero, the output at the last step uses lambda at t forty-nine, and each lambda t is a diagonal of per-channel scales computed at that step. It is the equation form of the drifting curve in figure 3, and the reason ARQ recomputes scales online.

Equation 11 is the delta-GBS rule. For each step t i, add up the relative L1 change of the model output, the size of the output difference between consecutive steps divided by the size of the previous output, over all steps since the last reset t p. If that sum is below the threshold delta, use b low, four bits; if it reaches delta, use b high, eight bits, and reset. F t is the model output at step t. Figure 6 and figure 2 show it in action.

Table 3 removes one component at a time to show both are needed. Each row ticks whether BGR, ARQ, or both are used, at W4A6 and at W4A4. With both, Imaging Quality is 61.93 at W4A6 and 58.93 at W4A4, the best in every column. Dropping ARQ hurts most at W4A4, where Aesthetic Quality falls to 43.26. Note that the W4A4 full-method score here is lower than the 61.82 in Table 1, so the ablation setup seems to differ slightly.

Quantization and caching stack. Here DVD-Quant is combined with TeaCache, which skips denoising steps whose output barely changes. The total speed-up reaches 4.01 times at W4A8 and 4.85 times at W4A4, with Imaging Quality of 62.96 and 58.20. For the thesis this is a useful precedent: weight compression and step caching are complementary on a video transformer.
