section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Take BGR into the thesis and treat the rest as ideas to test. BGR produces an ordinary INT4 grid, one scale and zero-point per row, which OpenVINO already decompresses, so it can be computed in PyTorch with Algorithm 1, extend it to NNCF-style groups of 64 or 128, write it into the compressed weights, and compare it with NNCF's data-aware options without spending CPU hours on calibration. ARQ needs INT4 activation kernels and a fast Hadamard op that OpenVINO lacks; its closest built-in match is dynamic INT8 activation quantization. Delta-GBS would need two compiled model variants, but its signal could also drive TeaCache-style step skipping.

label: Primer
text: Every quantizer needs a scale for each tensor, and the two kinds of tensor behave very differently. Weights never change, so their grid can be computed once, offline, from the weights alone. On the right, the bars are activation ranges across the denoising steps. A single calibrated scale, the dashed line, clips the tall steps and wastes levels on the short ones. DVD-Quant measures a fresh scale at every step, which is why it needs no calibration data.

label: Primer
text: A four bit grid is just sixteen evenly spaced levels, stored as the integers zero to fifteen. The step size is the gap between levels and the zero-point says which level means zero. Weights are bell shaped, so the MinMax grid on top wastes levels on a few rare extremes. Clipping the tails, bottom row, packs the same sixteen levels where the weights really are. BGR, the paper's weight method, searches for the best clip and then refines the grid.

label: Primer
text: One huge activation forces a wide range, and then every small value is rounded coarsely. Multiplying the activations by a Hadamard matrix, a grid of plus ones and minus ones, and the weights by its transpose, leaves the layer output exactly the same. But the spike is now shared across all eight channels, so a narrow range is enough. ARQ, the activation method, starts with this rotation and then adds a live scale per channel. The numbers here are illustrative.

label: Primer
text: This map places DVD-Quant in the atlas. ViDiT-Q already used live per-token scales for video but still chose bit-widths with calibration, and SVDQuant reached four bit weights and activations on images with a sixteen bit side branch. DVD-Quant removes calibration completely and reaches W four A four on video with plain low-bit kernels. SmoothQuant is one of its baselines, its bit switching uses the same kind of step-change signal as TeaCache, and QVGen, next, adds training.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. The most important are calibration data, which DVD-Quant avoids, and the step size and zero-point, which define every grid it builds. Hadamard matrix and online scaling are the two halves of ARQ. The hardware and benchmark entries matter for reading the results: all speed numbers come from an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with custom Tensor Core kernels, and quality is measured with VBench.

QVGen asks whether a video diffusion transformer can be squeezed to four bits, or even three, for both weights and activations without the videos falling apart. Its answer is yes at four bits, through quantization-aware training plus a temporary low-rank helper that absorbs quantization error during training and is then faded out completely, so the shipped model is a plain W four A four network that scores close to BF16 on VBench. The tab moves from a big-picture diagram to the problem, the method and algorithm, every equation including the proofs, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the training-based member of the diffusion quantization group, after Q-Diffusion, PTQ4DiT, ViDiT-Q, SVDQuant and DVD-Quant, and just before the SVDQuant with GPTQ study on Wan 2.2. For the thesis it marks the floor: even with expensive training, four bits is the limit.

Read left to right as three stages. On the left, naive four-bit training suffers large quantization error and spiky gradient norms, and the video breaks. In the middle, QVGen adds a low-rank helper called phi next to each layer, which calms the gradients, while its rank is halved from 32 down to nothing. On the right, the deployed model is ordinary W four A four with zero overhead, about four times smaller and 1.21 to 1.44 times faster.

Video is harder to train in low bits than images. The left bars compare the average gradient norm during four-bit Q-DM training on two models of the same two-billion size: about 0.33 for the CogVideoX video model against about 0.20 for the SD3 image model. The right bars show high-motion training clips give the largest norm. Because the theory later says large gradient norms slow convergence, this is the problem QVGen sets out to fix.

The helper phi cannot stay in the final model. At inference it would need a second matrix multiply in FP16 beside the fast INT4 one, and its full-rank FP16 weight would take far more memory than the four-bit weight itself. That would defeat the point of quantizing. This is why the method needs the rank-decay schedule: phi must help during training and then disappear before deployment.

The recipe has two halves. First, set up four-bit fake quantization and attach a helper to every linear layer that starts out equal to the weight's rounding error, compressed by SVD into two thin rank-32 matrices. Second, train by distillation from the BF16 teacher while repeatedly fading the weakest half of the helper's components, cutting them off, and re-factorising: rank 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, then zero. What remains is a plain low-bit model.

The algorithm is one outer loop wrapped around ordinary training. First, the model is quantized and each helper starts as the quantization error. Each pass of the outer loop factorises the helpers at the current rank, builds the mask gamma, runs a fixed number of distillation steps while the weakest half fades out, then truncates and halves the rank. When the rank is tiny, a last phase fades everything, so the returned model has no helper left.

This is the forward noising step of diffusion. x tau, the noisy latent video at timestep tau, equals alpha tau times the clean latent x zero plus sigma tau times Gaussian noise epsilon. Alpha and sigma set how much signal versus noise remains at that step. QVGen uses it in the training loop to create noisy inputs that both the teacher and the quantized student must denoise.

This is the standard training loss for a diffusion model. The network epsilon theta sees the noisy video, the text condition C and the timestep tau, and tries to predict the noise that was added; the loss is the expected squared difference. QVGen does not train with this directly. It replaces the true noise with the teacher's prediction in equation 6, a distillation version of the same idea.

Here is the basic object being compressed: one linear layer. In full precision the output Y is the weight matrix W times the input X. In the quantized version, Y hat is the quantized weight times the quantized input, both at b bits. The gap between Y and Y hat is the quantization error, and every later equation is about keeping that gap from spoiling training and the final video.

This is the quantizer itself: asymmetric uniform min-max quantization. The step size s is the value range divided by two to the b minus one levels, and the zero-point z shifts the grid so the minimum maps to zero. Each value is divided by s, rounded, shifted by z, clipped to the allowed integer range, then mapped back. It is exactly the INT asymmetric format OpenVINO and NNCF use, so nothing exotic is needed on the thesis side.

Rounding has zero gradient almost everywhere, so training through it needs a trick: the straight-through estimator. The derivative of the quantizer is simply taken as one when the scaled value falls inside the clipping range and zero when it is clipped. This lets gradients reach the weights and the learned scales during quantization-aware training, and the gradient norms the paper worries about are measured through this path.

This is the loss QVGen actually trains with, a knowledge distillation loss. The quantized student, epsilon hat, and the full-precision teacher, epsilon theta, see the same noisy video, condition and timestep, and the loss is the squared difference of their outputs. The student therefore learns to copy the BF16 model rather than fit raw data, which is the usual choice in diffusion quantization-aware training such as Q-DM and EfficientDM.

Regret is the yardstick for the convergence theory. R of T sums, over T training iterations, how much worse the loss at the current parameters theta t is than the loss at the best fixed parameters theta star. If average regret, R of T divided by T, goes to zero, training is converging. Theorem 3.1 bounds exactly this quantity.

This is plain gradient descent. The next parameters theta t plus one equal the current parameters minus the learning rate eta t times the gradient g t. It is the update rule assumed in the convergence analysis, and it is why the size of g t appears in the bound that follows.

label: (Thm 3.1)
text: Theorem 3.1 is the paper's key theoretical motivation. Average regret is at most two terms: the first shrinks as training length T grows, and the second is the average over iterations of the learning rate times the squared gradient norm. So after long training, convergence is governed by how large the gradients are. The takeaway is simple: shrink the gradient norm and quantization-aware training converges better, which the helper phi is designed to do.

This introduces the helper. The quantized layer's output becomes the usual quantized weight times quantized input, plus phi applied to the quantized input, where phi is just an extra full-precision weight W phi times that input. W phi starts as the weight's rounding error, W minus its quantized version, so at the start the layer behaves almost like full precision. That softer start is what lowers the gradient norm.

This is the singular value decomposition of the helper weight. W phi is written as a sum of d rank-one pieces, each a singular value sigma s times an outer product of vectors u s and v s, sorted from largest to smallest sigma. Figure 4 shows most sigmas are tiny and get tinier during training. That observation is what makes it safe to keep only the top few and later discard them.

The helper is stored in factorised form: phi equals L times R times the quantized input. L collects the top r left singular vectors and R the top r right ones, each scaled by the square root of its singular value. With r equal to 32, far below the full dimension, the helper is cheap. Column s of L carries the s-th strongest direction, which lets the next equations fade the weakest columns first.

This is the training-time forward pass with the rank regularizer. It is the same layer as before, except L is multiplied element by element by the mask gamma before being combined with R. Gamma lets training gradually switch off selected columns of L, so the helper's contribution shrinks smoothly instead of vanishing abruptly. Equation 13 defines what gamma looks like.

Gamma is built from two blocks. The first one minus lambda times r columns are all ones, keeping the strongest components untouched. The last lambda times r columns are set to u, a number annealed from one to zero with a cosine schedule. With lambda equal to one half, the weakest half of the helper fades out during each phase while the model learns to compensate.

Once u reaches zero, the faded columns are removed for real. L prime keeps only the first one minus lambda times r columns of L, and R prime the matching rows of R, and their product becomes the new, smaller helper weight. The rank halves, from 32 to 16 and so on. The loop then re-factorises and repeats until the rank is zero and phi no longer exists.

label: (A)
text: The appendix proof of Theorem 3.1 starts here. This is gradient descent written for one single entry p of the parameter vector, with its own learning rate eta t p and gradient g t p. Working entry by entry lets the proof handle adaptive, per-parameter learning rates like those in AdamW.

label: (B)
text: The proof now measures how far one parameter entry is from its optimum. Squaring the distance after one update and expanding gives three parts: the old squared distance, minus a cross term of two times distance times learning rate times gradient, plus the learning rate squared times the gradient squared. That last term is where the gradient norm enters the bound.

label: (C)
text: Rearranging the previous expansion isolates the gradient times the distance to the optimum. It equals the drop in squared distance over one step, divided by two times the learning rate, plus half the learning rate times the gradient squared. The first part will telescope across iterations; the second is the gradient-norm penalty that survives into Theorem 3.1.

label: (D)
text: This is where convexity is used. For a convex loss, the gap between the current loss and the optimal loss is at most the gradient dotted with the distance to the optimum. It links regret to the expression rearranged in the previous step. It is an idealising assumption: real diffusion training is not convex, which is why Appendix C repeats the argument without it.

label: (E)
text: Summing over all parameter entries and all iterations bounds the total regret. The distance terms telescope, meaning consecutive terms cancel, leaving the starting distance, a correction for changing learning rates, and the accumulated sum of learning rate times gradient squared. The gradient sum is untouched by the telescoping, which is why it ends up dominating.

label: (F)
text: Assuming parameters stay in a bounded region, every distance to the optimum is replaced by the largest possible distance, D infinity. Now the first two terms depend only on the learning rates and the problem size, while the last term is still the sum of learning rate times squared gradient. That split is exactly the shape of Theorem 3.1.

label: (G)
text: To tidy up, every per-entry learning rate is replaced by the smallest rate at the end, eta T m, in the first term, and by the largest rate at each step, eta t M, in the gradient term. The result is a compact bound: a constant depending on dimension d and distance D, plus the sum of the maximum learning rate times the squared gradient norm.

label: (H)
text: Dividing by T gives average regret and completes the proof; this line is Theorem 3.1 itself. The first term fades like one over T, so for long training the average squared gradient norm is what limits convergence. This is the formal reason QVGen adds the helper phi: it lowers the gradient norm, as Figure 3 then confirms empirically.

label: (I)
text: Appendix C redoes the analysis without assuming convexity. Here the objective is a single fixed function F, and the update is ordinary gradient descent, with g t defined as the gradient of F at the current parameters. This setting is closer to real deep-network training and checks that the gradient-norm argument does not depend on the convexity idealisation.

label: (J)
text: This is the L-smoothness assumption. The gradient cannot change faster than a constant L times the distance between two parameter points. Careful with the letter: this L is a smoothness constant, not the low-rank matrix L from the method. Smoothness is the standard condition that makes a small gradient step reliably reduce the loss.

label: (K)
text: This descent inequality is an equivalent form of smoothness. The loss at a new point is at most the loss at the old point, plus the gradient dotted with the step, plus L over two times the squared step length. It upper-bounds the loss with a simple bowl-shaped curve, which the proof uses to show every gradient step makes progress.

label: (L)
text: This assumption keeps learning rates in a safe range. Every learning rate eta t lies between a positive minimum eta m and a maximum eta M, and the maximum is at most one over the smoothness constant L. Rates that are too large could overshoot, so this cap guarantees each gradient step actually lowers the loss.

label: (M)
text: Theorem C.4 is the non-convex counterpart of Theorem 3.1. The average squared gradient norm over T steps is at most two times the gap between the starting loss and the best possible loss, divided by T times the minimum learning rate. So it falls like one over T. The paper reads it the same way: smaller gradient norms mean a tighter bound after a finite number of steps.

label: (N)
text: The smallest squared gradient norm seen during training is no larger than the average, and the average goes to zero as training gets longer. So training reaches a first-order stationary point, a place where the gradient vanishes. This is the standard convergence guarantee for non-convex optimisation, restated here to support the paper's gradient-norm focus.

label: (O)
text: The proof of Theorem C.4 begins by plugging the gradient descent step into the descent inequality. After simplifying, the new loss is at most the old loss minus eta t times one minus L eta t over two, times the squared gradient norm. In words, each step lowers the loss by an amount proportional to the squared gradient, as long as the learning rate is not too large.

label: (P)
text: Because the learning rate is capped at one over L, the factor one minus L eta over two is at least one half. So each step lowers the loss by at least half the learning rate times the squared gradient norm. It is a clean per-step guarantee of progress that the next line adds up over all of training.

label: (Q)
text: Summing the per-step decrease over all T steps makes the intermediate losses cancel, a telescoping sum. The total of half the learning rate times squared gradient norm is at most the starting loss minus the lowest achievable loss, F star. The loss cannot drop forever, so the gradients cannot stay large forever.

label: (R)
text: Replacing each learning rate by its minimum and dividing by T turns the previous sum into an average. The average squared gradient norm is at most two times the loss gap divided by T times the minimum learning rate. This line proves Theorem C.4, the statement shown earlier as equation M.

label: (S)
text: This closes the non-convex proof. The minimum squared gradient norm is bounded by the average, which is bounded by a quantity that shrinks like one over T, so it tends to zero. Remark C.5 draws the practical link: in both the convex and non-convex settings, lowering the gradient norm tightens the finite-time bound, which justifies the helper phi.

label: (T)
text: This is one of the alternative ways to remove the helper that the paper compares against, called residual quantization. W phi is written as a four-bit copy of itself plus four-bit copies of successive leftover errors E one, E two and E three, and one term is dropped per phase. Table N shows it scores below rank decay and costs about 2.6 times the GPU time.

label: (U)
text: This defines the throughput figure in Table R. For a matrix product of sizes M by K and K by N, the number of operations is two times M times N times K; dividing by the measured INT4 GEMM time and by ten to the twelfth gives tera-operations per second. It shows how close the kernel gets to hardware peak, separate from quantize and dequantize overhead.

label: (V)
text: This Amdahl-style formula projects speed-up if the quantize and dequantize steps were fused into the matrix multiply. G is the fraction of time spent in the GEMM, and r is the fraction of the remaining non-GEMM time that fusion removes. With r at 0.6 the paper projects about 1.18 to 1.38 times, and with r near 0.8 about 1.25 to 1.57 times. Kernel engineering, not only bit width, sets the real speed-up.

text: Each row is three frames of one prompt and seed on CogVideoX two B, a girl in a war-torn city. The top row is BF16 and the second is QVGen at four-bit weights and activations, which keeps the same girl, ruins and detail. label: Fig. 2

This table covers the large models, CogVideoX 1.5 five B and Wan fourteen B, and only QVGen is run. At four bits most scores sit near BF16, for example an overall consistency of 25.70 against 26.17 on Wan fourteen B, although scene consistency drops noticeably. The component ablation on Wan 1.3B at four bits. Naive is plain distillation training; plus phi adds the helper and keeps it; plus rank adds the rank-decay that removes it. Adding phi lifts every score, with overall consistency going from 21.63 to 22.98. Removing phi through rank decay costs almost nothing, 23.01 overall. So the benefit survives even after the helper is gone, which is the whole point of the design.

This ablation varies the shrinking ratio lambda, the fraction of the helper's rank removed in each phase. One quarter, one half and three quarters all perform similarly, with one half slightly best at 23.01 overall consistency. Lambda equal to one, removing everything in a single phase, drops to 21.81, almost back to the naive baseline. Gradual removal matters.

This ablation varies the helper's starting rank r, where zero means no helper. Any helper helps: rank 8 already lifts overall consistency from 21.63 to 22.81. Gains flatten around rank 16 to 32, and rank 64 brings nothing more. Rank 32 is chosen, consistent with Figure 4's finding that only a few singular directions matter.

This table compares ways of removing the helper. Linear simply scales all of it down, sparse variants prune entries, with Wanda and MaskLLM as smarter pruning criteria, and residual quantization peels off quantized layers of it. Rank decay wins on every column, 23.01 overall versus at most 22.57 for the others, while the pruning methods also need 1.8 to 2.1 times the training time. Removing whole weak singular directions is both better and cheaper.

Two line charts summarise Tables 4 and 5. On the left, overall consistency against the shrinking ratio lambda peaks at one half and falls sharply at one, where the helper is removed in one shot. On the right, against starting rank, the score climbs from 21.63 with no helper and plateaus from rank 16 to 32. Both defaults sit at the sweet spot.

Training cost on H100 GPUs for the four training methods on the two small models: GPU-days and memory per GPU. QVGen costs about 9.4 and 11.1 GPU-days, only about two percent more time and one percent more memory than Q-DM. The helper is cheap to train with. Still, around ten GPU-days per small model is far beyond a bachelor thesis project, which the thesis box stresses.

Total GPU-days of QVGen per model, with the extra cost over plain distillation training in brackets. The small models need about 9 to 11 GPU-days, only 0.14 to 0.18 more than naive training. The large models need about 51 days for CogVideoX five B and about 182 for Wan fourteen B. For a model the size of LTX-2.3, full quantization-aware training is out of reach, which is why the thesis leans on post-training quantization.

A milder setting: six-bit weights and activations on Wan 1.3B. Here every method is close to BF16, and QVGen scores highest on most columns, even slightly above full precision on overall consistency, 25.53 versus 24.67. The point is that QVGen does not only rescue extreme bit widths; it also holds up where the others already work. At six bits the choice of method matters much less.

This is the numeric source of the left bars in the problem figure. Both models have two billion parameters and use the same four-bit Q-DM training recipe for two thousand steps. The video model's average gradient norm, 0.3283, is about 1.6 times the image model's 0.2047. That is the paper's evidence that video quantization-aware training is intrinsically harder to converge.

This table trains four-bit QVGen on CogVideoX two B with eight thousand clips of high motion, low motion, or half of each. High-motion data gives the largest gradient norm, 0.1972, and the lowest imaging quality, but the highest dynamic degree. The mixed set balances both. Motion makes training harder, which is why the paper uses mixed data.

An obvious alternative to the helper is simply clipping gradients to keep them small. This table tests it on Wan 1.3B at four bits, where a threshold of 1.0 is the Q-DM baseline. Clipping at 0.5 changes almost nothing, and 0.1 makes things worse. So artificially capping gradients is no substitute; the gradient norm has to come down because the model is easier to fit, which is what phi achieves.

This table combines QVGen with SVDQuant, the post-training method that keeps a permanent low-rank branch in high precision. SVDQuant alone at four bits reaches 21.91 overall consistency, QVGen alone 23.01, and the two together 23.89, the best. Freezing the diffusion weights and training only the other parts, marked by a heart, loses most of that gain. The two ideas are complementary, though keeping a branch means some inference overhead.

Instead of VBench quality, this table measures how closely the four-bit videos match the BF16 videos from the same seed, using PSNR and SSIM, where higher is better, and LPIPS, where lower is better. QVGen is far ahead on both models, for example a PSNR of 16.74 against about 12 for the baselines on CogVideoX. This fidelity check is cheap and easy to reuse when comparing int8, int4 and mixed-precision LTX variants.

Handle this table with caution. It is meant to compare methods at four bits on CogVideoX 1.5 five B, but its rows repeat numbers from the decay-strategy ablation, and two baselines are identical. The tab transcribes it as printed and flags it as a likely typesetting error in the paper, so do not draw conclusions from it.

This ablation swaps the curve that fades u from one to zero: cosine, logarithmic, exponential, square or linear. All five land within a fraction of a point of each other, with cosine slightly best on overall consistency at 23.01. The method is robust to this detail; what matters is that the fade is gradual, not its exact shape.

This table tests how the helper weight is initialised on both small models. Starting from the rounding error W minus its quantized version, or from a layer-wise pre-trained helper, gives the same results. Zero initialisation is only slightly worse. Random initialisation is disastrous, with overall consistency falling to about 11 or 10. A sensible starting point is essential, and the error-based one is free.

This is the full eight-column version of the component ablation, with one extra row: minus decay, where the rank-32 helper is kept and never removed. Minus decay scores almost the same as plus phi, so rank 32 captures what a full helper does. Plus rank, which removes it, matches minus decay, 23.01 versus 23.03. Removing the helper is essentially free, so the deployed model loses nothing by shipping without it.

The complete shrinking-ratio results across all eight VBench columns. They confirm the short Table 4: lambda of one half is best or tied on most columns, and lambda of one, removing the helper at once, is worst almost everywhere, with subject consistency dropping to 90.04. Gradual halving is the safe choice.

The complete initial-rank results across all eight columns. Rank 32 is best or near best everywhere; rank 64 matches on scene consistency but slips elsewhere, and the no-helper row, rank zero, is clearly worst. It backs the short Table 5: a modest rank is enough because the helper's useful information is concentrated in a few directions.

The complete decay-strategy comparison across all eight columns, for sparse pruning, residual quantization and rank decay. Rank decay leads on every column. The caption adds the cost side: sparse needs 1.81 times and residual quantization 2.60 times the GPU-days of rank decay. It is both better and cheaper.

This ablation asks which helper components should be faded. Fading the smallest singular directions, the paper's choice, gives 23.01 overall consistency. Fading random directions, averaged over three runs, gives about 21.9, and fading the largest directions gives 22.24. The ordering from the SVD matters: dropping the weakest directions first lets the model absorb their loss gently.

This table varies how long each decay phase lasts, from three quarters of an epoch to one and a half epochs, on Wan 1.3B at four bits. All three settings score within a few hundredths of each other. The schedule is not sensitive to phase length, so the shortest option, three quarters of an epoch, is kept as the cheapest.

QVGen applied to an image model, SD3-medium, at four bits, scored with FID, where lower is better, CLIP score and GenEval. QVGen reaches an FID of 12.24 against 11.92 for full precision, clearly better than the baselines at 13.8 to 15.2, while matching on CLIP and GenEval. The method is not video-specific; it generalises to image diffusion transformers.

This profiles each quantized linear layer shape of Wan 1.3B on an A800: time for quantizing activations, the INT4 matrix multiply, and dequantizing, plus the achieved throughput. Quantize and dequantize together take roughly a quarter to nearly half of each operation's time because they are not fused into the multiply. This overhead explains why the end-to-end speed-up in Figure 6 is modest, and equation V projects what fusion could gain.

The time breakdown of one Wan 1.3B transformer block in PyTorch on an A800. Attention takes 51.8 percent, linear projections 24.5 percent, and everything else 23.7 percent. Since QVGen only quantizes the linear layers, at most about a quarter of the block's time can speed up. For LTX-2.3 on Intel hardware, it is a reminder that attention, not the linears, often dominates, so caching or sparse attention may matter more.

The linear-projection share from Table S, split by layer type in milliseconds. The feed-forward up and down projections dominate, at about 5.3 and 3.9 milliseconds, while the attention projections are under one millisecond and the cross-attention key and value projections almost free. If only some layers get the most aggressive compression, the feed-forward layers are where it pays off.

The attention share from Table S, split in milliseconds. Self-attention over the long video token sequence takes about 31.5 milliseconds, while cross-attention to the text is about 0.6. Self-attention is the single biggest cost in the block, and quantizing linear layers does nothing for it. That is why the paper pairs quantization with sparse attention.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Treat QVGen as a boundary, not a recipe. Full training costs 11 to 182 GPU-days, so for LTX-2.3 use post-training compression and do not aim below four-bit weights. Use NNCF weight-only compression, INT8 or group-wise INT4 asymmetric, with activations in FP16 or at most INT8, since Figure B shows four-bit activations destroy video. Try data-aware options like LoRA correction or AWQ with a small calibration set, expect memory savings more than speed, and reuse its VBench plus PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS protocol.

label: Primer
text: Two ways to get a low-bit model. The top row is post-training quantization: the weights stay frozen and only the scales are chosen from a few samples, which takes hours. The bottom row is quantization-aware training: the rounding is simulated in every forward pass and the weights are updated to cope with it, which takes GPU-days. Every earlier quantization paper in the atlas used the top row. QVGen uses the bottom one.

label: Primer
text: Rounding has no useful slope, so how can training pass through it? The left plot is the forward pass: a staircase, flat almost everywhere, next to the dashed ideal line. The right plot is what the straight-through estimator uses in the backward pass instead: a slope of one inside the clipping range and zero outside. This is equation five of the paper, and its noise helps explain the spiky gradients QVGen sets out to calm.

label: Primer
text: A big matrix can often be rebuilt from two thin ones. On the left, W is approximated by a tall matrix L times a short matrix R, with a small inner size called the rank. On the right, singular value decomposition sorts the pieces by importance: keep the tall bars, drop the tiny ones. QVGen's helper starts as the rounding error at rank thirty-two and is shrunk by halving the rank until nothing is left.

label: Primer
text: The map shows QVGen's neighbours in the atlas. SVDQuant kept a low-rank high-precision branch at inference, and DVD-Quant pushed post-training quantization on video. QVGen is the first training-based method here: it retrains the weights at four and three bits and uses a helper branch only during training, so the final model is plain W four A four. Next, the SVDQuant with GPTQ study returns to post-training quantization on Wan 2.2.

These are the words the paper takes for granted. The most important are quantization-aware training versus post-training quantization, the straight-through estimator, knowledge distillation from a full-precision teacher, and the gradient norm, which the paper's theory links to convergence. SVD and rank describe the helper branch. The rest names the baselines, the CogVideoX and Wan models, the VBench benchmark, and the H100 and A800 GPUs used for training and timing.

Can a fourteen billion parameter per expert video diffusion transformer, Wan 2.2 image to video, run with four bit weights and four bit activations, called W four A four, without retraining? The answer is yes for quality and memory: combining an SVDQuant low-rank branch, GPTQ rounding and a clip ratio looked up per timestep bin cuts peak memory by 59 percent for a VBench drop of under one percent, but it runs 1.8 times slower because the H100 had no fused FP4 kernel. The tab moves from the big picture, to the three problems of outliers, timestep drift and two experts, then the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it is the last of the diffusion quantization group, after QVGen, stitching GPTQ, SVDQuant and timestep-aware calibration together on a large video model, which makes it the closest analogue to the LTX-2.3 project.

Three known tools are stacked on every linear layer, and only one of them touches inference. Read the top lane as offline work done once: smooth the weight, split it into a sixteen bit low-rank part and a four bit GPTQ residual, then search a clip ratio rho for every expert, layer and timestep bin. The bottom lane is each denoising step, where the step number picks a bin and a lookup table supplies the activation scale. Everything later in the tab zooms into one of these boxes.

Four bits give only sixteen levels, so one extreme channel decides the step size for everyone. The grid spans plus or minus alpha to cover the outlier, and the bulk of normal values ends up sharing just two or three codes. This is the first problem the paper names, and it is the reason for the smoothing and low-rank branch in equations five and six.

The activation range shrinks as denoising proceeds, so no single clipping threshold fits every step. The flat line is one global alpha: it over-clips the wide early steps and wastes levels on the narrow late ones. The indigo staircase is a separate alpha per timestep bin, which tracks the drift. This is the second problem, and it motivates the per-bin clip search in equations eight to ten.

Wan 2.2 has two experts, and the low-noise one that paints texture is more fragile than the high-noise one that sets layout. The bars compare peak cosine error in the attention output projection, roughly 0.0065 against 0.011, read approximately from Figure 4. The third problem follows: one calibration policy for both experts ignores this gap, so the paper searches clip ratios separately per expert.

The method runs in two phases. Offline, each layer is first smoothed so activation outliers move into the weight, then the weight is split into a high precision low-rank part and a residual, and that residual is rounded to four bits with GPTQ instead of plain rounding. Next the denoising trajectory is cut into a few bins per expert, and for every layer and bin a clip ratio is chosen by comparing outputs against BF16. At inference the current step simply picks its bin and fetches the stored scale.

The clip ratio is found by brute-force grid search, not by training. For one layer and one bin, calibration samples go through the BF16 layer as a reference, then through the fully quantized layer once per candidate rho, and the rho with the smallest squared output error is written to the table. In the reported model almost every choice lands on 0.8 or 0.9. The paper has no algorithm box, so this loop is drawn from its section three C.

The procedure is a loop over the two experts, then over their layers. For each layer the weight work happens once: smooth, split by SVD, and round the residual with GPTQ. Only then does the inner loop over timestep bins run, measuring a reference activation magnitude and picking the best clip ratio, which becomes a stored scale. The final line is inference, where the bin lookup and equation eleven are all that remain. This listing is transcribed from the text, since the paper gives no algorithm box.

The starting point is an ordinary linear layer. Y equals X times W, where X holds N tokens with C in input channels, and W maps those to C out output channels. Every projection in the transformer, the query, key, value and output projections and the feed-forward layers, has this form, so it is the object all later equations quantize.

Quantized inference replaces both factors with four bit versions. Y hat is Q A of X times Q W of W, where Q A is the activation quantizer and Q W the weight quantizer. The goal of post-training quantization is to keep Y hat close to Y on calibration data without any retraining. The rest of the method is about making these two quantizers lose as little as possible.

This is the basic quantize then dequantize step. Divide the value z by the scale s, round to the nearest integer, add the zero point z zero, clip to the integer range from q min to q max, then subtract the zero point and multiply back by s. Rounding and clipping are the two sources of error. The experiments actually use MXFP4, a block-scaled four bit float format, but the idea is the same.

With a symmetric grid and zero point zero, the step size is set by one number. The scale s equals the clipping threshold alpha divided by q max. Choosing alpha is the whole trade-off: too small and large values get clipped, too large and the sixteen levels are spread thin. Equations eight and nine turn this choice into something searched per layer and per timestep bin.

Smoothing is a free rearrangement. X l times W l equals X l times D l inverse, times D l times W l, where D l is a diagonal matrix of per-channel factors. Dividing the activations by D l shrinks outlier channels, and multiplying the weight by it moves that magnitude into the static weight. The output is mathematically unchanged; only where the difficulty lives has moved, and that fix is the SmoothQuant idea.

The smoothed weight is then split in two. W hat l equals L one times L two, a low-rank product, plus a residual R l. The low-rank branch is kept in sixteen bits and captures the dominant outlier directions, so the residual that must go to four bits is much tamer. This is the SVDQuant decomposition, and it answers the outlier problem shown in the first problem figure.

This is the finished quantized layer. Y hat l is X hat l times the low-rank branch, plus the four bit quantized X hat l times R hat l GPTQ. The low-rank path sees unquantized activations and sixteen bit weights, while the residual path runs on four bit activations and four bit weights rounded with GPTQ, which uses second order information to compensate rounding error. The timestep-aware part will only change the activation quantizer in the second term.

The clip threshold is expressed as a fraction of a measured size. Alpha for layer l and bin k equals rho times m l k, where m l k is a reference activation magnitude recorded on calibration data in that bin, and rho is a candidate ratio such as 0.8 or 0.9. Searching over rho rather than alpha makes one small candidate set work for every layer.

Each candidate threshold becomes an activation scale. The scale s A for layer l and bin k is alpha divided by q max, which is just equation four applied separately to every layer and timestep bin. These are the numbers that end up in the lookup table used at inference.

The search objective picks the best ratio. Rho star for layer l and bin k is the rho from the candidate set that minimises the expected squared difference between the BF16 output Y l of t and the quantized output Y hat l of t, averaged over the steps t in bin B k. Because the full SVDQuant-GPTQ layer is inside the loss, the chosen clip accounts for the weight error too.

At inference the layer is equation seven with one change. The activation quantizer now uses the stored scale s A for the bin k that contains the current step t. Finding k and fetching the scale is a table lookup, so the timestep awareness adds almost no runtime cost. This is the bottom lane of the big picture diagram.

All methods generate videos of the same size: 720 by 1280 pixels and 61 frames. This fixes the workload behind every quality and efficiency number in the results tables, so memory and latency comparisons are like for like.

The headline savings come straight from Table II. Peak memory drops from 64.4 to 26.2 gigabytes, a 59.3 percent cut, and model size from 64.0 to 25.9 gigabytes, a 59.5 percent cut. Notice this is well short of the four times one might expect from sixteen to four bits. The paper does not break this down, but the likely reasons are the sixteen bit low-rank branches, the block scales and any layers left unquantized.

The shape is redrawn from the paper's 3D surface and the cell values are illustrative.

In calibration, each sensitive layer's weight is split into a four bit main part and a sixteen bit low-rank part, and the trajectory is cut into early, middle and late bins with a clip ratio searched for every layer and bin. In inference, the latent and timestep pass through blocks zero to thirty nine using that precomputed table. The ratios in the table are illustrative, not measured.

This sensitivity map is what motivates the Ours dagger run and the thesis box's mixed-precision advice.

text: Four bit weights and activations keep the video recognisable. Five frames from one sample show a man with a bouquet as the camera pulls back to a stage. W4A16 looks like BF16, while W four A four smooths texture slightly on the face and flower edges but keeps identity, pose and layout with no collapse. Imaging quality reads 0.769, 0.767 and 0.759, matching the small losses in Table I.

The main quality table climbs row by row toward BF16. Plain round-to-nearest W4A4 falls to a VBench average of 0.733 and an imaging quality of 0.389. Adding SVDQuant, then GPTQ, then timestep clipping raises the average to 0.783, 0.793 and 0.799, against 0.806 for BF16. The last row keeps two sensitive module types in higher precision and reaches 0.803. The starred subject consistency for RTN beats BF16, probably because near-static or blurred output looks consistent, not a real gain.

Efficiency tells a split story. Model size and peak memory drop from about 64 gigabytes to about 26 for both W4A16 and the full W4A4 method. Latency, however, rises from 520.7 seconds to 955.1 per video for W4A4, because the four bit values are dequantized in Python before a BF16 matrix multiply with no fused kernel. W4A16 gets nearly all the memory gain at almost BF16 speed.

Each ingredient adds a visible step in VBench average: round-to-nearest 0.733, plus SVDQuant 0.783, plus GPTQ 0.793, plus timestep clipping 0.799, with BF16 at 0.806. The axis starts at 0.70, so the bars exaggerate the differences; the whole gap from worst to BF16 is only 0.073. SVDQuant contributes the largest jump, and timestep clipping the smallest.

SVDQuant does most of the rescue on imaging quality. Plain round-to-nearest W4A4 nearly halves it, from 0.705 to 0.389. The low-rank outlier branch brings it back to 0.671, while GPTQ adds 0.013 and timestep clipping another 0.005. Here the axis starts at zero, so the RTN collapse is shown at true scale.

Memory and speed move in opposite directions. The left panel shows model size and peak memory falling by about 59 percent for both four bit variants; the right panel shows latency per video rising from about 521 to 955 seconds for W4A4, roughly 1.8 times slower. The cause is simulated quantization without a fused FP4 kernel. The lesson is that fewer bits do not mean faster inference unless the hardware kernels exist.

Wan 2.2 and LTX-2.3 are similar in scale but differ in how much runs at once. Wan has two experts of about fourteen billion parameters with only one active per step, while LTX-2.3 runs roughly fourteen billion video and five billion audio parameters together. The paper does W4A4 on an H100; the thesis targets INT8 and INT4 weight-only compression through NNCF on CPU and Arc. The LTX figures come from the thesis brief, and its quality loss is still to be measured.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Borrow the sensitivity map, not the W4A4 recipe. A first NNCF experiment is INT4 weights everywhere except the attention output and feed-forward down projections, kept at INT8 through an ignored scope or a mixed-precision setting in compress weights, then check whether LTX shows the same pattern. GPTQ, AWQ and LoRA correction in NNCF are the weight-only counterparts and need calibration inputs captured from every timestep. Skip the clip lookup table unless static W8A8 is tried, and report real memory and time per step, since memory savings are not speed.

label: Primer
text: Wan two point two does not use one denoiser but two. The high-noise expert runs the early, very noisy steps, where layout and motion are decided, and then hands over to the low-noise expert, which refines texture and detail. The gold line is the denoising timeline, and the dashed line marks the switch. Only one expert of about fourteen billion parameters runs at a time, but the two behave differently, so the paper calibrates each expert on its own.

label: Primer
text: W four A four means both weights and activations are stored in four bits. In the MXFP4 format, every block of thirty two numbers shares one power of two scale, and each number has only sixteen possible codes, dense near zero and sparse far out. The magenta outlier forces a large shared scale, so its neighbours collapse onto a few small codes. The paper's outlier branch and clipping exist to limit exactly this damage.

label: Primer
text: Saving memory is not the same as saving time. A kernel is the routine that performs one operation, such as a matrix multiply. The top row is this paper on the H100, which has no native four bit math: it stores four bit numbers, converts them back to BF16, then multiplies, so each step gets slower. The bottom row is a fused kernel working on low bit data directly, as OpenVINO offers for INT4 and INT8 weights.

label: Primer
text: This paper closes the diffusion quantization group of the atlas. QVGen, just before it, reached four bit video models by retraining. This paper gets to four bits with no training at all, by stacking GPTQ for careful rounding and SVDQuant for outliers, and it adds clipping ratios chosen per timestep bin and per expert. Its missing speed-up is exactly why the next group, starting with FlashAttention-2, is about fast kernels.

These fourteen terms are the vocabulary the paper takes for granted. The most important are the mixture of experts, meaning Wan two point two's two denoisers; the timestep bin, a group of steps that shares one activation scale; MXFP4, the four bit block format; and pseudo-quantization, which saves memory but not time. Keep this list open while reading the method and results sections of the tab.

Why is attention so slow on a GPU, and how close can it get to the speed of a plain matrix multiply? Tri Dao's answer is that attention is limited by memory traffic and by poor work splitting, not by arithmetic, and that reorganising the loops of FlashAttention roughly doubles its speed again while giving exactly the same output. The tab opens with the big picture of data movement, then the hardware problem, then the method: the swapped loops, the online softmax, and the new split of work across thread blocks and warps. After that come every equation, every figure from the paper, the benchmark results, and a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers, this one sits in the acceleration group with DeepCache and TeaCache. It speeds up attention without touching any weights, so it complements the quantization papers from GPTQ to SVDQuant rather than competing with them.

Both panels compute the same attention, but they move data very differently. On the left, standard attention runs three separate kernels, and each N by N matrix, first the scores S and then the probabilities P, is written to slow HBM memory and read back. On the right, one fused kernel streams small tiles of Q, K and V into fast on-chip SRAM, keeps a running state per row, and writes only the final output O plus one log-sum-exp number per row. That is why extra memory drops from N squared to N.

Two speed gaps on the A100 explain the whole design. The left panel shows the memory hierarchy: 108 streaming multiprocessors, each with 192 kilobytes of fast SRAM at about 19 terabytes per second, against HBM at only about 2. The right panel compares arithmetic: Tensor Core matrix multiplies run at 312 teraflops, while other operations like exp and max run at 19.5, so one non-matmul flop costs about sixteen matmul flops. FlashAttention attacked the first gap; FlashAttention-2 attacks the second.

Each bar is the fraction of the A100's peak throughput that a kernel actually reaches. An optimised matrix multiply reaches 80 to 90 percent, but the original FlashAttention reached only 30 to 50 percent forward and 25 to 35 percent backward. FlashAttention-2 lifts this to 50 to 73 percent forward and up to 63 percent backward. The paper blames v1's gap on how work was divided among thread blocks and warps, which is exactly what the method section fixes.

Here is the forward algorithm as a picture. The outer loop runs over blocks of query rows, and those blocks run in parallel; the inner loop walks through key and value blocks one after another. One thread block loads its query block Q i once, streams every K j and V j through SRAM, and updates three running quantities: the row maximum m, the row sum l, and an un-normalised output O tilde. Only after the last key block does it divide by l and write O i and the log-sum-exp L i to HBM, exactly once.

The online softmax is the trick that makes tiling possible. Reading left to right, the state starts at m equal to minus infinity, l equal to zero and O tilde equal to zero, and each new block of scores updates it. Whenever a larger maximum appears, the old contributions are shrunk by e to the power of old max minus new max, a number at most one. After the last block the state equals the exact softmax-weighted sum. FlashAttention-2's change is to postpone the division by l to the very end.

Version one and version two side by side, with identical output. In v1 the outer loop is over key and value blocks, so the output, l and m for every query block must be read from and written back to HBM at each step, and parallelism covers only batch times heads. In FlashAttention-2 the outer loop is over query blocks, the running state stays in registers, rescaling uses only the cheap exponential factor, and the grid also spans the row blocks. This loop swap is the heart of the paper.

These are the paper's four practical changes plus the tuning knob that ties them together. The first two cut expensive non-matmul work: divide by l once at the end, and store only the log-sum-exp. The next two fill the GPU better: give each row block its own thread block, and split queries rather than keys across warps so no warp waits for another's partial sums. With a causal mask, blocks above the diagonal are simply skipped. Block sizes of 64 or 128 are hand-tuned per head dimension, trading fewer memory loads against register pressure.

Long sequences usually mean a small batch, and that starves the GPU. In this illustrative example, whose numbers are the tab's own, batch one with sixteen heads gives v1 only sixteen thread blocks, so only sixteen of the A100's 108 multiprocessors are busy. FlashAttention-2 also splits each 8k-token sequence into 64 row blocks, giving 1024 thread blocks and a fully occupied chip. Batch-one video generation, as in the thesis, is exactly this situation.

In the grid, rows are query blocks and columns are key blocks. With a causal mask, every block entirely above the diagonal is skipped, which is roughly half of them, and only the single diagonal block in each row needs the element-by-element mask. That gives about 1.7 to 1.8 times speed-up over unmasked attention. It matters for language-model training, but a video diffusion transformer like LTX-2.3 uses bidirectional attention, so this optimisation does not apply there.

The backward pass flips the ownership. Each thread block now owns one column block, meaning one K j and V j, and loops over all query blocks. The gradients for K and V accumulate on chip and are written once, but the query gradient dQ is shared by every column block, so it is updated in HBM with atomic adds. Instead of storing S and P, the kernel recomputes them from Q, K and the saved log-sum-exp L. Inference never runs this part.

Algorithm 1 is the whole forward pass in one place. It cuts Q into row blocks and K and V into column blocks. Then, for each query block, and these can run in parallel, it initialises the running maximum, sum and output, and walks through all key blocks. Each step computes a score tile, updates the maximum, exponentiates, rescales the old sum and output, and adds the new contribution. At the end it normalises the output once and writes the log-sum-exp. This is the only algorithm that matters for inference.

Algorithm 2 computes the gradients for training. It first computes D, the row-wise sum of the output gradient times the output, which makes the softmax derivative cheap. Then, for each key and value block, it loops over query blocks, recomputes the scores and probabilities from the stored log-sum-exp, accumulates the gradients for V and K on chip, and adds its share of the query gradient into HBM with atomic adds. Recomputation trades extra arithmetic for never storing an N by N matrix.

label: §2.2a
text: Standard attention takes three steps. S equals Q times K transposed, where Q, K and V are N by d matrices, N is the sequence length and d the head dimension, so S is N by N. P is the row-wise softmax of S, and the output O is P times V. The problem the paper attacks is that S and P are N by N, so for long sequences they are huge and end up in slow memory.

label: §2.2b
text: These five lines are the backward pass by the chain rule, where dO is the gradient of the loss with respect to the output. The gradient for V is P transposed times dO; dP is dO times V transposed; dS applies the softmax derivative to dP; and the gradients for Q and K are dS times K and Q times dS transposed. That is five matrix multiplies against two in the forward pass, which is why backward is harder to make fast.

label: §2.2c
text: Here is the derivative of softmax for one row. If p is the softmax of the scores s, then a small change dp in the probabilities maps back to ds equal to the diagonal matrix of p minus p times p transposed, all times dp. Row by row this simplifies to p times the quantity dp minus one number per row, the dot product of p and dp. That number is exactly the D vector that Algorithm 2 precomputes.

label: §2.3.1a
text: This sets up the toy example for the online softmax. One row block of scores S is split into two column blocks, S one and S two, each B r rows by B c columns, and V is split to match into V one and V two. B r and B c are the row and column block sizes. The next two equations compute the same output, first the standard way, then block by block.

label: §2.3.1b
text: Here is the standard, numerically safe softmax on the two blocks. It first needs m, the maximum over the whole row, and l, the sum of exponentials of the scores minus m across both blocks. Only then can the division give P and multiply by V to get O. The catch is that m and l depend on the whole row, so every block must be seen before normalising. The next equation removes that requirement. As the tab notes, the division by l is meant to apply to both terms.

label: §2.3.1c
text: The original FlashAttention's online softmax processes block one alone, getting its own max m one, sum l one, and a correctly normalised partial output O one. When block two arrives, the new max m two and the rescaled sum l two turn out to equal the full-row m and l. The partial output is then corrected by the ratio of old to new sums, so after the last block the result is exact, without ever holding the whole row.

This ratio motivates the paper's first two tweaks. On the A100, half-precision matrix multiplies run at 312 teraflops per second, but single-precision operations that are not matrix multiplies, like exp, max and division, run at only 19.5. Divided, that is about sixteen, so each non-matmul flop costs as much as sixteen matmul flops. Even a small amount of softmax bookkeeping can therefore eat a large share of the runtime.

label: §3.1.1a
text: Here is the version one update that FlashAttention-2 improves. To merge block two, v1 rescales the old output O one by the ratio of old to new sums, and also divides the new term by l two. Both terms are divided by the current sum at every block, so this expensive rescaling is repeated T c times per row. The next equation shows how to postpone it.

label: §3.1.1b
text: Tweak one: keep an un-scaled output, O tilde, carry the sum l alongside it, and divide only once after the last block. The equation is reproduced as printed in the paper; in the fully un-scaled form the first term should be e to the power of m one minus m two, times O tilde one, as the tab's equation 3.1.1d shows. The idea is the same either way: fewer non-matmul operations inside the inner loop.

label: §3.1.1c
text: Tweak two. The backward pass needs each row's softmax statistics, and instead of storing both the maximum m and the sum l, FlashAttention-2 stores just L equals m plus the log of l, called the log-sum-exp. Backward can then rebuild the probabilities directly as exp of S minus L. That is one vector per row instead of two, and a simpler recomputation.

label: §3.1.1d
text: Here is the full two-block example redone with FlashAttention-2's un-scaled output. Block one gives m one, l one and O tilde one without any division. Block two updates the max and sum, and O tilde two is the old O tilde shrunk by e to the power of m one minus m two, plus the new block's contribution. Only at the very end is O tilde divided by l to give the exact output. Compare with equations 3.1.1a and b to see the division leave the loop.

label: Alg. 1
text: These are the general forward recurrences of Algorithm 1, for any number of blocks. T r and T c count the row and column blocks: N over B r and N over B c, rounded up. For query block i and key block j, the score tile S equals Q i times K j transposed, the max m and sum l are updated as in the two-block case, and the un-scaled output is rescaled and extended. At the end, O i is divided by l once and L i is stored.

label: §3.1.1e
text: Algorithm 1 guarantees an exact result: the output equals softmax of Q times K transposed, times V, with no approximation. The work is still proportional to N squared times d, the same as standard attention, but extra memory beyond inputs and output is only proportional to N, since the only stored statistic is L. The speed comes from fewer memory trips and better scheduling, not from skipping computation.

label: Alg. 2
text: These are the backward recurrences of Algorithm 2. D is the row sum of dO times O, element by element. For each tile, the probabilities are recomputed as exp of S minus L, the V gradient gains P transposed times dO, dP equals dO times V transposed, and dS equals P times the quantity dP minus D, element by element. Then dS updates the gradients for Q and K. Precomputing D turns the softmax derivative into a cheap element-wise step.

Benchmarks count work this way. Forward flops equal four times sequence length squared, times head dimension, times number of heads. With a causal mask the count is halved, and backward is counted as 2.5 times forward, matching five matrix multiplies against two. Figures 4 to 7 divide these flop counts by measured time to get teraflops per second, so a taller bar means a faster kernel on the same work.

The Megatron-LM formula for total training flops is used to report Table 1. The first term, six times sequence length times number of parameters, covers the weight matrix multiplies; the second, twelve times layers times hidden size times sequence length squared, covers attention. The attention term is not halved for causal masking, to stay consistent with earlier work. Dividing by time per GPU gives the utilisation figures in the table.

label: Fig. 1
text: The paper's Figure 1 shows the original FlashAttention forward pass with K and V split into two blocks. The first key block gives scores, exponentials and a partial output normalised by l one. The second block gives new scores, the sum grows to l two, and the old output is rescaled by l one over l two before the new part is added. The scores and probabilities are computed in SRAM and never stored in HBM. As in the paper, the row-max subtraction is left out of the drawing.

label: Fig. 2
text: Figure 2 shows which worker, meaning which thread block, computes which part of a causal attention matrix. In the forward pass each worker owns a horizontal strip of query rows, so workers never need to talk to each other. In the backward pass each worker owns a vertical strip of key columns and accumulates its K and V gradients locally, while the shared query gradients are combined with atomic adds. This row split is the sequence-length parallelism from the method section.

label: Fig. 3
text: Figure 3 shows how the four warps inside one thread block share the forward work. In panel a, version one splits K and V across warps, the so-called split-K scheme, so each warp holds only a partial result that must be written to shared memory, synchronised and summed. In panel b, FlashAttention-2 splits Q across warps and lets all of them read the same K and V, so each warp writes its own slice of the output directly, with no inter-warp traffic.

The two head-dimension-128 lines sit highest, reaching about 2.3 to 2.5 times, while head dimension 64 reaches about 1.6 to 1.8 times. section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: For the thesis, the job is to verify, not to implement. Export LTX-2.3 so that its attention becomes OpenVINO's ScaledDotProductAttention operation, check in the execution graph that these fused nodes really appear, and measure latency with the fused op on and off. NNCF's weight-only int8 or int4 compression does nothing for attention, which has no weights, so this is a separate, exact speed-up that stacks with quantization and caching. Treat A100 numbers as qualitative, and keep attention in FP16 with FP32 statistics on Arc.

label: Primer
text: Attention is two matrix multiplies with a softmax in between. Queries times keys gives a score matrix S with one number for every pair of tokens, softmax turns it into weights P, and P times V gives the output. The teal matrices grow with the number of tokens, but S and P grow with its square. For a video with thousands of tokens, storing S and P is the real cost that FlashAttention removes.

label: Primer
text: Softmax turns a row of scores into weights that add up to one. The largest score is subtracted, the exponential taken, and the result divided by the sum, as the top row works through for three numbers. The bottom row shows the online version: process one block, keep a running maximum and sum, and shrink the old sum when a bigger maximum arrives. The result is exactly the same, so the full row never has to sit in memory.

label: Primer
text: A GPU is organised in layers. Thirty two threads form a warp that runs the same instruction together, a few warps form a thread block, and each thread block runs on one streaming multiprocessor, or SM, with its own small, fast SRAM. All SMs share the big, slow HBM. FlashAttention keeps work in SRAM, and FlashAttention-2 splits the work across blocks and warps so every SM stays busy. On Intel Arc, Xe-cores play the SM role.

label: Primer
text: FlashAttention-2 is the first acceleration paper, right after ten quantization papers that ended with SVDQuant-GPTQ for Wan2.2. Quantization makes numbers smaller; this paper instead reduces how much data moves through memory during attention, and changes no output value at all. Attention has no weights, so NNCF weight compression cannot speed it up, which is exactly the gap this fills. Next come DeepCache and TeaCache, which skip work that repeats across denoising steps.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The most important pairs are HBM and SRAM, the slow big memory and the fast small one, and thread block and warp, the two levels at which the paper splits work. Tensor Cores make matrix multiplies fast, so every exponential or division counts. Remember too that the thesis needs only the forward pass, and that video transformers use no causal mask.

DeepCache asks a simple question: if a diffusion model's deep features barely change from one denoising step to the next, why recompute them every time? It answers: run the full U-Net once, cache the deep feature, and for the next few steps run only the cheap shallow path that plugs into that cache. It needs no training and no data, and reaches 2.3 times faster Stable Diffusion with almost the same CLIP score, and over four times faster ImageNet generation with FID moving only from 3.39 to 3.59. The tab goes from the big picture and the problem, to the method, every equation, every figure, the result tables with three charts, and finally a thesis box. Among the sixteen papers it belongs to the acceleration group with FlashAttention-2 and TeaCache: it saves steps' worth of compute rather than bits, so it can stack on top of the quantization papers.

Compute the deep part once and reuse it for the next steps. The left column is the normal sampler, running the full U-Net at every step. The right column is DeepCache with an interval N of three: one full step that stores its deep feature, shown in indigo, then two steps where only the shallow blocks run in teal and the deep blocks are skipped in grey. The rest of the tab explains where the cache sits and how often to refresh it.

Diffusion sampling is a long chain of calls to the same expensive network, and each call costs about the same. Samplers like DDIM cut the number of calls, and pruning or distillation make each call cheaper but need retraining. The key observation drawn here is that adjacent steps have deep features with cosine similarity often above 0.95, so most of the deep compute is repeated work. That redundancy is the gap DeepCache exploits without any retraining.

The cache lives at the junction of a skip branch. A U-Net pairs each down block D with an up block U through a skip connection; the grey main branch is deep and expensive, the teal path cheap. DeepCache stores the output of U two, the deep feature entering U one, and on retrieve steps runs only D one and U one. For Stable Diffusion branch one is about six percent of the compute, though the paper actually uses branch two, about eleven percent.

Two ways to spend the same budget of ten full steps out of fifty. The top row, uniform, refreshes the cache every fifth step. The bottom row, non-uniform, uses equation 7 with centre fifteen and power 1.4, and packs full steps near step fifteen, where features change fastest, spreading them out further away. The point is that the refresh schedule is a free design choice, and placing refreshes where similarity dips gives better quality at large intervals.

The procedure alternates two kinds of step. A cache step runs the whole network and saves the deep feature. The following N minus one retrieve steps run only the first m down blocks on the new input, join them with the saved feature, and finish with the first m up blocks. A larger interval N or a shallower branch m means more speed and less quality. The paper uses branch three for DDPM, one for LDM, and two for Stable Diffusion.

The first part of Algorithm 1 is an ordinary U-Net pass: go down through all blocks, through the middle block, then back up, and on the way up save the feature arriving at branch m. The second part loops over the next N minus one steps, runs only the shallow down blocks, pulls the saved feature from the cache, and runs the shallow up blocks. Each pass ends with the usual sampler update, so only the network evaluation changes, not the sampler.

A DiT like LTX-2 has no U-Net long skips, so DeepCache's recipe cannot be copied directly. The left side is the U-Net case, where fresh shallow detail travels around the cached deep part through the skip. The right side shows the DiT alternative: cache the change, delta, that a span of middle blocks adds to the hidden state, or cache the whole model's output as TeaCache does. This drawing is the tab's own illustration, and the saving scales with the fraction of blocks skipped.

The forward diffusion step. q of x t given x t minus one is a Gaussian: the previous sample x t minus one is scaled by the square root of one minus beta t, and noise with variance beta t is added, where beta t is the noise schedule and I is the identity matrix. Repeating this turns an image into pure noise. It is background only; DeepCache does not change the diffusion process itself.

The reverse, denoising step that sampling repeats many times. The network epsilon theta looks at the noisy sample x t and the timestep t and predicts the noise; the sampler subtracts a scaled version of it, divides by the square root of alpha t, and adds fresh noise with variance beta t. Alpha t is one minus beta t, and alpha bar t is the running product of the alphas. Every one of these network calls is what DeepCache makes cheaper.

The input to up block U i is the concatenation of two features: the low-level feature from down block D i arriving over the skip branch, and the high-level feature from the deeper up block U i plus one on the main branch. This structural fact is what makes DeepCache possible: the deep half can be replaced by a stored copy while the skip still delivers fresh shallow detail.

The cache step. At time t, F cache is set to the output of up block U m plus one, that is, the deep main-branch feature that is about to enter up block U m. Here m is the chosen skip branch. This stored tensor is the only thing carried between steps, and equation 5 is where it gets reused.

The retrieve step at time t minus one. Up block U m receives the fresh shallow feature from D m, computed on the new input, concatenated with the stale F cache saved at time t. Nothing deeper than branch m runs. This is equation 3 with the expensive main-branch input swapped for the cached one, and Table 5 shows the cache matters: replacing it with zeros destroys the images.

The uniform refresh schedule. The set I holds the steps where the full network runs: every multiple of N, i times N, for i from zero up to k minus one, where k is T divided by N rounded up and T is the total number of steps. With fifty steps and N equal to five, that means ten full steps. It is the simple baseline that equation 7 improves on.

The non-uniform refresh schedule. Take k evenly spaced points between minus c and T minus c, but in a p-th-root space; raise them back to the power p, shift by the centre c, round to integers and remove duplicates. Here c is the step where features change fastest and p controls how strongly refreshes cluster around it. The result is dense full steps near c and sparse ones far away. Tables 7 to 10 tune c and p.

label: Alg. 1
text: The sampler update used inside Algorithm 1. It is the same as equation 2, except that u one, the output of the first up block, stands in for the predicted noise epsilon theta; sigma t times z adds fresh Gaussian noise. It makes explicit that on a retrieve step the shallow path's output is treated exactly like a full network prediction.

label: §4.5
text: A way to count the work in the ablation of section 4.5. DeepCache equals K full network passes, the same as K DDIM steps, plus N minus one times K extra shallow passes. Framed like this, the question becomes whether those cheap shallow passes add quality on top of plain DDIM with K steps, which Table 6 answers with a clear yes.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Treat caching as a separate layer on top of NNCF weight compression, and measure the two together, since quantization noise and stale features add up. For LTX-2.3, cache the residual of a middle span of transformer blocks, or the whole model output TeaCache-style, by exporting the model as two or three OpenVINO sub-models and letting the Python loop decide per step. text: A U-Net is shaped like the letter U. The down blocks on the left shrink the image into abstract features, the middle block is the deepest point, and the up blocks on the right grow it back. The teal dashed skips carry fresh detail straight across. The indigo dot marks where DeepCache stores the deep feature, so on cheap steps only D one and U one need to run.

label: Primer
