Below each call sits its deep feature, and neighbouring ones are nearly identical. The bottom row is DeepCache with an interval of three: one full step stores the deep feature, then two shallow steps reuse it, and the pattern repeats.

label: Primer
text: The paper judges quality with two scores. On the left, FID compares the features of real and generated images as two clouds, and a smaller distance between them is better. On the right, CLIP score encodes the prompt and the image and measures how well they agree, and a higher score is better. Speed is reported separately, as arithmetic work and as images per second.

label: Primer
text: Read the column from top to bottom in atlas order. The quantization papers and FlashAttention-2 make a single network call cheaper. DeepCache, in indigo, is the first to save work across calls, by reusing deep features from an earlier step. TeaCache comes next and carries that reuse idea over to diffusion transformers like LTX-2.3, and VBench closes the atlas by scoring video quality.

These are the words the paper uses without explaining. The two knobs to remember are the cache interval N, how often the full network runs, and the branch m, how deep the cheap path goes. FID and CLIP score measure quality, MACs and throughput measure cost, and all timings come from a single RTX 2080 graphics card, so Intel numbers will differ.

TeaCache asks a simple question: if consecutive denoising steps of a video diffusion transformer give almost the same output, can we skip some of them without training anything? The answer is yes, as long as the steps to skip are chosen from a cheap signal, the change in the timestep-modulated input, rescaled by a small polynomial and summed until it crosses a threshold. The tab starts with the big picture and the problem of fixed skipping, then walks through the method, every equation, every figure, the results tables, and a thesis box on LTX-2.3. Headline numbers are 1.86 times faster on Latte and 1.55 times on Open-Sora with no VBench loss, and up to 4.41 times on OpenSora-Plan for a loss of 0.07 points. Among the sixteen papers it is the last of the acceleration group, after FlashAttention-2 and DeepCache, and just before VBench. It cuts how often the model runs, so it stacks with int8 or int4 weights.

Every sampler step is kept, but the expensive transformer only runs when the input has drifted enough. On the left, the baseline runs six full passes for six steps, while TeaCache runs three and patches the other three by adding a cached residual. On the right, one step zoomed in: a cheap indicator from the first block's modulation feeds a running sum, and if the sum is below the threshold the step costs almost nothing. The rest of the tab explains each box.

A fixed reuse pattern fails in both directions. The curve is the output change between consecutive steps, a schematic U shape like Open-Sora's. Uniform every-other-step caching reuses stale outputs at the start and end, the magenta points where the output moves fast, yet still recomputes in the flat middle where three or four skips in a row would be safe. The note at the bottom adds the second problem: the true output change is only known after running the model, so a cheaper proxy is needed.

The method is a chain of five decisions. First choose an indicator that is cheap yet tracks the output: the timestep-modulated noisy input at the first block wins over the text embedding, the raw input, and the timestep embedding alone. Then measure its relative change from the previous step, correct that number with an offline-fitted polynomial, and add it to a running sum. When the sum crosses the threshold delta, run the full model and reset; otherwise reuse the cached residual, output minus input.

Skipping is decided by a sawtooth. Gold bars are the rescaled input change at each step, and the indigo line is the running sum since the last computed step, with a threshold delta of 0.1. While the sum stays below the line the step reuses the cache; when it reaches 0.1 the model runs and the sum drops to zero. The toy numbers show the key behaviour: small changes in the middle give long reuse streaks, while large changes near the end force a compute at every step. This is equation 7 in action.

TeaCache stores a residual, not a finished output. After a computed step it keeps one tensor, the transformer stack's output minus its input. On a skipped step the sampler has already updated the input, so adding the old residual to this fresh input gives a new output that still moves along the trajectory. That is why skipping with TeaCache differs from simply dropping a step, which figure 6 shows costs much more quality. The second implementation equation writes this as a formula.

The polynomial that rescales the indicator is fitted once per model, offline. The model runs without caching on seventy prompts from T2V-CompBench, record pairs of input change and output change for every consecutive step, and fit a low-order polynomial with numpy. The coefficients are then hard-coded, and at inference the only extra work is evaluating that polynomial on one number per step. The threshold delta is chosen afterwards, 0.1 for the slow setting and 0.2 for the fast one.

The whole method fits in a normal sampling loop; the paper has no algorithm box, so this is reconstructed from its sections three point three and three point four. Each step computes the cheap timestep embedding and the first block's modulated input, then updates the accumulated rescaled change. The first step is always computed. If the sum has reached delta, all transformer blocks run, the residual is cached and the sum resets; otherwise the cached residual is added to the input. Either way the sampler takes its normal step, so the schedule is untouched.

Equation 1 is the forward diffusion process that adds noise. x t, the sample at step t, equals the square root of alpha t times the previous sample x t minus one, plus the square root of one minus alpha t times fresh Gaussian noise z t. Alpha t is between zero and one and sets how much signal survives each step. TeaCache does not change this; it is background for the reverse loop in equation 2.

Equation 2 is the reverse, denoising step. p theta of x t minus one given x t is a Gaussian whose mean mu theta and covariance sigma theta are predicted by the network from the current sample x t and the step t. Generation repeats this step many times in sequence, and each repetition is one full transformer pass. That sequential loop is exactly the cost TeaCache shortens by reusing work between neighbouring steps.

Equation 3 builds the timestep embedding. The scalar step t is turned into sinusoidal features, then passed through a small MLP to give the vector T t. This vector produces the scale and shift that modulate every transformer block, as figure 4 shows. It is cheap to compute, which is why TeaCache can afford to look at it, and at the input it modulates, at every step.

Equation 4 measures how much a tensor changed between steps. The relative L1 distance of O at step t is the L1 norm of O t minus O t plus one, divided by the L1 norm of O t plus one, where t plus one is the previous, noisier step. A large value means new information, so the model should run; a small value means the output could be reused. Applied to outputs it is the ideal but unavailable criterion; TeaCache applies it to the cheap input F instead.

Equation 5 is the naive skipping rule. After computing at step t a, keep summing the relative input change from equation 4; while the sum up to the step before t b stays at or below delta, reuse. The first step t b where the sum exceeds delta is recomputed, and the sum restarts. F here is the timestep embedding or the modulated noisy input. The flaw is that input change and output change are on different scales, which equation 6 fixes.

Equation 6 is the rescaling polynomial. y equals f of x, which is a zero plus a one times x plus a two times x squared, and so on up to a n times x to the n. Here x is the measured change in the modulated input and y is the estimated change in the output. The coefficients a zero to a n are fitted offline, as in the fitting diagram, and they remove the scaling bias visible in figure 5. Table 3 shows first order already captures most of the gain.

Equation 7 is the final TeaCache rule: equation 5 with every term passed through the polynomial f first. So the running sum is of estimated output changes, not raw input changes, and a step is recomputed the moment that sum exceeds delta. Delta is the only knob users turn: 0.1 is the slow, near-lossless setting and 0.2 the fast one, with 0.15 and 0.25 also shown in figure 1.

label: impl.
text: This formula is not printed in the paper; it writes figure 4 as an equation. F t, the indicator, equals one plus gamma of T t, multiplied element by element with the layer-normalised input tokens h in, plus beta of T t. Gamma and beta are the first block's adaptive layer norm scale and shift, both computed from the timestep embedding. This F t is the tensor whose relative change goes into equation 4, and it costs only one modulation layer to get.

label: impl.
text: This formula is also not printed in the paper; it restates section three point four. On a skipped step t between t a and t b, the output h out at t is approximated by the current input h in at t plus the residual saved at the last computed step, h out at t a minus h in at t a. Because the fresh input enters the sum, the output keeps moving with the sampler, which is why caching loses less than dropping steps.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Treat caching as a separate ablation next to NNCF quantization: report quantization alone, caching alone, and both together, since skipping transformer passes likely saves more CPU time than int8 versus int4 kernels. To implement it, split the OpenVINO model into embedding plus modulation, the block stack, and the head, so the loop in Python can read F t and cache the residual. Refit the polynomial on the quantized LTX-2.3 with a few dozen uncached prompts, decide once per step for both guidance branches and both audio and video streams, and use a conservative delta on a distilled few-step checkpoint.

label: Primer
text: A diffusion model does not make a video in one go. It starts from pure noise and cleans it a little at a time, and every one of those steps runs the whole diffusion transformer once. Read the picture left to right: noise at the top left, a clean video on the right, one DiT pass under each arrow. The frames in the middle barely differ from their neighbours, and that redundancy is exactly what TeaCache turns into skipped passes.

label: Primer
text: The timestep number reaches the transformer in a specific way. It becomes a vector through sinusoidal features and a small MLP, and that vector sets a scale called gamma and a shift called beta. These are applied to the normalised video tokens before attention, which is called adaptive LayerNorm modulation. The result of the first modulation, F sub t, is cheap and reflects both content and noise level, so TeaCache watches it instead of the expensive output.

label: Primer
text: To decide whether a step is worth computing, TeaCache needs one number for how much things changed. The relative L1 distance adds up the absolute differences element by element and divides by the total size of the previous tensor. In the toy example the differences sum to 0.6 and the previous values to 6, so the change is ten percent. Small values mean reuse the cache, large values mean run the model again.

label: Primer
text: Every paper before this one either made each transformer pass cheaper, like the quantization methods, or sped up one part of it, like FlashAttention-2, or reused features inside a U-Net, like DeepCache. TeaCache skips entire transformer passes and decides when from the input side. VBench, next in the atlas, explains the quality score it reports. For the thesis the key point is that quantization and caching are independent, so their savings multiply on LTX-2.3.

These are the terms the paper assumes. The most important ones are the denoising step, the timestep embedding and its adaptive LayerNorm modulation, the relative L1 distance and the threshold delta that controls how much is skipped. Also note the two kinds of quality metric: VBench judges a video on its own, while LPIPS, PSNR and SSIM measure how close the cached video stays to the uncached one. All timings are on an NVIDIA A800, a data-centre GPU.

VBench asks a simple question: how can one tell whether a generated video is good, and in what way? Its answer is to replace one opaque number like FVD with sixteen separate scores, each with its own small prompt set and its own off-the-shelf judge network, and to check every score against human votes. The tab starts with the big picture and the problem, then walks through the method one dimension at a time, lists every equation, redraws every figure, and ends with the results tables and a box on how to use VBench in the thesis. VBench is the sixteenth and last paper in the atlas and the only one about evaluation. The other fifteen describe the model and how to make it cheaper; VBench is the ruler that shows the cheaper model still makes good video.

One opaque score becomes sixteen explainable ones. On the left, metrics like FVD, IS or CLIPSIM give a single number that says nothing about why a model is good or bad, and it often disagrees with people. On the right, VBench runs a dedicated prompt suite through the text-to-video model, scores the samples with one judge model per dimension, and checks each dimension against human pairwise preferences. That last check is what lets the scores stand in for human judgement.

Consistency and motion pull in opposite directions. The bars compare LaVie and VideoCrafter from Table 1: LaVie wins background consistency and flicker, but its Dynamic Degree is about 50 percent against almost 90 for VideoCrafter. The sketch on the right shows the trap: a frozen clip scores near perfect on consistency and flicker. This is why VBench adds Dynamic Degree as a counterweight and never reports one averaged number.

Here is the whole dimension tree, with the judge behind each leaf. Teal branches are Video Quality, seven dimensions that ignore the prompt and ask whether the video looks good. Gold branches are Video-Condition Consistency, nine dimensions that ask whether the video matches what was requested. The small mono labels name the evaluation model for each leaf, such as DINO for subject consistency, RAFT for dynamic degree and GRiT for object detection. The method section below explains each leaf in turn.

The pipeline has four stages. First, build small prompt suites, about a hundred prompts per dimension that each probe one ability, plus eight content categories of a hundred prompts each sorted by a language model. Second, sample one video per prompt from every model with a fixed seed. Third, score each video with that dimension's judge and average into a model score, reading it against reference baselines. Finally, confirm the dimension ranks models the way humans do.

Subject Consistency asks whether the main subject keeps its identity across the clip. Every frame goes through DINO, which is good at telling individuals of the same class apart, and each feature is compared by cosine similarity with the first frame and with the previous frame. Averaging those two similarities over time gives equation one. A cow that slowly changes its markings drops the score, as figure A8 shows.

Background Consistency is the same recipe as Subject Consistency, but uses CLIP image features instead of DINO, because CLIP captures the overall scene rather than one object's identity. Each frame is compared with the first and the previous frame, giving equation two. The prompts come from Places365 scene names, so there is always a background worth tracking.

Temporal Flickering measures high-frequency jitter between frames. VBench first keeps only videos that RAFT says are static, so real motion is not mistaken for flicker. It then averages the mean absolute pixel difference between consecutive frames, equation three, and flips it into a zero to one score where higher means less flicker, equation four. Quantization noise that changes from frame to frame would show up here.

Motion Smoothness uses the idea that smooth motion is predictable. VBench drops every odd frame, asks the AMT frame interpolator to rebuild them from their neighbours, and measures the pixel error against the real frames. Small error means the motion follows a smooth path and the score is high. The error is normalised the same way as flicker in equation four. Step-caching methods that skip computation could hurt this score.

Dynamic Degree is simply the fraction of a model's videos that actually move. RAFT computes optical flow between consecutive frames, VBench takes the mean of the largest five percent of flow magnitudes, and a video counts as dynamic if that value passes a threshold. It exists to balance the consistency dimensions, which a frozen clip would otherwise win.

Aesthetic Quality asks whether frames look artistically pleasing: layout, colour harmony, realism. The LAION aesthetic predictor rates each frame from zero to ten, VBench divides by ten and averages over frames. It is a per-frame judgement, so it says nothing about motion.

Imaging Quality looks at low-level distortions such as noise, blur and over-exposure. The MUSIQ quality model, trained on the SPAQ dataset, gives each frame a score from zero to a hundred, which is divided by a hundred and averaged over frames. For the thesis this is the most direct check that four-bit weights have not added visible noise or blur.

Object Class checks that the requested object actually appears. For prompts built from 79 COCO classes, the GRiT detector runs on every frame, and the score is the fraction of frames in which the named class is detected. It is the simplest semantic test of whether the text conditioning still works.

Multiple Objects tests composition: when the prompt asks for two things, both must be detected by GRiT in the same frame. The score is the fraction of frames where every requested object is present. It is much harder than Object Class, and the results section shows it is where video models lag image models most.

Human Action uses a hundred Kinetics-400 actions phrased as a person doing something. VBench samples sixteen frames, runs the UMT video classifier, and counts a hit if the prompted action is among the top five classes with a logit above 0.85. Because it needs a video classifier, it judges the clip as a whole rather than frame by frame.

Color checks that the object has the requested colour. GRiT's dense captioner describes each frame, and only frames where the object is detected are counted, which keeps this score separate from Object Class. The score is the fraction of those frames whose caption contains the right colour word. The results show it is the least human-aligned dimension.

Spatial Relationship checks prompts like a clock to the left of a vase. From GRiT's boxes, the relation counts as correct if the distance along the named axis is larger than along the other axis. Heavily overlapping boxes are down-weighted, following the rule from T2I-CompBench. The results show image models are far better at this than video models.

Scene checks that the video shows the requested place. The Tag2Text captioner describes each frame, and a frame counts only if every word of the scene name appears in the caption, in any order. So a caption saying river does not satisfy a prompt asking for ocean.

Appearance Style asks whether frames look like the requested style, such as Van Gogh or oil painting. Each frame's CLIP image feature is compared by cosine similarity with the CLIP text feature of the style phrase, then averaged. The raw values are small, around twenty to thirty percent, so only differences between models are meaningful.

Temporal Style covers camera effects like zoom, pan or slow motion, which cannot be seen in a single frame. So instead of per-frame CLIP, VBench uses ViCLIP, which encodes the whole video, and compares it with the text of the camera instruction. This is one of the few dimensions that truly needs a video-level judge.

Overall Consistency is a catch-all that compares the whole video with the whole prompt using ViCLIP's video and text encoders. The paper calls it an aiding metric: it covers semantics and style together on general prompts, rather than isolating one ability like the other dimensions do.

Human annotation is how VBench earns trust. For each prompt, the four models each produce videos, arranged into five groups, and within each group all six model pairs are compared. The annotator picks A better, B better, or same, judging only the dimension being tested. Wins count one and ties half, giving a human win ratio per model, which is correlated with the VBench win ratio. The quality checks with re-labelling keep the votes reliable.

As a side contribution, the human votes and VBench scores are turned into about thirty thousand instruction pairs to fine-tune a video language model. The tuned model first picks which dimensions matter for a prompt, then describes the video and gives a score from zero to ten per dimension. Training took about an hour on eight A100 GPUs. It is an extension, not part of the core benchmark.

This is the exact prompt used to sort the category prompts. A language model is asked to act as a language expert and tag each text with one or more of eight categories, such as Food or Vehicles, with no explanation. The logic is cheap automatic labelling followed by a human check: the tagging was about 95 percent accurate, then corrected by hand to give a hundred clean prompts per category.

This chain-of-thought template is how the tuned video language model starts an evaluation. Given a prompt, it first selects which of the sixteen dimensions apply, and only then scores the video on them. In the phone booth example, the model leaves out object and colour checks and keeps the quality, scene, style and overall ones. Choosing dimensions first mirrors how VBench itself matches prompt suites to dimensions.

Raw percentages mean little without anchors, so VBench gives three per dimension. Empirical Min comes from noise clips or frames spliced from different videos. WebVid-Avg is the average score of real WebVid clips retrieved for each prompt. Empirical Max is the best real clip where a hundred percent is unreachable. For example, Appearance Style tops out at about 28.6 percent even for real videos, so LaVie's 23.6 is not bad.

Equation one is Subject Consistency. S subject is one over T minus one times the sum from frame two to frame T of one half times the dot product of d one and d t, plus the dot product of d t minus one and d t. Here d t is the unit-length DINO feature of frame t, so each dot product is a cosine similarity. It rewards frames that match both the first frame and their neighbour, and is averaged over all of a model's videos.

Equation two is Background Consistency, identical in form to equation one. The only change is that c t, the unit-length CLIP image feature of frame t, replaces the DINO feature. Each frame is compared with the first frame and the previous one, the two cosine similarities are averaged, and the result is averaged over the T minus one frame transitions.

Equation three computes raw flicker. For each of N videos, it takes the mean absolute error between frame t and frame t plus one, averages over the T minus one pairs, and then averages over all videos. Because it is only applied to static scenes, any pixel change is treated as flicker. A larger value means worse flicker, which equation four then flips.

Equation four normalises flicker: 255 minus S flicker, all divided by 255. Since eight-bit pixels range from zero to 255, this maps the error into zero to one, with higher meaning less flicker. Motion Smoothness reuses exactly this normalisation. One consequence is that scores cluster near the top, around 96 to 99 percent, so small differences matter.

This is Motion Smoothness written out from the paper's text. Every odd frame is removed, and AMT reconstructs frame f two k minus one from the frames on either side, giving f hat. The mean absolute error between f hat and the real frame, averaged over the n dropped frames, is subtracted from 255 and divided by 255, as in equation four. Low reconstruction error means predictable, smooth motion.

This is Dynamic Degree. For each video, take the RAFT optical flow magnitudes, average the largest five percent, and check whether that exceeds a threshold tau. The indicator is one for moving videos and zero otherwise, and S dynamic is the average over N videos, so it is the share of non-static clips. The paper does not give the threshold value.

These two formulas give the frame-wise quality scores. S aesthetic averages the LAION aesthetic rating of each frame divided by ten, and S imaging averages the MUSIQ rating divided by a hundred, both over T frames. They are simple linear rescalings to zero to one, so they inherit whatever the judge models consider good.

These are the object scores. S obj is the fraction of the T frames in which GRiT detects the requested object o. S multi is the fraction of frames in which both requested objects, o one and o two, are detected together. The indicator makes each frame count as one or zero.

Human Action is scored per video. For each of N videos, the indicator is one if the prompted action a i is among UMT's top five classes with a logit above 0.85, and the score is the average of these hits. UMT sees sixteen uniformly sampled frames, so it judges the motion, not a single still.

Color is a ratio of frame counts. The numerator counts frames where the object is detected and its caption contains the requested colour c; the denominator counts all frames where the object is detected. Dividing by detected frames only means a missing object does not lower the colour score, keeping the two dimensions separate.

Spatial Relationship is scored per frame in three cases. If the relation is correct and the boxes overlap little, meaning IoU below tau, the frame scores one. If it is correct but the boxes overlap heavily, it gets a reduced score kappa of IoU. Otherwise it scores zero. The exact form of kappa is not given in the paper, so treat this as a sketch of the rule.

Scene is the fraction of the T frames where every word of the scene name appears in Tag2Text's caption. The indicator is strict about vocabulary but ignores word order, so partial matches do not count.

These are the style and overall scores, all cosine similarities between a visual and a text embedding. S app averages, over frames, the similarity between the CLIP image feature of frame t and the CLIP text feature of the style phrase s. Temporal Style and Overall Consistency instead compare one ViCLIP embedding of the whole video v with the ViCLIP text embedding of the prompt p.

This counts human comparisons. For each of N prompts there are five groups of four model videos, and four models give four choose two, which is six pairs. So each dimension collects N times five times six pairwise votes. This is the data behind the win ratios in equation fifteen.

The win ratio of model m is the sum over all pairs involving m of one for a win plus one half for a tie, divided by the number of pairs involving m. It is computed twice, once from human labels and once from VBench scores, and the Spearman rank correlation between the two is the human-alignment number reported for each dimension in figure five.

This is only for drawing radar charts. The score s of model m on dimension d is min-max normalised across models, then stretched into the range a to b. Figures two, six and A26 use a of 0.3 and b of 0.8, so the best model sits at 0.8 and the worst at 0.3. Figure seven uses zero to one over all 32 model and category values. It changes the picture, not the underlying scores.

label: Fig. 1
text: Figure one is the paper's overview and reads left to right. The dimension suite splits video quality into temporal and frame-wise parts, and video-condition consistency into semantics, style and overall. Each dimension gets a prompt suite, the models generate videos, and a designated evaluation method scores them. Human preference annotation sits alongside and verifies every dimension. The rest of the paper fills in each box.

label: Fig. 2
text: Figure two is the headline result as a radar chart, redrawn from Table 1 with the best model per dimension at 0.8 and the worst at 0.3. No model wins everywhere. LaVie, in gold, is broad and strong on most axes. VideoCrafter, in indigo, spikes on Dynamic Degree and Spatial Relationship. CogVideo, in magenta, wins Subject Consistency and Motion Smoothness but is weak on semantics. This is exactly the per-dimension diagnosis a single score cannot give.

label: Fig. 3
text: Figure three describes the prompts. The word cloud on the left shows common words like person, view, style and tranquil. The bars on the right show prompts per dimension, in gold, between about 72 and a hundred, and a hundred per content category, in teal. Some suites are shared, for example Motion Smoothness and Dynamic Degree reuse Subject Consistency's prompts. The small size is deliberate, since sampling video is slow.

label: Fig. 4
text: Figure four is the annotation screen. At the top are the prompt and a question about one dimension only, here whether the style is Van Gogh. In the middle are two videos, on the right three choices, and at the bottom playback controls. In this example the annotator should pick A, the swirly painted skyline, even if it flickers more, because only style is being judged.

label: Fig. 5
text: Figure five is the main validation. Each small plot is one dimension, each dot is one model, with the human win ratio on the horizontal axis and the VBench win ratio on the vertical. Dots near the fitted line mean VBench ranks models as people do, and rho is the Spearman correlation. Agreement is high everywhere, from 0.61 for Color to 0.998 for Motion Smoothness, which justifies trusting the scores in the results tables.

label: Fig. 6a
text: Figure six a compares video models with image models on the frame-level dimensions, redrawn from Table A8. The image models, especially SDXL, reach far out on Multiple Objects and Spatial Relationship while the four video models stay near the centre. The paper's conclusion is that video models lag in compositionality, perhaps because modelling time costs frame-level semantics. The bar chart in the results section shows the gap directly.

label: Fig. 6b
text: Figure six b places the video models next to real data, redrawn from Table A6. Real WebVid clips beat every model on subject consistency, motion smoothness and overall consistency. But LaVie beats the WebVid average on aesthetic and imaging quality, because WebVid footage is often low quality with watermarks. Real video is a reference point, not an upper bound on every axis.

label: Fig. 7
text: Figure seven shows one radar per model, with one coloured line per content category, redrawn from Table A7 and normalised to zero to one over all 32 values. Look for lines that stick out. CogVideo's Food line is high on aesthetics. Human and Vehicles are the most dynamic but lower elsewhere, and Architecture and Scenery are the most static. Performance depends on what is being filmed, so a test set should cover several categories.

label: Fig. A8
text: Figure A8 illustrates Subject Consistency. In the top row the cow keeps one appearance and scores about 96.8 percent. In the bottom row its look drifts from frame to frame, marked by the magenta boxes, and the score drops to about 83.3 percent. It shows what the DINO similarity in equation one is actually picking up.

label: Fig. A9
text: Figure A9 illustrates Background Consistency. In the top row the street stays the same as the camera moves, scoring about 93.4 percent. In the bottom row the church warps and the scene changes within a few frames, scoring about 88.1 percent. A five-point drop here already signals a visible problem.

label: Fig. A10
text: Figure A10 illustrates flicker. The lower strip in each example stacks the same small patch of pixels from every frame, so smooth columns mean stable pixels. The top example has mild flicker and scores about 99.7 percent, the bottom has severe flicker and scores about 96.0. The range is very compressed, so a drop of one or two points is meaningful.

label: Fig. A11
text: Figure A11 checks whether measuring flicker only on static scenes is fair. Human win ratios for flicker on static, dynamic and semi-dynamic video sets correlate with each other at about 0.99 in every pairing, so models rank the same way whatever the motion. That justifies the static-only filter in figure A10's metric. The dot positions here are approximate.

label: Fig. A12
text: Figure A12 illustrates Motion Smoothness. The top bear walks smoothly and plausibly, scoring about 96.0 percent. The bottom bear jumps erratically between frames, marked by the boxes, and scores about 88.5. Jerky motion is hard for the frame interpolator to predict, so its reconstruction error rises.

label: Fig. A13
text: Figure A13 illustrates Dynamic Degree for the prompt of a motorcycle turning a corner. In the top row both the bike and the camera move, so the video counts as dynamic and scores one. In the bottom row the bike barely changes from start to end, so it counts as still and scores zero. The model's Dynamic Degree is the share of its videos that look like the top row.

label: Fig. A14
text: Figure A14 illustrates Aesthetic Quality with one beach prompt and three videos of increasing score: about 46, then 70, then 82 percent. The dark silhouette looks flat, while the balanced, well-lit beach scores highest. For comparison, SDXL images in row d reach 80 to 87 percent, showing that image models still lead on per-frame beauty.

label: Fig. A15
text: Figure A15 illustrates Imaging Quality. The sharp, well-exposed bee scores about 70.6 percent on MUSIQ, while the blurry, over-exposed one scores about 31.3. This is the kind of degradation to watch for when weights are pushed to low bit widths.

label: Fig. A16
text: Figure A16 illustrates Object Class for the prompt a person. In the top row GRiT detects a walking person, scoring one. In the bottom row the model produces a pattern of letter A badges, reading the article as a letter, and no person is found, scoring zero.

label: Fig. A17
text: Figure A17 illustrates Multiple Objects for the prompt a dog and a horse. In the top row both animals appear together in every frame, scoring one. In the bottom row only the horse appears, so the pair never co-occurs and the score is zero. Getting one of two objects is common for video models.

label: Fig. A18
text: Figure A18 illustrates Human Action for the prompt a person is barbequing. In the top row UMT recognises a man at a grill, scoring one. In the bottom row the video shows only food on a plate, with nobody performing the action, scoring zero. Getting the objects right is not the same as getting the action right.

label: Fig. A19
text: Figure A19 illustrates Color for the prompt a pink chair. In the top row the chair is pink in every frame, scoring a hundred percent. In the bottom row it is partly pink and white striped, so only about 77 percent of frames are captioned with the right colour. Partial colour errors give partial scores.

label: Fig. A20
text: Figure A20 illustrates Spatial Relationship for a clock to the left of a vase. In the top row the two objects are separate and correctly placed, scoring a hundred percent. In the bottom row the clock and vase are fused into one shape, so the relationship is missing and the score is zero.

label: Fig. A21
text: Figure A21 illustrates Scene for the prompt bedroom. In the top row Tag2Text's caption contains the word bedroom, scoring one. In the bottom row the model produced a flower field, so the scene word never appears and the score is zero.

label: Fig. A22
text: Figure A22 illustrates Appearance Style for the Bund in Shanghai in Van Gogh style. The swirly painted skyline scores about 33.1 percent CLIP similarity, the plain photo about 20.9. Both numbers look low, because CLIP similarities are small in absolute terms. Only the gap between videos carries meaning.

label: Fig. A23
text: Figure A23 illustrates Temporal Style for a corgi prompt ending in zoom in. In the top row the camera really zooms from far to close-up, scoring about 30.5 percent on ViCLIP. In the bottom row the camera instruction is ignored, scoring about 8.7. A per-frame metric could not tell these apart.

label: Fig. A24
text: Figure A24 illustrates Overall Consistency for a corgi playing a drum kit. The top video matches the whole prompt and scores about 40.1 percent. The bottom video shows hands on drums but no corgi, scoring about 28.9. Missing one key element of the prompt costs about eleven points here.

label: Fig. A25
text: Figure A25 shows why the tuned video language model helps. Before tuning, VideoChat misreads subject consistency as a question about content and gives an unexplained low score. After tuning on VBench scores and human votes, it describes the phone booth frame by frame, notes that it stays the same, and gives eight out of ten. The tuning taught it what each dimension means.

label: Fig. A26
text: Figure A26 uses the same category data as figure seven but grouped the other way: one radar per category, with the four models as lines, normalised to 0.3 to 0.8. Two patterns repeat in every category. VideoCrafter's Dynamic Degree spike is always there, and CogVideo's Overall Consistency is always lowest. So these are model traits, not category effects.

label: Fig. A27
text: Figure A27 shows how WebVid-10M, a common training set, splits across the eight categories. Human clips are 26 percent and Scenery 21 percent, while Architecture and Lifestyle are only 4 percent each and Food 11 percent. The next figure uses this to argue about data quality versus quantity.

label: Fig. A28
text: Figure A28 gives the average aesthetic score of WebVid clips per category. Food scores highest at about 45.1 percent despite being only 11 percent of the data, and Animal lowest at about 41.1. Since models also do well on Food aesthetics, the paper argues that the quality of training data matters more than its quantity.

Table one, part one, gives the raw scores for the quality dimensions plus Object Class, with Empirical Min and Max rows as anchors. No model wins everything. CogVideo leads subject consistency and motion smoothness, LaVie leads background, flicker, aesthetics, imaging and object class, and VideoCrafter is by far the most dynamic at about 89.7 percent. Note how close the flicker scores are, all around 98 percent, which is why small changes matter there.

Table one, part two, covers the condition dimensions. Semantics is where models separate: Multiple Objects and Spatial Relationship sit around 18 to 39 percent, far below the maximum. LaVie leads most columns, while CogVideo collapses on Temporal Style and Overall Consistency at under 8 percent. The Empirical Max row shows that style and overall scores top out near 28 to 36 percent even for real video.

This bar chart ranks the sixteen dimensions by how well they agree with humans, using the Spearman correlations from Table A5. Teal bars are quality dimensions and gold bars are condition dimensions. Color, at about 61 percent, Object Class at 80 and Dynamic Degree at 82 are the weakest, while Motion Smoothness, Appearance Style and Multiple Objects are near perfect. Lean more on the tall bars when a result is borderline.

Table A2 checks the three benchmarks used to validate flicker. Every model scores zero Dynamic Degree on the static benchmark, confirming it is truly static, and the semi-dynamic and dynamic sets show increasing motion. This supports the claim in figure A11 that flicker rankings hold regardless of motion.

Table A5, part one, gives the numbers behind figure five for the quality dimensions and Object Class. Each cell shows the VBench win ratio then the human win ratio for one model, and the last row is their Spearman correlation. Motion Smoothness agrees almost perfectly at 99.8 percent, while Object Class and Dynamic Degree are lowest at about 80 and 82. The orderings of models usually match even when the exact ratios differ.

Table A5, part two, covers the condition dimensions in the same format, VBench win ratio then human win ratio. Most correlations are above 89 percent, but Color stands out at about 61, because the four models are close and small differences flip the ranking. CogVideo's near-zero VBench win ratios on Temporal Style and Overall Consistency match humans ranking it last.

Table A6 adds the WebVid-Avg row, the average score of real clips retrieved for each prompt. Real video wins subject consistency, motion smoothness and overall consistency, but LaVie beats it on aesthetic and imaging quality, and VideoCrafter on dynamic degree. It is the numeric source for figure six b and a useful reminder that real data is not the ceiling on every axis.

Table A7 breaks seven dimensions down by content category for each model, with the best category marked. Consistency scores barely move across categories, while Dynamic Degree swings a lot, for example LaVie ranges from about 5 percent on Architecture to 39 on Human. It is the data behind figures seven and A26, and shows why prompts from several categories are needed for a fair comparison.

Table A8 compares the four video models with three Stable Diffusion image models on dimensions that can be judged per frame, using CLIP for overall consistency so images can be scored. SDXL reaches about 70 percent on Multiple Objects and 86 on Spatial Relationship, roughly double the best video model. Image models also lead on aesthetics. This is the evidence for the compositionality gap.

The compositionality gap in one chart. For Multiple Objects and Spatial Relationship, the best video models reach about 34 to 37 percent, while SD2.1 and SDXL reach 51 to 86. The gap on aesthetics is smaller. The paper reads this as a cost of temporal modelling: learning motion seems to take capacity away from getting frame-level semantics right.

section: Why it matters for this thesis
text: Use VBench as a before-and-after test, not a leaderboard. Pick six to eight dimensions that compression can break: imaging and aesthetic quality, flicker and consistency for quantization, motion smoothness and dynamic degree for caching, plus one or two semantic checks. Generate FP16 and quantized videos with OpenVINO on the same prompts and seeds, save frames as PNG, and score them in PyTorch on any machine. Always report Dynamic Degree next to consistency, and remember VBench does not cover audio.

label: Primer
text: A pretrained network like DINO or CLIP turns each video frame into a long list of numbers, a vector. Frames that show the same thing give vectors pointing in almost the same direction, so their cosine similarity is close to one. VBench's subject and background consistency scores are simply averages of these cosines across the frames, and CLIP can also compare a frame with a sentence.

label: Primer
text: Optical flow is a field of arrows saying how far each pixel moved between two frames, and VBench estimates it with a network called RAFT. If the largest arrows are big, the clip is moving; if they are near zero, it is frozen. Dynamic degree is the share of clips that move, and it matters because a frozen video would look perfectly consistent on the other scores.

label: Primer
text: People judge two videos side by side on one dimension, and each model's win ratio is the share of comparisons it won, with a tie counting as half. Spearman's rank correlation then asks whether VBench orders the models the same way humans do. One means the same order, zero means no relation. In the toy example a single swap gives zero point eight.

label: Primer
text: The first fifteen papers in the atlas cover the model, how to quantize it and how to speed it up, ending with TeaCache. VBench is the last paper and the only one about evaluation. It gives the scorecard to compare full precision LTX-2.3 with its int8 or int4 version, dimension by dimension, on the same prompts and seeds.

These are the terms the paper uses without explaining. Most are names of the judge networks: CLIP and DINO for frame features, ViCLIP and UMT for whole-clip understanding, RAFT for motion, AMT for frame interpolation, MUSIQ and the LAION predictor for image quality and beauty, GRiT and Tag2Text for objects and scenes. Win ratio and Spearman's rho are how the paper checks it agrees with people.
